supervisory role regarding the structural funds, addressing this issue among other things. the third issue in the report relates to the declaration of financial interests and, in particular, to the results of an independent comparative study launched in july 2006, in the context of the european transparency initiative, and published in 2007. the study concluded that most of the european institutions are regulated more intensively than institutions at national level. the commission and the european investment bank have the most comprehensive ethical rules of the eu institutions. while the study noted that the commission has a relatively well developed system for notification of conflicts of interests, it suggests that consideration be given to enlarging the mandate of our ad hoc vice-president of the commission. − mr president, mr musotto’s report covers two years of efforts to improve the protection of the financial interests of the european union. a sound system of effective and thorough controls. when i presented the commission report in july, i emphasised the need for member states to ensure a correct, complete and timely communication of data on irregularities. a good flow of information between the member states and the commission is essential for effective recovery and joint action against fraudsters. many of them are doing this, but for vice-president of the commission. − mr president, addressing radicalisation into violence is at the core of the commission’s counter-terrorism policy, and i therefore welcome the report being discussed today and the very vital issues it tackles. i also welcome the progress in interinstitutional cooperation in the area of recognition of the enormous challenge we face in developing a coherent eu policy that prevents, interrupts or reverses radicalisation processes. after a series of initiatives in recent years, since my first communication on the subject in september 2005, a communication will be presented to the council and parliament in july this year, identifying good practices in the member states and making concrete recommendations for the way forward. i notice that the report makes a recommendation to the commission in this regard. we have devoted time and resources in the last three years to better understanding this phenomenon, its trends, its manifestations and its dynamics. we have commissioned four separate comparative studies which are now being completed. we have sent a questionnaire to all the member states and are currently analysing the answers received. we have organised a conference on the role of education in preventing radicalisation, which brought together educators, religious leaders and policy-makers to brainstorm new ideas. we are working on drafting the communication at the moment. the first three studies – on trigger factors, narrative and mobilisation tactics – are to be approved in the coming month. a fourth study on civil society engagement (best practices) is likely to be published around the time of the communication’s adoption in july. its main results will by that stage already have been incorporated into the communication. analysis of the questionnaire sent to the member states is ongoing and will also feed into the reflection on the communication. we can therefore now formulate our policy with much will also be talking about the role of education, and civil society engagement in countering radicalisation. members will be aware that, in relation to incitement, we have presented a proposal for the amendment of the framework decision on combating terrorism that is one part of the ‘terrorism package’ introduced last november. that instrument aims to introduce into the framework decision offences parallel to those covered in the council of europe convention on the prevention of terrorism: public provocation, recruitment and training for terrorism – including via the internet – and in particular internet instructions on how to produce home-made bombs. the commission is strongly committed to supporting the victims of terrorism. we have, since 2004, demonstrated our support through financial assistance to numerous projects intended to help associations of victims of terrorism and to promote solidarity among european citizens. we envisage creating, in 2008, a european network of associations of victims of terrorism, in order to represent victims’ interests at european level and to strengthen european citizens’ solidarity with victims of terrorism. in conclusion, in order to tackle the terrorist threat at european level, it is absolutely necessary to implement a global prevention policy on the factors leading to radicalisation and recruitment, in order to explore its deep roots, while never justifying terrorist behaviour. jihadist terrorism remains the biggest threat to democratic societies, including thousands of millions of honest muslim people in the eu and in many other parts of the world.

although it exists in most member states and is essential for the quality of market surveillance organisations. in the light of the european single market and the free movement of goods within the eu, it is of particular importance to consumers that the apparent differences in the quality and effectiveness of market surveillance organisations be compensated for by european rules on accreditation bodies. the european parliament has imposed significantly stronger obligations on these authorities and member states, in addition to the commission's proposal. the regulation clearly prohibits the commercialisation, profit-making and competition of accreditation bodies and safeguards their independence and public-law status. secondly, although consumer and environmental safety and protection system of market surveillance. this position has not only been shared by the european parliament but has been developed in many ways, and the obligations on member states and market surveillance right to know. i am glad that the council and the commission have followed parliament's request. thirdly, i personally regard the inclusion of consumer goods as the greatest success of parliament and started the preparatory work because i believe that this project is urgent and that we will present this study as soon as possible. the ce marking was not created for the information of the consumer at the time. it's a misunderstanding that keeps happening. the ce marking merely confirms the conformity of a product with all the rules applicable to it. the consumer can only take action with the ce marking if he knows what regulations actually apply to a particular product. but that is clearly too much to ask, and it is not possible to ask that of the consumer. it is true that the ce marking is surveillance system will be optimized in the future according to uniform criteria, and this is necessary. if the market is open, then there must be market surveillance systems. it is easier to detect vice-president of the commission. - madam president, ladies and gentlemen, the commission has not yet adopted a position on the proposal for a directive. let me say a few words about the direct economic impact. it is true that the rules on mutual recognition apply to 21% of all european industrial production, which is a very large amount indeed. and if this system of mutual recognition were to work perfectly, i.e. if it were to be applied fully and everywhere, then we would have an increase in european gross domestic product of 1.8%, i.e. already on a macroeconomic scale. the opposite is also true: if mutual recognition does not work, we estimate that the potential of the internal market is reduced by about 10%, which means that the fact that mutual recognition is not practised actually costs about eur 150 billion a year. mrs roithová asked a question about the registration of the ce mark. we were able to do this last year because it required a change in european law. the process is underway, and i expect that today's decisions will help us to accelerate it. it is not in our hands alone, but we are doing everything we can to complete this registration as quickly as possible. mr csibi mentioned - and with a critical tone - that i had already pointed out last year that there could be no 100% safety of products. i would like to say again, very specifically: there really is no such thing as a 100% product safety. even if we have all our products certified by an independent third party, this does not mean that every single part of a series can be tested. the problem is not that the prototype is being tested, but that the problems arise in normal production. even in the areas where we have the most stringent regulations in terms of product safety, like prescription drugs or cars, there are always production errors and there are always recalls. the idea of telling the consumer that there can be a 100% safety is an illusion. that is why we must - and this is the only way we have - insist that all those who are responsible in the chain are also fully held accountable. this starts with the suppliers, then the manufacturer, and if it is an imported product, the importer. and that is also the answer to mr purvis's question: what we are doing with the new regulations is to make it clear that an importer in europe is responsible for ensuring that the products he imports are safe and that where standards exist they also meet those standards. this means that the european importer assumes responsibility for the safety of a product coming from a third country and that the person who suffers damage from a dangerous or defective product does not have to look for any manufacturer in any country far outside the european union but keeps his claim to the european importer. i am sure that this is a regulation which will have a considerable practical impact. so much for the questions that have been asked. i would like to take this opportunity to thank you once again for the positive and constructive spirit of this debate. if malcolm harbour is still around, i tell him, if it were up to me, he could have a birthday any day, if his birthday is decorated with such beautiful results. prime minister of sweden, member of the european council. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, ladies and gentlemen, i have to say that i am very pleased with the way the commission has been working. be prepared in case something unexpected happens. in other words, there must be a great deal of flexibility and the ability to adapt to the prevailing situation which may, after all, affect the process. climate and energy issues are one of the major societal challenges of our time. we have a great responsibility to future generations to ensure that we succeed in formulating a policy for the united states. estimates show that the world's total energy demand is not declining but is projected to increase by 50 percent by 2030. the key to tackling climate change, of course, lies in how we deal with this supposedly increased energy demand. first, we have to think: how can we become better at saving and being more efficient? but the climate challenge also requires a new political approach. we need to dispel the myth that growth is the enemy of the environment. sweden is a living example of the opposite. since 1990, the beginning of the kyoto year, our economy has grown by 44 failures of national reform efforts, which also exist, are no longer just an internal matter but in fact concern us all. our future prosperity in europe depends to a large extent on how we, the member transnational environmental challenges. progressive energy and environment policies within the union are a prerequisite for long-term sustainable growth and thus prosperity in europe, but they are also an important factor for our future competitiveness. with the lisbon strategy for sustainable growth and jobs, the eu has created the means to meet these challenges. the strategy is there. sustainable growth and employment also in the next decade. a few words about the eu budget. we're saying it's long past its expiration date. the budget should be the main instrument for achieving the discussion about what should be financed at eu level and what should be financed at national level? europe is facing a demographic development with a rapidly ageing population, a development that will put our welfare systems under increasing pressure in the coming years. i can only paint the picture of how quickly this has changed sweden. in 1913, almost 100 years ago, sweden introduced a retirement age of 67. then you should be aware that the average life expectancy in sweden at that time was around 56 years. the truth was that the pension system was for the few who managed to survive the years in the work force and a few years after that. most of them worked and died. and worked from a young age. now, while we have seen a real decline in the retirement age, we have also seen a development where the average age in sweden is now 80 years. we have gone from a situation where we worked almost all our lives to the fact that the swede who is now born can see a life ahead of him where he may only work half his life. a remarkable development in just a few generations. but it leads to fewer and fewer people supporting more and more people. this, together with a significant degree of exclusion from the labour market, reinforces the need for job-creating policies. more people need to be in work to maintain a good standard of living in the face of these challenges. more people have to work for longer periods of their lives as we do. the growing proportion of older people in europe is not matched by those who will be of working age. this also partially addresses questions of migration. properly handled, it can be an important and indeed necessary piece of the puzzle in maintaining a well-being worthy of the name. remember that all these newcomers who are positive, expectant and eager to do the right thing are being treated with this positive energy. we must create the political conditions for people who have sought to come to europe, conditions which never be the only answer to the challenges posed by increased migration. anyone who thinks that strengthening borders is enough to solve the many issues of migration is making it too easy for will require intensive work on this very issue. sweden also sees it as a priority to bring together the eu's external relations and to increase the coherence between migration on the one hand and development policy on the other. secondly, we must remember that only by addressing the causes of migration in poverty and oppression in the long term can we achieve truly good results. a global approach is needed, not least in the context of the un high-level dialogue on migration. the eu has an important role to play in giving this thinking more substance, not least in the form of broad and partnership-based cooperation with the african countries concerned. we want to work for an ambitious and forward-looking programme for the years 2010 to 2014 to replace the hague programme. we attach great importance to the active participation of the european parliament in this process. international terrorism is one of the greatest global threats to our open societies. as terrorist networks grow, we see more and more individuals acting independently and terrorist attacks becoming less predictable. organised crime is a growing problem in europe. it is becoming increasingly difficult for individual countries to combat serious international organised crime on their own. much of organised crime often originates outside the eu. the lisbon treaty now gives us new tools in the fight against terrorism and other crossborder crime. the european parliament will play an important role in this. there will be a process of approximation of legislation which will continue. the turkmenistan and uzbekistan. the five republics became members of the osce after the collapse of the soviet union, but they also undertook to adopt the values, standards and principles that we share within the osce. under the german presidency of the council, the european council adopted a common strategy for central asia on 20 and 21 june 2007. the central asia strategy offers the five countries to share experience and expertise in key areas such as good governance, rule of law, democratisation, human rights, education and training. the european union's dependence on external energy resources and the need for a diversified energy supply policy to guarantee energy security are a common interest of the european union and the central asian republics. we have common interests in this respect. however, when it comes to the supply of energy sources, we are talking about two countries in particular, namely turkmenistan and kazakhstan. uzbekistan and tajikistan, for example, as we have recently learned, have their own energy problems. kyrgyzstan is an energy-rich country when it comes to water, and we mentioned it deliberately. in this respect, we are following the proposal of the instruments of bilateral cooperation with states. the agreements with kazakhstan, kyrgyzstan and uzbekistan have already entered into force, while the agreement with tajikistan has not yet been road ahead, however - and this must be said at this point - is still a very long one. we welcome the first steps towards opening up that have been taken. we hope, however, that this is only the beginning of what is desirable. this report clearly sets out the objectives and priorities for relations with these five countries. it's about bringing together country-specific and regional approaches. it is about democracy and the rule of law, without overlooking human rights. we want clear benchmarks, defining indicators and targets so that our partners know what they are dealing with. in writing. the lisbon treaty will make a militaristic europe possible. the current ec and eu treaties forbid a permanent eu military budget of its own. the 'stimulus fund' (article 28 (3)) can now also be used to pay for operational eu military expenditure. this means that in addition to national military budgets, there is an eu military budget. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the use of the term 'competent authority' in the context of the directive. institutional cooperation between the eu and nato is laid down in a treaty (article 28a (7)). the right of the bundestag to decide on the deployment of the bundeswehr abroad is being significantly eroded. the reform treaty will make a military core europe possible through the instrument of 'permanent structured cooperation'. this creates a primary legal framework for the increased deployment of eu battle groups (article 28, protocol 4). the court of justice of the european union has no jurisdiction (article 11, 240a). the european parliament is also not competent and is merely kept informed (article 21). this will remove future military operations from democratic control. the possibility of a militaristic europe is accompanied by repressive closure of the external borders. the new article 62 of the treaty on reform is intended to introduce 'an integrated border control system at the external borders'. the undemocratic implementation of the lisbon treaty by the circumvention of referendums, the imposition of a neoliberal economic policy and the militaristic elements are taking europe in the wrong direction.
in writing. - it is a success for the greens that the commission's proposal for this regulation was not simply passed by parliament. the greens have been persistent in ensuring that the collection of sensitive data on population and housing is protected under this regulation. the voluntary annex, which provided for the collection of micro-data and questions on highly sensitive data such as sexual behaviour or reading skills , has now been completely deleted. the european data protection supervisor was also called on twice by the greens. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the protection of personal data. the regulation contains our amendment, which refers to compliance with data protection rules both in the member states and at eu level. in addition, there are now clear references to data protection rules for data transmission and processing. the regulation, which has been clearly supported, is now doing what it was originally intended to do. the aim is not to collect new data but simply to harmonise the collection of statistical data on the main social and economic characteristics of regions already carried out at national level, so that these data can be compared throughout europe. a common european data base will allow regional aid to be used where it is needed most.
the chairman of the council. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, ladies and gentlemen, on balance, and if i'm to leave out a few details, i have to say that we, the members of my generation and, of course, our younger colleagues, have been quite fortunate. we've spent a great, perhaps the best part of our lives in a time of open doors and windows of opportunity. this period began in 1975 with the helsinki final act and was most marked in eastern and central europe, where the berlin wall and the communist system collapsed in 1989. through the broken wall, through the open doors and windows of the eastern front of the euro-atlantic community, a new view has been opened. we saw the vast, sunny and rugged landscape of a united and free europe, as represented by this mighty european parliament building. i just couldn't imagine, in my youth, that i would ever be in it. in our country, the period between the 1980s and the early 1990s was called the slovenian spring. unfortunately, at the very beginning of the democratic awakening, we were hit by the yugoslav crisis, which tried to stop democratic development and which caused the nations of the western balkans to lag behind in a huge way. most of the countries of eastern and central europe, the ten new members of the european union, have accepted the historic challenge. but in the balkans, time stopped. the gaerc general affairs and external relations council, which i chair, has amongst other difficult tasks the task of promoting the european perspective of the western balkans. this means integrating countries such as croatia, the former yugoslav republic of macedonia, serbia, montenegro, bosnia and herzegovina, kosovo and albania into the european membership, candidacy and agreement system. the yugoslav crisis must end. the doors and windows are open. the wall is gone. the european union announced in the thessaloniki agenda that the western balkan countries would sooner or later become members of the european union. now is the time to remember our commitments. we must make sure that macedonia, or the former yugoslav republic of macedonia, starts negotiations for membership of the european union this year. serbia must shed the burden of the past, that is, the fears and shadows of the milosevic regime. milosevic was the one who was responsible for the stalemate in the western balkans. and we must not forget albania, bosnia and herzegovina, montenegro and kosovo. in this context, the european union western balkans forum will be held in slovenia at the end of march. the commission is preparing a specific communication on the western balkans in cooperation with the slovenian presidency. the forum will also discuss strengthening regional cooperation in various fields, such as transport, civil protection, research and development, and so on. in accordance with the conclusions of the january general affairs and external relations council, the european commission is holding talks on visa liberalisation with all countries in the region. the enormous importance of visa liberalisation for the region cannot be underestimated. in this connection, mr president, we would like to point out a paradox. citizens of the former yugoslavia travelled to most european countries without a visa before 1990. now, a generation of young people who grew up after this turning point in europe's history need a visa to travel. ladies and gentlemen, at the january council, the foreign ministers unanimously invited serbia to sign a political agreement, which represents a new step towards membership of the european union. the election victory of the european-oriented candidate tadić has given us hope that serbia will join us as soon as possible after years of slow development and isolation. the european union has already deployed a european security and defence policy mission to kosovo. the establishment of relations with kosovo is a matter for each member. but we will probably not differ on the basic assessments announced by the european council in december. the most important thing is to take into account and respect serbia. the european union needs serbia and serbia needs the european union. intercultural dialogue, in my view, is not an empty phrase. if negotiations are exhausted, the possibilities for dialogue are not exhausted. the time has come for practical dialogue between serbs and albanians in kosovo, between serbia and kosovo, between serbia and the european union. the fate of kosovo has been a burden for many years. kosovo was once part of the federal system of yugoslavia, but after 1974 it was virtually equated with the yugoslav republics. slobodan milosevic took away kosovo's autonomy in the late 1980s and then occupied it militarily in 1999, causing a tragedy of global proportions. the case of kosovo is truly unique, having been taken under the protection of the international community for humanitarian reasons, and then administered by it for almost nine years. monday's decision by the general affairs and external relations council was not an easy one, however. it, like the declaration of independence in pristina, was not unexpected. the following facts led us to her conclusion. first, there is a growing recognition that a return to the status quo is not acceptable, nor is the current status quo. the new formula for kosovo's status was not found by either side, and it is clear that continuing negotiations would not bring it. kosovo has been under un administration since 1999 and serbia has not exercised effective authority in kosovo during that time, pursuant to resolution 1244. kosovo, and in particular its majority population, had been subject to systematic repression, including ethnic cleansing and humanitarian catastrophe, for several years prior to that year. all of the above, ladies and gentlemen, which was initially agreed by all the members of the contact group, including the russian federation, supports the argument that kosovo is indeed a special case, a case sui generis, and therefore does not call into question the validity of the principle of sovereignty and territorial integrity of states. the council has long been convinced that the european union must take responsibility for kosovo. this belief was confirmed at the gaerc meeting in february by the conclusions you are familiar with. after all the prophecies of disunity, we have achieved unity. the decisions were adopted unanimously after lengthy negotiations and coordination. the european union is an interesting and unique community. of course, we share common interests and values. among them are respect and tolerance for differences. you could say we're all about our differences. at the end of the february meeting of the general affairs and external relations council, we reached a common position. an important finding in it is that we expect to act in accordance with the national, domestic practice of each country with regard to the recognition of kosovo. some may have expected the european union as a whole to recognise kosovo, but that is not possible because the european union is not the same as a state. the european union has adopted a joint assessment of developments in kosovo and the western balkans. first, the european union has confirmed the fact that kosovo has adopted a resolution on independence. secondly, the european union notes that kosovo has committed itself to democratic principles through this resolution, for example with regard to the serb minority and cultural monuments. thirdly, the european union confirmed the continuation of the international mission and its readiness to play a leading role in the region. fourthly, the european union has confirmed the european perspective of the western balkans. fifth, the european commission will prepare concrete, for example economic, measures for the wider region. and sixthly, the european union is aware of the principles and decisions of the international community, but the declaration of independence of kosovo, because of its specific nature, does not compromise those principles. kosovo, of course, also contains and includes serbian people, serbian heritage and culture. and i would say, and i would stress this, that this is a particularly valuable part of european culture. many european nations, including slovenia, which i represent, have important monuments of their cultural and ethnic heritage outside their modern national borders. this is a fact that in modern europe no longer constitutes a barrier but, on the contrary, a link. the same applies to ethnic minority communities. we believe that it is essential for serbia at this moment not to close its door to the european union with its reactions to the declaration and recognition of kosovo's independence. we reiterate that the issue of kosovo is separate from the issue of serbia's european integration. serbia should not link these two issues. in this sense, we find it particularly incomprehensible that serbia opposes the european union or its mission in kosovo, which is primarily in the interest of the serbian population there. i'm finished. the european union is one of the most successful peace-keeping organisations in the world. the peoples and countries of europe are united and in solidarity for peace and a better life. such an attitude includes tolerance and generosity, and above all, understanding and compassion for the plight of others. ladies and gentlemen, the european union has also opened doors and windows for the western balkans, including kosovo, with the decisions i have just mentioned.

draft opinion of the consultative committee on regional development. the commission has already made a number of proposals in this area. the effects of demographic change are very different. while the suburbs of paris are constantly shaken by social unrest due to the high rate of migration, in our home in brandenburg, the regions are shrinking, people are migrating and the population is aging much faster. the ageing of society is putting a burden on public budgets for social spending, and the lisbon strategy is aimed at reducing this burden. but given the real causes of demographic change, i wonder whether such a reduction is not counterproductive to the lisbon strategy. the commission finds it very easy to blame the ageing of society on women because they are not having more children. the causes are more likely to be present and past political mistakes. i would like to mention just three of the factors which have led to this distortion in society. the first point is that the analyses show that the desire to have children is very much there, the parents - and not only the women - but still do not have children because the framework conditions are not right, because they do not have social security, because - as already mentioned - the employment opportunities for parents are more difficult and because career and family life are not compatible. but the solution to this would be to think about work-life balance in a whole new way. the key is to divide income and time for family and career equally between the sexes; there are excellent studies on this from the dublin foundation. and it would be crucial that children do not become an individual at risk of poverty, as is the case in many member states. for the policies of the member states in the eu, this actually means sustainability in social security systems, and this is an unpopular cost factor, but it would bring demographic change back on track. the second aspect is illustrated by an interesting study in my own region. it was found that the migration of young women was not caused by the question of reconciling family and work, but by massive discrimination after school. they're the best people, they're the best in their class, they're the best graduates, and yet they get the worst educational placements, the worst career opportunities. this means that the european commission can be effective in combating discrimination in the area where it has real competence, namely in the area of gender mainstreaming, equal opportunities for men and women, by introducing improvements in legislation and, above all, by putting pressure on the member states to implement legislation so that something finally happens. thirdly, as the author of the opinion of the committee of the regions, i would like to refer again to the subject of the shrinking regions. in our opinion, we criticise the fact that the public administrations still erect huge barriers to effective civic engagement, to the development of innovation and creativity, and thus prevent successful regional development concepts. at the same time, there is a tendency for policy makers to simply write off regions, to withdraw from the state's responsibility for basic services and simply give them up. this cannot be a european solution, because in the long term, over generations - as history shows - it will be very expensive. it is therefore the task of the public administrations to take up the impulses of civil society and work with it to help the region to overcome this dilemma. in this context, i call on the european commission to incorporate civil society impulses into regional cooperation, to promote it by bringing regions to exchange experience where this is working well and by showing good examples of good practice. these would be very concrete solutions where the european commission can really be active and not always blame demographic change on women.
i would like to thank the commissioner for his reply. the european union is facing an unprecedented demographic change. by 2030, more than 20 million people of working age will be missing. two employees have to cover one pensioner. the good news is that people are living longer, and older people are healthier than ever. the bad news: there is a lack of young people, which has dramatic implications for the organization of work, urban planning, housing and education systems. we need a more family-friendly environment in our member states, more childcare facilities, more company day-care centres, better reconciliation between family and work, more women in active working life, more part-time work for parents and safe re-entry after the family phase. and above all, stable career prospects and sufficient income to facilitate the desire to have children. we also need much higher investment in people to improve education and skills. lifelong learning programmes should not only benefit young people, but also older people who want to be employed for much longer, who are resilient, highly competent and highly motivated. the castex own-initiative report must not be overloaded. the legal status of social services of general interest remains controversial. we are against an eu-wide framework directive or binding legislation. the voluntary earnings-related pension should not be subject to additional obligations, such as family policy criteria. this is a social security issue, a tax issue, a classic member state issue. the report contains substantial content, based on these considerations and the amendments tabled by the epp-ed group. they will enable us to have the necessary broad discussion on the consequences of the dramatic changes in demography.

the commission is therefore proposing to extend the period of validity of the directive to the period of 1 january 1999. the commission has already made a number of proposals. in the late 1990s, the european union had a philosophy of measuring its capacity for integration by the achievements of the internal market. the hope that the internal market's development strategies, which were exclusively geared to economic growth, would solve the problems in the european union was not fulfilled. the european single market concentrated the growth in economic activity on the centres of gravity that attracted further activity, at the expense of the less-favoured regions and the natural environment. and even in these centers, not everyone was part of the successes, but poverty was increasing, and that caused tension and unrest. today the commission is making the same mistakes: it places cohesion policy under the lisbon strategy. instead of giving real priority to the problems of the most disadvantaged regions and promoting exclusively sustainable development projects, it relies on old-fashioned infrastructure concepts and, consequently, only on economic centres. the municipalities and regions have been made dependent on the big european banks for generations. i think this is a huge problem, because in the end the next generation will pay the price for a failed development policy. and this in turn is triggering migration movements - as my colleague mrs krehl has already indicated - and it is also leading to anti-european sentiment because a part of the population is not involved in the successes. these are dead end strategies. i believe that we must be careful not to jeopardize the internal cohesion of the union. economic and social cohesion must really remain a policy in its own right, and the gains must be available to all regions and all people in europe. this can only be achieved if cohesion policy is really supported by a model of society based on solidarity and by sustainable development patterns that do not come at the expense of the environment.

vice-president of the commission. − mr president, i should like to begin by pointing out that directive 95/46/ec (the ‘data protection directive’) applies to data controllers established in the community. it also applies to controllers not established on the territory of a member state when such a controller uses equipment situated on the territory of a member state, unless such equipment is used only for purposes of transit through the territory of the community. the directive ensures rights to all individuals, whatever their nationality or place of residence and regardless of whether they act as consumers or not. it lays down substantive provisions imposing obligations on data controllers and recognising the rights of individuals. it also prescribes sanctions and appropriate remedies in the event of breaches and establishes enforcement mechanisms to make them effective. we follow closely developments in technology and associated challenges, in particular those relating to the protection of privacy and personal data. as far as transatlantic cooperation is concerned, we maintain regular contact with the united states authorities responsible for monitoring safe harbour – the department of commerce and the federal trade commission – in the context of which questions relating to the protection of personal data are addressed. issues posed by new technologies and their worldwide deployment are also examined. in this particular case, which is the merger of google and double click, the case is still being analysed by the commission in order to decide whether the envisaged merger is in line with regulation 139/2004/ec (the ‘merger regulation’). we will adopt a decision soon. however, it can be said that the commission has carried out an extensive analysis of the economic aspects raised by the proposed merger in order to determine whether it is compatible with common market rules. companies are required to comply with national data protection laws implementing the data protection directive, and national data protection authorities are the bodies responsible for enforcing compliance by those entities which process personal data within their territory. a merger between different entities does not exonerate the parties to the merger from their obligations under national data protection principles. indeed, any decision the commission may take to approve a merger is without prejudice to the obligations imposed on the parties by community legislation on the protection of privacy with regard to the processing of personal data. irrespective of the approval of the merger, the new entity, in its day-to-day business, will have to respect the fundamental rights recognised by all relevant instruments, including, but not limited to, privacy and data protection. national data protection authorities are therefore charged with the task of ensuring this compliance and, if necessary, taking appropriate measures to enforce compliance.
the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used effectively. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council and parliament. the internet is a great blessing. new technologies none of us can imagine our work today without the internet. this new technology also leads to an unprecedented exchange of data. but where there's light, there's shadow, and that's what we're seeing here when billions of data sets are stored for a long time. in the specific question, commissioner frattini made it clear that the merger of google and doubleclick now required the application of the european union legal framework and that the merger had to be examined. we shall wait for that examination and then draw our political conclusions from it. the basic question is how we deal with data protection on the internet, because it is not a matter of concern to large or small companies - to the user - how data protection is handled. there are no easy answers because at the heart of the question is whether the ip address is also personal information. this is the case with fixed providers, but there are also a plethora of other providers where the ip address does not automatically reveal the identity of the user. in our view, there would be a negative impact on data protection, and even the disclosure of data would be possible. the need for legislation must always be assessed in the context of necessity and proportionality. there are also a lot of benefits for the user in making the data public. the key is that he consciously decides on the data transfer and can also have it. this means that the user must have information rights be able to find out about the data stored about him and there must be clear rules on how to deal with the transfer of data, the sale of data. the commission has already taken a number of initiatives to improve the quality of internet services, and it is hoped that the commission will be able to take a number of initiatives to improve the quality of internet services.
i would like to thank the commissioner for his reply. i have to admit, i like this catch-the-eye rule, especially when the clock isn't running. we certainly have a lot to discuss in the area of data protection. some colleagues from the green group raised the issue of the collection of data from private companies and individuals. certainly, mergers such as google and doubleclick raise some questions. however, you should also be careful not to mix things up. if many frogs quack, it's still a quake. so that means we should not forget to understand the technical processes behind it. we are very close to the subject - and this is particularly true of my group - particularly on the internet and, of course, also on the question of data protection, and we are often very emotional. but to understand how the internet and data collection work, i first have to understand the technology behind it. in that regard, i do not think that mr weber's approach is so wrong as to first examine the extent to which ip addresses may constitute personal data within the meaning of directive 2002/58 on the protection of personal data in the electronic communications sector. in some cases, this can be combined with user data to obtain very personal information. on the other hand, with the technological development we have today, when, for example, refrigerators automatically retrieve recipes from the internet, the question of whether the ip address of my refrigerator is really personal data is obsolete.

member of the commission. − mr president, first of all i would like to say that i agree with the comments made by the rapporteur, mr capoulas santos, that fisheries and the revenue that is derived from the fisheries partnership agreement form a very important part of the budget of guinea-bissau. we are now working in a spirit of partnership as against the traditional fisheries agreements where the objective was to go and catch fish, pay for the fish caught and leave. these fisheries partnership agreements are modelled on the basis of helping the country concerned to build its fisheries infrastructure and to build related sectors so that there could also be a diversion from pure fishing to fish-related activities like aquaculture, where that is possible. the aim is also to see to it that the fishing activities that are carried out by our fleets under a fisheries partnership agreement relate only to the surplus. for example, in this case, at our request, an evaluation study was carried out at the end of 2005 by an independent external consultant, whose recommendations in terms of management and conservation of resources have been taken into account, together with the scientific advice provided by guinea-bissau’s research institute following the 2006 trawling campaign. furthermore, the protocol includes a number of binding measures in its annex iii, with a view to implementing a management plan for the global fishing effort in the guinea-bissau exclusive economic zone. according to the fisheries plan, guinea-bissau committed itself to reducing the fishing effort on shrimps and cephalopods, maintaining in 2007 the existing agreements with third countries and the european community, preventing the mobilisation in 2008 and subsequent years of fishing opportunities granted to third countries from 1 january 2007 which have remained unused, not granting any fishing opportunities for chartering in these categories, and revoking and formally terminating all agreements with european companies, associations or enterprises. in addition, datasheets 1 and 2 of annex ii, applicable to fin-fish, cephalopod and shrimp trawlers, provide for the possibility of biological recovery periods. with regard to shrimp fishing, guinea-bissau has also undertaken to increase the mesh size from 40 to 50 mm, in keeping with existing legislation in the subregion. i would say that it is in spite of these fisheries partnership agreements that a lot of illegal fishing activity is carried out and a lot of private licensing is granted to third countries not belonging to the european union, and it is by virtue of these fisheries partnership agreements that we can control and manage our own fishing fleets so that they fish in a sustainable manner in guinea-bissau and other waters. so i have to say that, yes, i believe that it is beneficial to the third country concerned for the european union, for the european community, to negotiate and enter into such fisheries partnership agreements under the new regime. i agree with you, however, that the previous regime did exploit the resources, but the new arrangement is that we are only interested in negotiating agreements on the surplus, so that if the stock in the third-country waters is already fully exploited or overexploited we do not enter into a fisheries partnership agreement. if it is underexploited, then we only enter into an agreement for the surplus, and we do our utmost to see to it that our own fleets, at least, do carry out and do maintain the commitments undertaken under the agreement.

president of the republic of estonia. - dear friends, first of all, happy birthday. good friends, respected colleagues, colleagues in the truest sense of the word. friends i've missed for the last year and a half. i look at you and i see all of you. from down here, you look a lot more like you do from the 131st chair i used to sit in. you have no idea how powerful you are. you, the european parliament. i'm imagining it; i had to leave here to figure it out. but now allow me to continue in my current role as president of my country. this year, as estonia enters its fifth year as a member of the european union, we are no longer beginners, we are no longer new members. i really believe it is time to discard the term 'new member state' as an anachronism that explains nothing. (applause) today we have no new and old members. it's members only. the term 'new member state' does not even mean 'poor' today, because many of us have adopted the 'old member states'. today we form coalitions within the community based on interests or party positions. these unions can take innumerable forms, consisting of large or small, industrial or commercial countries, etc. but it's not based on the length of membership. here and today, i want to look ten years ahead. the time when we're all old or senior members. the time of the first horrific european civil war of the 20th century. we say that our union is the answer to the second european civil war; that it is the way to organize things in our part of the world so that the horrors of the second world war cannot be repeated. but we must not forget that a third or more of what is now the european union grew into independent political entities from the ashes of the first world war. finland, estonia, latvia, lithuania, and after 140 years of absence, poland, the former czechoslovakia. like hungary and austria today, which emerged in the 20th century as empires collapsed, as international superpowers collapsed, and as new states were born, based on the right of nations to self-determination. i mention this because many of today's member states - my home country among them - began their journey by getting rid of forced membership in large, despotic or undemocratic multinational organisations. in other words, empires. estonia, like many others, managed to break out twice. yet we are all here together today to build our own, our own new transnational alliance. and the identity. our european union. not because we've been conquered or occupied, but because we have the freedom to do so. and because we believe it's the right thing to do. it's like our new right to self-determination. i mention this because for the first time in ten years estonia has the right and the responsibility to preside. i very much hope that when that time comes, we will no longer struggle with the questions we face today. and that's why i want to talk today about things that are important for at least a ten-year time frame. and the reason i'm talking about these things in the end is that our election cycle and our challenge cycle don't move in the same rhythm. we're good at dealing with problems that fit into a four- or five-year cycle. but the challenges and needs of the european union today - from energy to the environment, from competitiveness to enlargement, from a common foreign policy to the migration of peoples - are all strategic issues that require bold and courageous action over a period of time far longer than two or three elections. ladies and gentlemen. even if we cannot predict the future, certain developments and dangers are generally understandable. with two, or two seats, you can't complain about the lack of discussion. global warming and the decline of fossil fuels. yet these two problems are global, and the solutions, which are not possible without the european union, can also only come from a global perspective. but the union also faces other serious challenges. if we don't deal with them, in maybe ten years, certainly in a quarter of a century, we'll lose some of the relative prosperity and success that we enjoy today. these challenges and needs are all linked to the competitiveness of the european union. where are our competitors? within the eu or in the world? the answer is clear: both sides. we compete in the marketplace within the european union and globally. but if we look at the long-term trends of globalisation, we have to thank jean monnet and jacques delors for the internal market, because it was created at a time when globalisation was not yet a tangible phenomenon. it is the internal market that helps individual european countries to remain globally competitive. opening up europe, opening up to competitive pressure from market forces europe is the engine of global competitiveness. the current state of mind in the european union does not always give cause for optimism. for two reasons. firstly, the european union's lisbon process, the unfortunate failure to deliver on our own best-intentioned innovation and competitiveness programme. (applause) thank you very much. secondly, the growing protectionism in the european union, not only in relation to the rest of the world but also within our own borders. let me address these two issues next. at a time when my own country was just emerging from fifty years of soviet captivity, i wondered with anxiety: how long will it take to build the infrastructure needed for all of estonia? yet, in areas such as information technology, we were able to start at the same place as others. public and private investment in information technology allowed estonia to reach above the eu average. by the end of the 1990s, we had reached a point where few in europe could offer a comparable service to e-government and banking, for example. my country's contribution to the development of information technology has paid off, allowing us to increase our competitiveness. but that alone is not enough. in general and in the wider context, estonia, like the rest of europe, is lagging behind in the fields of innovation, research and development. innovation, let us admit, is now coming first and foremost from the united states, where maintaining a high level of competitiveness depends in turn on the input of brains. it depends on the brighter heads coming from europe, but also from india and china. we have to get serious about this for once. we're very tough on immigration. our children are increasingly choosing not to study math, science, engineering and science. we have made our own choice and restricted free competition within the european union to the services sector, which is the most competitive in the world. competition - or rather the lack of it - in the european union also has an impact on security. given the importance of energy, it is understandable that many countries in the european union want to protect their companies from competition and do not support the liberalisation of the energy market. that reaction is understandable. but today, europe's largest energy source is a country that has declared itself an energy superpower and proclaims on its foreign ministry website that energy is an instrument of foreign policy. in order to avoid the division of the european union into imperialist and imperialist policies and to prevent the manipulation of the member states in the interests of better gas supply conditions, the creation of a common energy policy is indispensable. the chairman of the council. − let me say first of all that the bureau welcomes the report by mrs jeggle on the proposal to increase milk quotas as a constructive and balanced contribution to a debate which has been going on for several weeks or longer. the european commission has proposed, on the basis of the favourable market opportunities presented in its report and analysis, an increase of 2% in the national milk quotas from the next quota year, 1 april 2008. the question of milk quotas cannot, of course, be confined to a question of percentages; it is a wider question linked to the review of the common agricultural policy. that is why the council has also confined itself, or not confined itself, to this question, but it has triggered a wider debate, essentially parallel to that which we have on the whole package of health inspections of the common agricultural policy. i have to say that very similar concerns have been raised in the council and in parliament in relation to this proposal. for example, calls were made for predictability and stability in the dairy sector. concern was expressed about areas with less favourable farming opportunities where there is little or no alternative to traditional dairy production. on the other hand, there were strong demands that european farmers be allowed to take advantage of the opportunities offered by the developing international market, as well as the european market. despite the complexity of these questions, these concerns, these matters, we are convinced that the health review of the cap can also provide balanced answers and solutions to all these concerns. and i would add here that the council also joins parliament in this regard in its initiative to have the commission draw up a comprehensive, long-term strategy for the european milk sector or a proposal for such a strategy. we believe that the so-called soft transition to the abolition of milk quotas should be a fundamental part of this strategy, ensuring a smooth transition to a more market-oriented milk policy and predictability in the sector. the council therefore intends to invite the commission to examine all appropriate means in this regard. we believe that the commission's proposal for a 2% increase in quotas from the next quota year can be considered as part of the package and that the other parts will be dealt with appropriately in the context of the health inspection. finally, i would like to add that the proposal will be on the agenda of the agriculture and fisheries council next week and i hope that it will be adopted. so, if the conditions are met, it will start to apply, as i said, this year, or the quota year 2008. finally, let me thank all those who contributed to the debate on this report, in particular the rapporteur. we believe this is a balanced and stable view, and we thank you for your work.
member of the commission. − mr president, i think it is a very good signal from the presidency that the minister for agriculture is present here today to participate in this very important discussion. i shall start my speech in the traditional way, by thanking the committee on agriculture and rural development and especially the rapporteur for the very constructive report on the proposal to increase the milk quota system by 2%, as was stated by the minister, for the coming milk year starting on 1 april 2008. many people have pushed the commission to alleviate the very tight dairy situation. in the council, a large majority of member states invited the commission to put a proposal on the table on increasing quotas. a resolution here in the european parliament, adopted in october 2007, on rising food prices also called on the commission, as a matter of urgency, to propose a temporary increase in milk quotas. in december 2007 the commission presented a market outlook report that showed that there clearly is, and will be in the future, a growing demand for dairy products. your report also confirms that we should increase the possibilities for producing more milk. i think everybody would agree that the commission’s proposal is fairly prudent and clear, with a predictable and equal outcome for all the member states. may i respectfully suggest that your amendments seem not to pay full attention to the need for predictability and equal treatment for farmers? the amendment to make the increase of 2% voluntary for member states, if applied, would be likely to create some difficulties. firstly, i think we would all agree that we are looking for more market orientation and higher productivity. therefore, i personally feel that the producer should be given the choice of whether or not to produce more milk. i think we would also agree that dairy farmers need predictability – certainty about their production possibilities within the quota system – and i do not think that a voluntary system would contribute to this. as a solution, member states have the opportunity to decide not to distribute the quota but to keep it in the national reserve. this is a possibility, although i would push the member states and i would be happy to see the quota distributed, because i think it is the most proper way. the amendment to use balancing-out of the quota at the end of the quota year is not a new idea. in fact, it is something that the commission has been looking closely into, since such a theory could facilitate the use in some member states of the unused quota in other member states. but i think we would also agree that theory is one thing and practice is another. firstly, i think it clearly introduces uncertainty for milk producers. they would then have to make their best guess of how the situation would look at the end of the production year and, on that basis, try to make a choice for their production, and only the following year would they know whether that production was levy free or not. i think, with all respect, this is not to the advantage of the decision taken on the dairy farm. it is obvious that milk production implies heavy investment, and we owe it to our farmers to have a predictable system until the quotas disappear in 2015. secondly, who would benefit from this? i do not have to point out that it would largely benefit only a small group of member states. this already makes it politically difficult. the most important thing is that it will benefit those producers who have already exceeded their quotas – those who have produced too much – and not those who have tried to keep within the limits of the quota system. so there is no certainty that this would lead to more milk being available on the market. thirdly, in my view, this also goes against the idea of simplifying the common agricultural policy. i fear that implementing rules in this area would be extremely complex, and i am not in favour of making our system more complicated in a situation where there are only seven years left of the lifetime of this quota system. all in all, i note with pleasure that we all agree on the necessity for increasing the possibilities for the dairy sector in europe to increase its production. it is an extremely important political signal to me and to all the member states that the agriculture committee unanimously chose this line after the very divided opinions at the beginning of this discussion. i therefore send my biggest congratulations to the rapporteur for that achievement. i hope i will have the same rate of success in the council.
the rapporteur. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. as i have said, the committee on agriculture and rural development unanimously rejected the commission's proposal to increase the quotas for the coming milk year by 2%, i.e. 2.8 million tonnes. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. on the basis of the 2003 decisions, 11 member states will have a quota increase of 0.5% on 1 april this year, which is equivalent to 700 000 tonnes more milk in the european union. the intensive debates with my colleagues on the committee on agriculture have shown that there will be no formula and no easy way forward for the debate. opinions were widely divided: all the positions were represented, from the general and fundamental rejection of any increase in quotas to an increase of 5%. we have nevertheless succeeded in reaching an inter-group compromise which was adopted unanimously without any objections or reservations. i would like to thank all the members for their constructive cooperation. the compromise adopted has two central points. commissioner, you said it. i have a different opinion on that. firstly, the establishment of a european balancing mechanism to compensate for under- or over-compensation of existing national quotas at eu level. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the quota system is not over-taxed. secondly, as from 1 april, member states may opt for a voluntary national quota increase for the quota year 2008/2009. we want flexibility, not rigidity! this compromise will enable us to make more efficient use of the quotas already in place. the commission has also proposed that the member states should be able to use the european quota system in the context of a common european internal market system. commissioner, you always stress that the existing milk quota in this system will expire in 2015. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. let us also think of the former lakes of milk! the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. we believe that this is the only way to ensure that the whole sector is promoted and preserved in a way that is future-oriented. in particular, this instrument should be used for dairy farmers in less-favoured areas and in areas of absolute grassland. i therefore ask you, commissioner, to incorporate this request from the european parliament in your legislative proposal on health checks. the application of article 69 is not, in our view, sufficient because it is not clearly defined in terms of concrete measures, particularly for the sector mentioned above. it is pure cynicism for a high-ranking commission official to say to a farmers' meeting that farmers should not complain about the fact that producer prices are falling again, since they have already been able to get by on 27 cents a litre of milk. this is a disregard for the legitimate interests of an entire profession, which i, as a member of a parliament which has put democracy on the map, cannot accept!
the commission has already made a number of proposals. i would also like to thank elisabeth jeggle for her work on this report. the current quota system is set to run until 2015. so it's going to be around for exactly seven years and a few days. i think it is wrong, madam commissioner, to increase the milk quota by 2% now. i would be perfectly willing to accept a 2% increase in the quota for the new member states, because their consumption of dairy products is still well below the eu average. the commission's proposals are not, however, in line with the commission's proposals. for the first time in many years, our dairy farmers have been able to obtain a decent price for milk for a few months. our dairy farmers, who milk their cows 365 days a year, 366 days this year, morning and evening, deserve to earn a better income than they have in the past. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the milk quota is not exceeded. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council and parliament on the subject. it will not be a soft landing, it will be a hard landing if what the commission has in mind for the quota sector is implemented. i think there are hoelgaards and rasmussens in the commission who would like to see a brutal drop in milk prices. you can't let them get away with this. we are already having problems without enlargement, and we must try to counteract this. the bavarian csu members will vote against the report tomorrow because they are against enlargement. this is not against elizabeth jeggle, it is against the quota increase.
the commission has already done so. two weeks ago, four and a half thousand dairy farmers from all over europe were in brussels. they have joined together in the european milk board and they are demanding adequate prices first. this has already had a considerable effect in germany. we have producer prices which were around 40%, they are now coming under pressure again. the dairy farmers are therefore calling for a quantity-oriented market policy. if this trend is to gain momentum, if it is to influence agricultural policy, can you imagine that in 2015 a commission could resist politically the demands of this movement to extend or re-establish the quantitative regime in a flexible way?

member of the commission. − madam president, the oral question tabled by ms berès on behalf of the committee on economic and monetary affairs gives me, on behalf of mr mccreevy and on behalf of the whole commission, the opportunity to inform you of the ongoing work on the review of the lamfalussy process. throughout last year, the european supervisory model in the field of financial services was examined at the highest political level. these discussions showed that there is a strong political will to strengthen the current supervisory architecture based on the lamfalussy committee structure. last year we saw the european parliament, the council and the commission each submit their assessment of the functioning of the current process. it is now time to move forward and to present concrete proposals. this stems from the ecofin council’s conclusions and the accompanying road map which were adopted last december. this road map sets out what needs to be done to improve the lamfalussy process and in particular to improve the committees of national supervisory authorities, the so-called ‘level three’ committees. the commission’s work is centred on three main areas following this agreement of the road map adopted last december. first, the commission was requested to consider how to clarify and strengthen the role of the level three committees and to set out concrete options for the informal ecofin council next april in ljubljana. the main objective here is to bring forth the contribution that the level three committee should make to supervisory cooperation, supervisory convergence and possibly to crisis prevention and management. the informal ecofin, by the way, will also discuss the work of a taskforce focusing on crisis management on cross border institutions. second, work is ongoing by a working group of the commission to review supervisory powers, voluntary delegation of tasks, supervisory cooperation and exchange of information. we are working together with the three level three committees on these tasks to deliver the requested results before the end of the year. considering the enormous scope of these reviews, it is, however, still too early to indicate today what the outcome of this work will be. third, the commission is looking into the possibility of financially contributing to the activities of the level three committees. this is an urgent problem as these committees in general, and in particular the committee of european securities regulators (cesr), have reached their budgetary limits. the commission will be looking for a stable legislative solution which would ensure continuity in eu financing. in our view, this could best be achieved by agreeing the modalities of eu funding in a decision adopted by the european parliament and the council. i have no time to give the parliament details of the road map adopted last december by ecofin, but allow me in half a minute just to read some of the commitments that were sent to the commission. we are working on all of these things. by april 2008 the commission should prepare an assessment of how to clarify the role of the committees and to consider all the different options towards strengthening the working of these committees. by mid-2008, the level three committees should for the first time transmit to the commission, the european parliament and the council draft work programmes, and thereafter start reporting annually on progress. this committee should also explore the possibility of strengthening the national application of guidelines, recommendations and standards; they should introduce in their charters the possibility of applying qualified majority voting coupled with a comply or explain procedure; they should study the possibilities of introducing a common set of operational guidelines for the operation of colleges of supervisors and monitor the coherence of the practices of the different colleges of supervisors. the level three committees and the commission should suggest – also by mid-2008 – a timetable for the introduction of eu-wide reporting format for single data requirements and reporting dates. by the end of 2008, the commission has also committed itself to conduct a cross-sectoral stock-taking exercise of the coherence, equivalence and actual use of sanctioning powers among member states. the commission should consider – also by the end of 2008 – financial support under the eu budget. and, as i said before, it should study the possibilities for eu funding under the eu budget of the development of tools to help build a common supervisory culture by the level three committees. the commission and the committees should review financial services directives to include provisions to enable the use of voluntary delegation of tasks, analyse the options for voluntary delegation of competences and so on and so forth. so we are working a lot and we should work a lot in the coming weeks, months and before the end of this year. but we are working at the same time on the financial turmoil by following the road map that was adopted in october 2007 by ecofin. a report on how we are working on this road map to tackle the financial turmoil consequences has been sent to the european council for discussions in a few days in brussels. we contributed to this report with a communication. the economic and financial committee the other day also presented its own report to ecofin. we discussed both reports at ecofin level and these reports are on the table for the discussions of the heads of state and government next thursday and friday. these reports convey the simple message: in order to respond to the concerns of our citizens and investors we must act swiftly and in a consistent way. we need to restore confidence and stability as soon as possible, having carefully considered all the options and in line with the better regulation principles. i think everybody acknowledges that this road map, adopted a few months ago by ecofin, provides the right answer to the problems identified. work on these road map commitments is on track. in the months to come it will be crucial to stick to the timetable and show that the eu is responding effectively to the crisis. our regulatory and supervisory framework must remain robust and keep pace with market developments. although the basle ii rules have only been fully implemented as of 1 january 2008 further improvements have already been planned in the capital requirements directive. this work has taken on increased importance in the light of the recent turmoil and maybe there will be other aspects of basle ii that we will need to address in the time ahead. we intend to adopt a new proposal for this directive in october so that discussion in parliament and the council can take place before the adoption of a new directive in april 2009. we appreciate very much the involvement of parliament in all these discussions. we need parliament’s contribution and we appreciate this involvement and this contribution. on 1 april – a few days before the next informal ecofin – mr mccreevy will go to the committee on economic and monetary affairs. economic and monetary affairs and in this parliament. finally, on macro-financial issues, it is true that we need to improve the supervisory and regulatory framework – it is absolutely true at european level and at a global level – but we will not put an end to these bubbles, this excess of liquidity, this risk to financial stability unless we seriously tackle global imbalances. this is the real origin of these imbalances. we cannot solve the current or previous problems, or perhaps the next challenges to the functioning of the global economy, without tackling the global imbalances that
