member of the commission. − mr president, before going into the context i would like to thank the committee on agriculture and rural development and the rapporteur, mr tabajdi, for this very interesting and important report. parliament’s report clearly underlines the benefits of biogas production to the agricultural sector, but also to society. i fully agree with the emphasis placed on the development of biogas production. it has environmental benefits by reducing the emission of powerful climate-altering gases, such as methane and nitrous oxides. for this reason, biogas production further enhances the environmental sustainability of agriculture – there has already been a 20% reduction in greenhouse gas emission since 1990 – and it also has obvious economic advantages as a useful alternative to natural gas in a situation where we now see that oil prices have exceeded usd 100 per barrel. the production of biogas from agricultural feedstocks has more than doubled in the period from 2004 to 2006. overall biogas production is increasing but i think that we can clearly do more. there is a large untapped potential in biogas production within the european union. on the commission side we are fully aware of this and we have put in place a number of important instruments to promote the production of biogas. our current green electricity directive with implementing legislation in some member states is an example of an important driving force. rural development policy also favours the development of biogas production. member states have the possibility to support investments, technical assistance and cooperatives and other activities enhancing biogas production and biogas use. implementation of the rural development programmes from the period 2007 to 2013 has only just started but i find that member states’ first programming is very promising and i am confident that biogas-related measures will be among those with the highest uptake in the area when we talk about bio-energy. measures included in the commission’s recent energy and climate package will give a further boost to biogas production in the coming years. particularly important is the 20% target for renewable energy. it is expected that biogas will contribute significantly to reaching those targets. biogas will also play an important role in delivering the 20% reduction targets for greenhouse gas emission from sectors that are not participating in the emission trading system. therefore we are in a very positive situation where we can kill two birds with one stone. i am convinced that biogas production will be a key element in the european union strategy to combat climate change and to make it possible for us to meet the kyoto targets. i agree with you that a coherent biogas policy is important. the eu initiatives are in my view coherent and they go in the same direction. nevertheless, i believe that this policy could be most effectively fleshed out and implemented at regional or at national level on the basis of local resources, needs and economic realities. in this respect, i welcome the recommendations concerning the simplification of the current legislative framework. they are in line with our ongoing discussions on simplification and better regulation, which represent a commission strategy very high on the agenda. finally i have to say that i have doubts on specific targets for biogas, and i heard a remark by the rapporteur. i think that the 20% target for renewable energy already encompasses biogas. biogas can also contribute to the achievement of the 10% biofuel target. if we introduce a special biogas target we would run the risk of not being focused enough. setting a specific target for biogas would introduce further administrative burdens for private operators and public authorities. in my view it would also lead to excessive political pressure for a particular type of renewable energy, which could be unfortunate draft opinion of the consultative committee on industry, research and energy. - madam president, i have to say that i am very sorry. i have the opinion of the committee on industry responsible for energy policy. i have no personal opinion on this, but the committee adopted my draft opinion by 45 votes to 0 with 0 abstentions. the committee on industry is aware of the positive contribution of biogas not only from manure, as the rapporteur says, but from all organic waste. we have stressed that competition for food is increasingly a problem, that there is a need to discuss this, that gas supply must be provided without discrimination, that new processes for second generation technical biogas should be encouraged. we have discussed the role of green genetic technology in relation to biogas and we believe that the young and innovative biogas sector needs start-up funding but not permanent subsidies. we also want uniform funding instruments at european level, and our 13 points make this clear: we want a simplified approval procedure for biogas plants. the committee on energy has not called for four new directives to be tabled, as the honourable member has done in his draft report. i share the commissioner's view that we do not need new directives, but that we should give biogas a proper role in the existing renewable energy directives. in this respect the committee on industry has made a slightly different assessment of the situation from the leading committee on agriculture!
the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used effectively. the commission has already made a number of proposals. as the shadow rapporteur for the epp group, i can largely agree with this report. the rapporteur has done a good job. i can emphasise what has already been said: biogas can make a significant contribution to achieving our renewable energy targets and to reducing our use of fossil fuels and thus our co2 emissions. the first condition is, of course, that the potential of biogas is exploited. in germany there are many biogas plants which produce only electricity. only about 38% of the energy available is used, and over 60% of the energy is blown into the environment as waste heat. this cannot be the point of biogas production! i therefore think it is right that the report calls for biogas to be fed into the gas grid. we must go in these two directions: either use waste heat for electricity generation or feed biogas directly into the grid. here we can achieve a high degree of efficiency in both procedures. i also believe that modern plant breeding can produce even better plants. but i don't necessarily think that you need genetic engineering to do that. i've heard from plant breeders that with conventional plant breeding, you can double the yield of biogas plants in good conditions. we can harvest about 5,000 litres of heating oil equivalent per hectare using biogas. with good crops created in the future by plant breeding, we can harvest up to 10,000 litres per hectare. this is a good way for biogas to contribute to climate change mitigation.
the commission is therefore proposing to amend the proposal. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. i would like to congratulate mr tabajdi on his balanced report. i think he has succeeded in showing the importance of biogas for a sustainable energy mix of the future. as a member of the european parliament for the north german region, i am particularly aware of the potential of biogas as an important and versatile form of bioenergy from agriculture. germany - and in particular my home state of lower saxony - is one of the leading countries in europe in terms of biogas plants. but we should not fail to develop strict and clear criteria for biogas technology as part of the introduction of an eu certification scheme for biofuels. this should also apply in particular to imports. however, no additional administrative burden should be imposed on local producers. this is the only way to effectively address concerns about the use of cereals and foodstuffs for biogas production, as food production must remain a priority for agriculture. only in this way can and will biogas technology make a meaningful contribution to energy security, to reducing our dependence on foreign imports, to climate protection and to rural development. european research and development programmes can also provide efficiency gains.
the commission is therefore proposing to extend the period of validity of the directive to the period of 1 january 1999. the commission has already taken a number of measures to combat fraud. the rapporteur has put forward a good report and he has put it to the committee on agriculture and rural development, and that is a good thing. we have just heard from mr langen that the industry is clearly seeing competition here. it's always like this: when something is successful, the industry tries to take it over. it doesn't have to be good. when i think that the pioneers of the biogas plants were farmers who were ridiculed 10, 15, 20 years ago when they tried to get energy out of the manure. because that's the idea, to put it bluntly, of turning shit into gold. the commission has already proposed a number of measures to improve the quality of the foodstuffs. and what is left of the manure is also a better fertilizer, more versatile than aggressive fertilizer. in other words, biogas is in the same category as renewable energy sources such as wind, water, sun, wood, and is indeed a renewable energy source if it is produced from organic waste. if we have a situation like we had last year and the year before in the dairy sector, where you paid 23.5 for the milk, the relative advantage of putting the corn directly into the biogas plant was much higher than if you sent the corn through the cow first and produced milk. this means that there is always a correspondence between food prices and energy prices, and this is due to the fact that we have an energy input law - at least in germany, but also in some other countries - which allows a better utilization of plant products in the energy sector than in the food sector. and here we have to be careful not to get into a competitive situation. the competition between the tank and the plate is there when we do it wrong. but if we take a balance sheet on biofuels, it is negative, whereas we had a positive balance sheet on biogas - and on biogas for cars. it is therefore essential that the policy of support and the policy of remuneration give a clear preference to smaller installations so that there is no migration to industrial production.
the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used effectively. the commission is not prepared to accept this. there is agreement that we want to reduce the harmful effects on man and the environment of pesticide use. in order to identify these effects, indicators need to be developed. to develop them, you need data. the collection of such data is the subject of this directive. i emphasize this to make it clear that this is not about the authorization of plant protection products or their use, but only about collecting data which will be useful for developing appropriate indicators. there is agreement on that. we have also, as mr staes has rightly said, made a very diligent effort to reach common positions, and we have succeeded to an astonishing extent. we agreed that the scope of application should be extended to the non-agricultural sector. we have also found a common position on the protection of trade and business secrets. two things have remained open between us: the first point is the inclusion of biocides. i fully share the commissioner's position. there are no objections in principle, but we do not have the knowledge at the moment to take this step in a meaningful way. i have no reservations, as i said, about the principle. this can be done at the appropriate time. the second point is more important. we have expressed our reservations about the inclusion of not only the use but also the production of plant protection products in the scope of application, because production as such does not give any information on the use. products are exported to third countries, products are stored before being used. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. i would like to say, however, mr staes, that if we succeed in sticking to the compromises we have worked out, your report will not fail in our final vote.
the commission is therefore proposing to extend the period of validity of the directive to the period of 1 january 1999. the commission is not prepared to accept this. i would like to congratulate the rapporteur. here in the eu pesticide package we are also discussing how we can - and this is our aim - protect people, animals and the environment from harm caused by dangerous pesticides. sufficient data is the basic requirement for this objective. i hope that this vote sends a strong signal to environmental and health protection. the collection and disclosure of data is not about trade secrets, but about ensuring the right of consumers to information and transparency. i support making as much data as possible available on the internet. that would also be fully consistent with my report on the pesticide authorization. the experience of authorisation shows that we need reliable figures on pesticide use in europe and harmonised data collection methods. only when good data is available can we hope to receive less misunderstanding and misinformation. finally, something that is not in the statistical report but is nevertheless very important to me. we have also adopted a pesticide passport for wholesale and retail trade at the first reading on the authorization of pesticides. again, this is data on pesticide use. the wholesale and retail trade want this data, and i hope the member states will not stand in the way of that. this is also a good complement to the statistics on pesticide data. i hope we will be united in the goal of achieving better protection of man, animals and the environment through more reliable figures and data.
the commission has already done so. the plant protection products are on the test bench and the statistics are part of a package which also includes the marketing authorization regulation and the directive on the sustainable use of plant protection products. the whole package aims to minimise the impact of plant protection products on both human health and the environment. the competitive pressures in the single market and the cross-border aspects of the environment require a common approach. but the access of food from around the world to our markets also makes it clear that restrictions must be appropriate to be effective. it is not in the interests of anyone if our fruit and vegetables and meat come only from third countries, because production is made too difficult by imposing conditions. we have no influence in europe on food from third countries. the only way is to establish maximum residue levels, and this is where we are still not properly positioned, let alone where we can have a pesticide pass. it is right to keep records and statistics on the sale of plant protection products in order to monitor the trends and developments in plant protection. the stated objective is to reduce risk. the collection of data shall ensure comparability, while minimising reporting requirements. the aim of registering the flow of substances is clearly out of the question here, since it is not yet clear whether the substance will be used to produce a plant protection product, a biocide or perhaps even a medicinal product. biocides must be considered separately and we are awaiting the commission's proposal on the authorization and use of biocides. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. the illegal use of plant protection products must be targeted more strongly. we need to strengthen the controls on existing legislation. i do not think that statistics can help here. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect.

the chairman of the council. - i am very pleased to present to you today the main themes of the european council which starts tomorrow. in line with the tradition of the spring summits, this session will also focus on economic issues, in particular the lisbon strategy, as well as climate change and energy and financial stability. the presidency looks forward to this exchange of views with the european parliament and i can assure you that parliament's views on the matters on the agenda for tomorrow's sitting will be duly taken into account. we are all aware that the european union is facing new challenges today, and that globalisation is bringing new opportunities, not only in the economic but also in the social and cultural fields. and these opportunities have already brought benefits to the union. we are also aware that globalisation also requires adaptation and the search for the right responses from the union and the member states. this is what the european council will be dealing with. the global economic environment is in a period of testing. we've been witnessing a turbulent period in the financial markets. we have seen a decline in economic activity recently due to the recession in the united states and the higher prices of oil and commodities. the foundations of the european union's economy are still firm, but in these circumstances we cannot stop, we cannot rest, we must continue with our reforms. in this context, the european council will assess the state of play of the implementation of the lisbon strategy for growth and jobs. it will welcome the positive results and confirm the good functioning of this strategy. he will stress the need to focus on implementation now, and in this spirit he will launch the new cycle of the renewed lisbon strategy. in the area of knowledge and innovation, the european council will give a new impetus to our efforts by introducing the so-called fifth freedom. it is intended to remove existing barriers to the free flow of knowledge by enhancing the cross-border mobility of researchers, students, scientists and university lecturers. the fifth freedom would, in our view, accelerate the transformation of the european union into an innovative, creative and knowledge-based economy. to strengthen the competitiveness of enterprises, in particular small and medium-sized enterprises, the european council will provide for measures to enable them to operate and develop better. it is expected to have easier access to funding sources and to strengthen incentives for innovation. the implementation of the better regulation plan will also be given high priority. the social dimension of the lisbon strategy, efforts to address demographic challenges, skills shortages and future policy measures to increase social cohesion will also receive a great deal of attention. the spring summit will instruct member states to implement the common principles of flexible security progressively, with national arrangements that ensure a balance between flexibility and security in the labour market. let me now turn to the other important matter to be considered by the european council. these are the challenges of climate change and energy. last year saw historic commitments in climate and energy policy. this year, we must focus on fulfilling them. this objective is both an economic and an ecological challenge of major long-term importance. if we respond to it with ambition, we can create a story not just of economic success, but also of environmental success. the legislative package presented by the commission is currently being considered by the council. and the first discussions reaffirmed the commitment of all member states to an ambitious response. however, it would be premature to expect that all aspects of the package would be agreed at this summit. however, we expect that it will be possible to reach an agreement on the principles and guidelines for the further consideration of the package. we expect leaders to express a desire to maintain the overall balance, while paying attention to the complexity of the package in terms of its economic and financial impact. the aim is to adopt the package as early as possible in 2009, certainly before the end of the european parliament's mandate. if all key partners are able to address the challenges of climate change, our efforts will be successful. when the copenhagen climate conference meets at the end of 2009, europe should be the leading force in negotiating an ambitious and comprehensive post-kyoto agreement. this is another reason to adopt the agreement as soon as possible in 2009. let me also briefly touch on some other energy-related issues. an efficient, functioning internal energy market is an essential condition for a reliable, sustainable and competitive energy supply in europe. in this context, we expect the european council to call for the adoption of an agreement on the third gas and electricity internal market package as soon as possible. it will also pay particular attention to further measures relating to security of supply and external energy policy. the european council will place efforts to tackle climate-related energy policy within the framework of developing new technologies and increasing investment in them. this was recently defined in the strategic energy technology plan. this would further contribute to the competitiveness of our companies. the heads of state or government will also consider the conclusions of the joint communication of the secretary-general, high representative solana and the commission on the impact of climate change on international security. the complexity of climate change requires more comprehensive policy coordination and the european council will call for a thorough follow-up to the report. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, allow me to touch on the third main item on the agenda of the european council. it is an exchange of views on the recent developments in international financial markets. the situation in the international financial system remains uncertain. to manage the risk of their impact on the real economy, the economic and financial policies of the european union should be geared to ensuring macroeconomic stability and implementing the structural reform agenda. the union's response has been prepared by the finance ministers and some adjustments in the financial markets have been under way since last autumn. the european central bank, national authorities, the institutions of the european union and financial institutions have taken a series of measures to stabilise the situation. however, the primary responsibility for risk management remains with the individual financial institutions and investors. the current situation has highlighted the need to further strengthen the financial stability framework through enhanced prudential supervision and improved financial crisis management tools. we expect the european council to call for action in four main areas: improving transparency for investors, markets and regulators, improving valuation standards, consolidating the credit rating framework and strengthening risk management in the financial sector, and finally improving market functioning, including the role of credit rating agencies. the spring european council, which starts tomorrow, will be devoted primarily to the implementation of the commitments made. the presidency wants to accelerate the work of transforming europe into the president of the commission. − mr president, traditionally, the spring european council is the time when we review the lisbon strategy for growth and jobs, and this meeting will be more important than most. i would like to start by thanking the slovenian presidency for the very careful preparation of this spring summit. whatever other messages come out of the european council this week, one should be clear: the lisbon strategy is working. no fewer than 6.5 million jobs have been created in the european union in the last two years. unemployment is at its lowest level for 25 years. the employment rate stands at 66%, getting close to the lisbon target of 70%. what is more, job creation has gone hand in hand with productivity improvements. productivity is now growing faster in the european union than in the united states. these are no mean achievements. of course, the lisbon process cannot shield us from negative economic developments whose origin lies outside europe. in today’s inter-connected economy, that is impossible. we have had to trim our growth forecasts slightly for this year but we are still predicting growth of 2% – a very respectable performance. the reforms already carried out have made our economies more resilient and flexible. this has left us better able to cope with external shocks. of course when conditions deteriorate it becomes all the more important to reassure those that feel threatened by an economic downturn. europe needs to protect – but it must avoid the temptation of becoming protectionist. a retreat into protectionism would be madness. europe has been a huge winner from globalisation. with just 7% of the world’s population, europe accounts for 30% of economic output. we account for seven of the ten most competitive nations in the world and, despite the rise of china and india, europe remains the world’s largest trading power. so europe has every reason to approach the future with confidence. at the same time, we need to remain vigilant and cautious as to further developments. but our general line should be one of confidence. it will not be with pessimism that we will win the next economic battles. this is what has inspired our reaction to the financial turmoil and our policy papers on the financial situation and on sovereign wealth funds, which are also on the table of the european council. and we hope the european council will support our proposals for a common european response to these challenges. when i say that the lisbon strategy is working – and indeed it is – this does not mean that all is rosy and that we can rest on our laurels. i have said, and the commission has said, time and time again, there is no room for complacency, especially when the economic situation seems to be deteriorating globally. a lot has to be done. in many regions of europe unemployment remains a serious problem. there are special social categories that are very much affected. rising energy and food prices are fuelling inflation, eating into the purchasing power, especially of those who depend on salaries and pensions for their income. so we need to continue our efforts. but the lisbon strategy is not a static process. far from it. the commission strategic report sets out a series of new policy initiatives to make europe even more resilient to economic turmoil, and to reinforce european efforts to shape and fully benefit from globalisation. first, the most important area. the most important area is people. the key to overcoming poverty and inequality is driving up standards of education and training throughout the union, making sure they are available to all. we have chosen to focus on one of the most vulnerable groups: early school-leavers. today in europe, one in six young people still leaves school without qualifications. one in five 15-year-olds does not have adequate reading skills. we cannot afford to allow their talents to go to waste. we must give young people the skills they need to realise their potential. another key pillar of the lisbon strategy we have returned to is research and innovation. to keep investment coming in, europe must increase its relative attractiveness. we need a fifth freedom in europe – the free movement of knowledge – to complement the other four freedoms on which the single market rests. we need to support open innovation but at the same time we need to ensure that knowledge is suitably protected by european patents and copyright. here i would like to welcome the adoption of the european institute of innovation and technology yesterday by this house. this is a crucial moment for europe. i would like to congratulate the european parliament on this achievement and to thank you for the support you have given to my proposal, which i remember met with so much resistance when i put it forward three years ago. but, thanks to the good cooperation between parliament and the commission and the member states, at the end we have got that agreement. the third priority we have looked at is the business environment. we need a single market that works for europe and in particular for smes, which are the backbone of our economy and the place where most jobs are created. that is why i will be asking the european council tomorrow to endorse the idea of a small business act to remove the impediments to the creation and the growth of smes. we have to keep in mind that the most important thing we can give to smes is a real internal market. this is the main difference between europe and the united states of america, when it comes to smes, not because of specific legislation. a small company in the united states can start in one state but can immediately reach the entire internal market of the united states. in europe it is still not like that. in europe there are a lot of barriers in practical terms in going from one country to the next. so we really need to complete the internal market if we want to develop smes and if you want more growth and more employment in europe. (applause) the final lisbon pillar we have revisited in our strategic report is energy and climate change, the defining challenge of our generation. it may be early days for the energy and climate package. but, as this house knows well, the momentum cannot be allowed to slip. the timing of an agreement is critical to its success. the earlier it comes, the lower the cost of adjustment, the bigger the benefits for early movers. and it is crucial to our number one goal: agreeing a comprehensive international agreement in copenhagen next year. the more countries are involved and the closer their ambitions are to ours, the more we will have a level playing field. nothing will bring this closer than the european union showing that it means business by reaching agreement by the end of this year. so i am really determined – the commission is really determined – to work with the member states so that we can have a basic political agreement on the energy internal market and on the climate protection and renewables package by the end of this year. of course, we would also like to have the final legislative process concluded with the european parliament at the beginning of next year. it is of course important to link the climate protection strategy with the internal market for energy. we all know this is essential for our vision of competitive, secure and sustainable energy for europe. i have been glad to see this dossier accelerating over the past weeks, and we are committed to finding ways of ensuring that the genuine market opening targeted in our original proposals is realised. the commission remains fully committed to the realisation of ownership unbundling or its functional equivalent. the efforts of this house to be ready for a first reading by june are central. reform is not about rolling back valuable social advances or our social market economy; it is about equipping people to succeed in times of change, giving them the chance to take control of their own lives. it is about modernising our social systems and securing their sustainability. access, opportunity and solidarity must be the watchwords and will be at the heart of the renewed social agenda that the commission will present before summer. it is about a dynamic business environment where entrepreneurs are spending their time and resources on producing high-quality goods and services that people from all over the world want to buy, not on filling in unnecessary forms and having to battle every day against red tape. it is also about transforming europe into a low-carbon economy that is good for the environment and good for business. an economy that provides rising living standards but which does not cost the earth. i am glad to see that the hard work of the last few years on the revamped lisbon agenda has helped foster a broad consensus on where we stand and where we want to go. this house has been a consistent source of critical support, and i want to thank you for this. i was pleased to note the large degree of support for the lisbon strategy expressed in the european parliament’s resolution of 20 february on the input for the 2008 spring council. i have also seen the amendments that this house voted the same day to the broad economic policy guidelines. i agree with the issues you emphasise, and indeed they are already part and parcel of european union policies on the basis of proposals from the european commission: social inclusion, sustainability of public finance, the need to fight inflation, r&d, improved economic policy coordination, the promotion of entrepreneurship and innovation, the external dimension of the internal market, and climate change and energy. so let us be clear: the commission agrees with these priorities. after consulting with various stakeholders, including the member states, the commission proposed in december to keep the guidelines of the strategy as they were, given their inbuilt flexibility, which allows adaptation to the evolving circumstances and accommodation of the priorities i have just cited and which the commission endorses. keeping the guidelines sends a much-needed signal of stability and predictability to member states and economic operators alike and, in doing so, reinforces the likelihood of delivery. as the presidency of the council just stated, the priority now is delivery. we have to deliver concrete results and we have to show consistency. this being said, after contacts with parliament’s committee on economic and monetary affairs, the commission tried to broker a compromise with the inclusiveness, is europe’s best response to the challenges of globalisation. (parliament adopted the resolution) almost exactly fifty years ago, on 19 march 1958, the joint parliamentary assembly of the three institutions - the european economic community, the european atomic energy community and the european coal and steel community - met for the first time here in strasbourg, in what was then the maison de l'europe, and was composed of representatives of the peoples of the states associated in the community, as stipulated in the treaties of rome, which had come into force a few weeks earlier. we are commemorating this anniversary today because we are in the continuity of this parliamentary assembly with its original 142 members . the first president of the joint parliamentary assembly was the great robert schuman. in his opening speech, he said that the assembly had an essential role to play in the development of a european spirit, and that 'the assembly has been and will remain the melting pot for this'. i think that is still true today. at the same time, he reminded his colleagues at the inaugural sitting that parliamentary work with 142 members - from six countries at the time - requires all the discipline, which is of course all the more true today, with 785 members from 27 countries, as we all know! shortly after the founding assembly, our predecessors began informally referring to their institution as the 'european parliament' - a phrase not found in the founding treaties of the european communities. four years later, in march 1962, the parliamentary assembly also decided to call itself the 'european parliament'. although the treaties establishing the european communities provided that 'the assembly should draw up drafts for direct general elections in accordance with a uniform procedure in all the member states' and that the council of ministers should 'unanimously adopt the relevant provisions and recommend them to the member states for adoption in accordance with their constitutional requirements', it was not until 1976 that the council of ministers, on the basis of a recommendation from the european parliament on 20 september 1976, adopted a corresponding legal act which decided to hold general and direct elections to the european parliament. the parliamentary assembly originally had little in the way of rights of its own. our predecessors foresaw that you would have a long road ahead of you in the process of european parliamentarisation, which would require from them and from the generations that followed a clear compass, bold initiative and patient perseverance. the european parliament has gradually acquired more and more rights, has become more and more aware of its responsibilities and its possibilities, and i think it is a great honour to be able to say this on behalf of all those present here today. (applause from the centre) we represent almost 500 million citizens of the union. we are the reflection of all the political currents in the european union. we are the freely elected parliament of the european union, united in the struggle for the best convictions. we have become self-confident and a force in european politics. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. the main stages of this process, which began in 1958, have always been milestones on a common path towards european unification: in 1971 the european community received its own budget; the european parliament has since then played a major part in the adoption of the budget. in 1979, the first direct elections to the european parliament were held. in 1986, the single european act finally gave legal force to the concept of the 'european parliament'. fifteen years ago, with the entry into force of the maastricht treaty, the european parliament was given full co-decision in the first areas of community policy, and thus the possibility of shaping draft legislation in a substantial way and, if necessary, of preventing it from being adopted against the wishes of the council of ministers. the treaty of amsterdam further extended the right to vote. the lisbon treaty will de facto make the codecision procedure the rule of european law and therefore appropriately also speak of the ordinary legislative procedure. today we are 785 meps from 27 european nations. we represent over 150 national political parties, most of which are grouped in seven political groups. we are a joint legislative and budgetary body, equal to the council of ministers. we control the european commission, we elect its president or its president, and the commission needs our confidence to be in office. we are advocates of the primacy of community law. we are the chamber of citizens of the european union. the lisbon treaty, which we approved three weeks ago, will further strengthen our rights. in future, major issues affecting citizens in the european union today will only be decided by a majority vote in the european parliament. this is also true of the important questions of internal and legal policy. all this is not a cause for complacency and it was by no means the result of a natural process. we fought for it! i would like to thank the many colleagues who, over the past five decades, under the leadership of our presidents, have worked to strengthen parliamentarism in the context of european unification and have done so with merit. i would like to thank the members of the european parliament yesterday and today. (applause from the centre) jean monnet once said: 'nothing is possible without people, nothing lasts without institutions.' i would also like to mention paul henri spaak, the first president of the joint parliamentary assembly of the european coal and steel community (ecsc), the predecessor of the european parliament, which played a major role in the preparation of the treaties of rome by its report after the messina conference in june 1955. the path of parliamentary democracy in the european union has followed a logic similar to that which we know from the history of the european nation states. the institutional balance we have created today between the national and european levels is a great success of the balancing of the different levels of co-government in europe. the european parliament has a duty to ensure that the european parliament is properly represented in the european parliament. i am pleased to see that almost all the national parliaments of the member states of the european union are represented here today at a high level. (applause from the centre) i ask all of you - us members of the european parliament and the national parliaments - to continue to work for this good cooperation. the lisbon treaty and the charter of fundamental rights will make a decisive contribution to the realisation of democracy and parliamentarism at all levels in the european union. we can be proud of the fact that we have always supported the reform treaty and the charter of fundamental rights without question, ladies and gentlemen. (applause from the centre) we need the critical public, the critical support of our work. but we also have a right to fairness. the european union, with its diversity, is more complex than any other community in the world. i would ask the media to take this into account, since we urgently need them to communicate with the citizens. the european union must not be used as a scapegoat for national failures. (applause from the centre) one of the greatest achievements of our european vision in the last 50 years has been the establishment of democracy and freedom throughout europe. the accession of estonia, latvia, lithuania, poland, the czech republic, slovakia, hungary, slovenia, bulgaria, romania and the reunified germany remains an achievement we dreamed of and which has become a reality in our own day. today we are as the berlin declaration of 25 march 2007 says united in our happiness. this is a cause for great joy. the first step in taking stock of the past 50 years is to look to the future. we should be self-critical in remembering which aspects of european parliamentarism remain unsatisfactory to this day: unlike the national parliaments, we still lack the possibility of deciding within the budgetary procedure whether to raise our own financial resources. parliamentary rule is usually accompanied by parliamentary control of the military; the european union's common foreign, security and defence policy will remain incomplete without a sensible combination of national and european responsibilities. we still lack a common, uniform electoral law. we are therefore missing an important prerequisite for having effective european parties running with common lists in the european parliament elections. the european parliament has been fighting for its place since the first meeting of the european parliamentary assembly, with patience, long breath and a clear compass. that's the way it is, that's the way it should be, and that's the way it has to be. as a directly elected supranational representative of the people, the european parliament - and i notice it and you notice it when you travel around the world - has become a model for similar efforts in other regions of the world. when robert schuman took office as the first president of the european parliamentary assembly on 19 march 1958, such a positive development of parliamentarism in europe was hardly foreseeable. but robert schuman had a vision. he spoke of the european idea which had to be revived, of 'la relance de l'idée européenne'. what could be a better guiding motive for the task ahead of us today, after the crisis-ridden developments surrounding the failed constitutional treaty? in his short speech on 19 march 1958, robert schuman expressed concern that a technocratic view of things could lead to european unity being marginalized. that is true today as well. robert schuman was realistic, modest and clear in describing the possibilities of the joint parliamentary assembly, which he chaired until 1960: 'we want to contribute', he said in his warm, humanitarian voice, 'to create a new core of the european structure'. robert schuman concluded his first speech as president of the european parliamentary assembly by declaring that he was committed to the unification of our continent, to the unification of europe, which must be seen as a community of values of the free peoples of our continent: 'ainsi seulement l'europe réussira à mettre en valeur le patrimoine total qui est commun à tous les pays libres'. i would like to follow that up. the european union is a community of values. our institutions are not an end in themselves, they serve our values: human dignity, human rights, democracy, the rule of law, economic and social well-being; the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial instruments are used in a proper manner. europe means respect for one another, respect for our diversity, respect for the dignity of all our member states, large and small. this respect cannot be imposed, but it is the necessary condition for our mutual understanding and for our common action. the respect for european law, which enables us to balance our interests peacefully and to resolve conflicts peacefully, must be supplemented by the unwritten rules of our european coexistence: respect for one another. (applause from the centre) i would like to encourage and call for this respect for one another, wherever we stand politically. if we can achieve this mutual respect - tolerance for each other while respecting our own convictions, but a commitment to compromise - then the european union and the european parliament can be a model for peace in the world. our european heritage is anchored in the freedom and unity of our peoples, united in the european union. we honour robert schuman and all the members of the first european parliamentary assembly by striving to prove worthy of their succession by working for a responsible, open and citizen-oriented european parliament, which must also be determined to take a political lead when necessary. if we continue to do so, we need not fear the judgment of those who will follow us and, in 2058, the year of the 100th anniversary of the european parliament, will assess our work today. the european parliament has been a great help to the people of europe in the past, and it is a great help to us in the present. (applause from the centre and the right)
the chairman of the council. - "my speech cannot be emotionally cold. " with these words, robert schuman, the first president of the european parliamentary assembly, addressed your house for the first time on 19 march 1958. fifty years later, on your anniversary, we feel the same way. i am not speaking to the 142 national members of the european parliament, but to the 785 directly elected members of the european parliament. looking back on the journey and the flowering of european democracy over the past five decades can fill us with pride and a deep sense of gratitude to the founding fathers of the european idea. at the same time, it places on us a responsibility to do our part to continue the european story of peace, cooperation and prosperity. let's turn our memories back to 1958, to a society facing the aftermath of two devastating wars, to a world of bipolar balance of power between east and west, to the cold war, the cuban revolution, the first chip, nuclear testing and the launch of satellites into space. the six member states of the european union then brought together 168 million europeans, healing the wounds of the post-war period, boosting economic growth and securing an area of freedom and democracy with the euro-atlantic alliance. sadly, much of the rest of europe lived in a totalitarian environment, stagnating or even declining economically and civilisationally. in 2008, we face a completely different picture: the multipolar world is no longer about economic or political competition, but increasingly about cooperation in finding answers to current challenges. the abolition of borders that have divided europe from the berlin wall, the iron curtain to internal border controls continues at the end of this month with the abolition of air borders within the enlarged schengen area. the european union today is more than three times the size it was fifty years ago, has three times as many people, 23 official languages, a strengthened internal market and a common currency, and its citizens live on average about eight years longer. twenty-seven heads of state and government, more than a third of whom lived under totalitarian regimes 20 years ago, will be sitting down tomorrow to decide. the wider europe is also now almost entirely free and democratic. this is an achievement that should be recognized and celebrated. the life and work of the european parliament from 1958 to the present day clearly reflect the progress made in integration over the past 50 years. after an initial consultative role, you acquired the first powers in the field of the european budget in the early 1970s and marked the first direct elections at the end of the 1970s. the new treaties give you greater powers to adopt legislation and appoint the highest european political representatives. the new european commission cannot be without your trust either. just as the treaties of rome in 1958 gave the parliamentary assembly new responsibilities, the treaty of lisbon fifty years later represents a major step forward for the european parliament. the codecision procedure will be extended to almost all european policies, and parliament's role in democratic control, the conclusion of international agreements and the appointment of the european high representatives will be strengthened. i am very pleased that you approved the report on the lisbon reform treaty by such a convincing majority in the plenary last month. i also congratulate all the member states that have already successfully completed their ratification procedures and hope that all the others will soon follow. if the first 50 years of the european union were devoted to the european agenda, our political and economic development and reforms, the next 50 years will surely be more focused on the global agenda. the list for tomorrow's european council is a good illustration of this. it is clear that we will only be able to respond adequately to the lisbon challenges, environmental and energy issues and financial market shocks if we take account of global trends and global actors and integrate all of this into our activities. this also applies to the field of human rights and intercultural dialogue, where you undoubtedly play a leading role in the european parliament. on behalf of the european council, i take this opportunity to commend you for your active role in raising awareness of human rights violations, in election observation and in the work of your delegations in international institutions such as the un human rights council. your role in the framework of joint parliamentary assemblies is also important, as it adds value to the european union's policies towards third countries and regions. through your activities and meetings with high-ranking guests, you will reinforce one of the fundamental european traditions: that mutual respect and understanding are the foundations of coexistence both at european and global level. the range of activities of the european union is ever-increasing, but the same rule applies to all: success grows in direct proportion to unity. unity between member states, sectors, stakeholders and generations, between regional, national, european and global factors. the institutions of the european union must set an example in this respect. "every man begins the world anew. only institutions that nurture the collective experience mature. " jean monnet brings us one step closer to explaining why the vision of the european union is often still different from reality, why many europeans, despite the more than obvious successes of the last fifty years, still doubt the merits of european integration. to understand and appreciate the freedom, peace, diversity, the boundlessness, the benefits and the prospects of a united europe, we must always be aware that there are other, much worse alternatives. it is therefore our common task to revive the collective european experience. it can give us the strength to face the challenges of our time. we must combine the past with the future. if we had not joined forces 50 years ago, we would probably not be living in peace and prosperity today. and the same is true for the next 50 years. if we don't work together to find low-carbon and energy-efficient solutions, we're not going to be able to slow down climate change. we will face more and more floods, hurricanes, droughts, new diseases, threatened ecosystems and climate refugees. it is essential that the results of european decisions and actions are sufficiently concrete and tangible to enable citizens to understand the decisive importance of the european union in maintaining and improving the quality of life. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i thank you for your contribution to the development of the european union over the past five decades. i know what that time in our generation's lives was like, because i was born the same year as the european parliament. i wish you much success in your work towards the end of this mandate and beyond, and a wealth of fresh ideas and unwavering commitment to the development of european values, european democracy and the european way of life. i am convinced that the next round of anniversaries of this european home of democracy will enable us to celebrate once again the progress europe has made, which is visible everywhere. i am not going to go into detail. i would like to tell you today how i dealt with the incidents of serious disturbance during the formal signing of the charter of fundamental rights on wednesday 12 december, here in strasbourg, which you will all remember. after the conference of presidents had dealt with these incidents, i invited a number of colleagues to speak on the basis of rule 147 of the rules of procedure in order to hear them before a decision was taken on possible sanctions. i explained to each of the colleagues the reason for the invitation to the interview. the basis of parliamentarism is freedom of speech. in a democratic parliament no speaker should be prevented from speaking by the systematic shouting of colleagues who hold a different opinion. this is of course all the more true of speakers who are here in the house as guests and representatives of other institutions. i made it clear that i had invited the members because, even after i had asked them to remain quiet in the chamber, they had continued to try to prevent the speakers from speaking by shouting. the sanction should not be imposed because they held up posters and banners. so it's about restricting free speech. following these discussions, i have decided to take the following measures in accordance with rule 147 (3) of the rules of procedure: in nine cases, the loss of entitlement to daily allowance for a period of between two and five days, in one case, for five days, in six cases for three days, in two cases for two days and in another case, the issuing of a reprimand. i should like to read to you first what i said to my colleagues in my letter informing them of the measure in question. i quote: 'i fully understand your right and the right of any member to oppose the adoption of the charter of fundamental rights or the treaty of lisbon and to express this position in accordance with the rules laid down in the rules of procedure. i also have a certain understanding of the great emotions that such topics sometimes bring. however, i believe that a line must be drawn between legitimate conduct under the rules of procedure and the disturbances as they occurred on 12 december. we cannot allow actions which would prevent other members or official guests - in this case the presidents of other institutions of the european union - from speaking with dignity and without deliberate interruption after they have been given the floor in accordance with rule 9 (2) of the rules of procedure, within the framework of the agenda decided by parliament itself. the very essence of parliamentarism and democracy is that freedom of expression also respects the right of others, in this case those who have been given the floor to speak in the plenary. in accordance with the chairman of the council. - first of all, i would like to congratulate the reports by the honourable members mr swoboda and mr meijer on the progress of croatia and the former yugoslav republic of macedonia. we are also pleased that the european parliament has included a debate on the progress of both candidates on the agenda. the slovenian presidency attaches particular importance to the european integration of the western balkan countries. in this context, i would remind you that the ministers for foreign affairs, at their informal meeting at the end of march, sent a positive message to the western balkans region on its european perspective. we consider that such a message is welcome and appropriate in this difficult period for the region. first of all, as regards croatia, i would like to stress that the accession negotiations with croatia are proceeding as planned. and here i would like to express my agreement with the assessment of the honourable member swobode that croatia has made substantial progress in meeting the requirements of the accession process over the past two years. sixteen of the 35 negotiating chapters have been opened, two chapters have already been provisionally closed. two accession conferences with croatia are planned in april and june, and if the criteria for opening chapters are met, some new chapters will be opened at these two accession conferences. i would stress that the slovenian presidency is committed to continuing the process of enlargement of the european union and to further progress in the negotiations. however, i would stress that the speed of the negotiations depends mainly on the candidate country and its progress in meeting the conditions. these are set out in the negotiating framework, the revised partnership for accession adopted by the council in february this year and other acts. i repeat, croatia has made significant progress, but the fact is that we still have a lot of work to do. in future, as mr swoboda points out, even more attention will have to be paid to the further transposition and effective implementation of the acquis communautaire. croatia should continue its efforts to meet the conditions and to make faster progress. in this context, i would like to highlight in particular: judicial and administrative reform, the fight against corruption, economic reform, minority rights, the return of refugees and full cooperation with the international criminal tribunal for the former yugoslavia. it is also essential, on the basis of the documents i have listed, that croatia continues to pursue good neighbourly relations, which of course includes efforts to resolve outstanding issues. i should like to continue with the former yugoslav republic of macedonia: as mr meijer points out in his report, it is the only country with candidate status since 2005 which has not yet opened accession negotiations. we believe that this should be exceeded this year, if the conditions are met. the main message of a recent european commission document was therefore that the autumn progress report on the former yugoslav republic of macedonia could be positive, provided the key priority tasks are fulfilled. and a similar message was sent from an informal meeting of foreign ministers in slovenia at the end of march. in this context, it should be borne in mind that the country has already demonstrated its role as a major factor of stability in the region. this role should be recognised and positive signals should be given to encourage this country to continue its constructive role in the region and to pursue reforms. one such signal is the recent launch of negotiations on a graduated visa regime, or visa liberalisation dialogue. we agree with the assessment of the rapporteur, mr meijer, that the government in skopje is consistently implementing the ohrid agreement, in particular in the area of decentralisation and the representation of ethnic minorities in public administration. we want to see progress as soon as possible in resolving some of the remaining issues that are critical to the albanian community. slovenia, as the presidency of the council of the european union, encourages all political parties to strengthen political dialogue and inter-ethnic cooperation in order to achieve the next step in the process of integration into the european union this year. in this context, i would like to express our sincere regret that the last negotiations on the name issue have not produced the desired results. we also regret that the former yugoslav republic of macedonia has not received an invitation to join nato. given the great effort the state has put into obtaining the invitation, we hope that it will soon join the other two candidates who have received the invitation. in a statement after the nato summit, the slovenian presidency called for the name negotiations to continue and be concluded as soon as possible. it called on all political leaders in the former yugoslav republic of macedonia to maintain the consensus already reached on the country's european and euro-atlantic future. at the same time, it recommended that the state make the best use of the remaining time until the commission's regular autumn progress report.
member of the commission. − mr president, i welcome mr swoboda’s report on croatia and mr meijer’s report on the former yugoslav republic of macedonia. on croatia, i find that the swoboda report been affected by the application of the ecological and fisheries protection zone – the famous, or infamous, zerp issue. i welcome the recent decision of the sabor, the croatian parliament, to suspend the rapporteur. the commission has already made a number of proposals. the budgetary procedure this year is special, because it is the last one to be held under the rules which have been in force until now. from next year we will draw up our budget according to the procedure described in the lisbon treaty. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. we will no longer have the opportunity to correct our errors in a second reading, to amend compromises that have been reached, to correct mistakes. the first, the only reading must be valid, it must be a viable basis for negotiations with the council until the end of the year. it is important for us to stress that we expect to make preparations with the council and the commission in parallel with the 2009 budgetary procedure in order to be able to start the budgetary procedure under the lisbon treaty. the budgetary procedure we have now is somewhat different. the committee on budgets, at the instigation of the reform working group decided to no longer bring our usual guidelines in response to the commission's annual strategic planning as the first resolution to the plenary, but to bring our proposal on the budgetary framework and priorities for 2009. the resolution on the jcp is the responsibility of the political groups. it covers all policy areas. we in the committee on budgets have concentrated on the overall budgetary concerns which are of particular importance to us and have put them into 11 paragraphs. i would like to draw attention to three aspects. first, we see that our budget suit is very tightly tailored, so to speak, to fit. the margins in each category are very small. new policy priorities that urgently need budgetary support, such as the implementation of our concrete role in climate policy, cannot be funded without jeopardising old priorities. the same applies to financing growth and jobs or to a sustainable europe. if we look at category 1a, for example, we know that we cannot finance new agencies with the funds we have. we must stick to our old, but simple and very clear principle: new tasks, new money. secondly, we see that category 4 is chronically underfunded. year after year, we have the same picture there. we expect the commission to present us with a preliminary draft budget which has analysed needs in detail and is realistic. we want to use the flexibility instrument for what it was designed to do, namely for the unforeseen. we do not want to have partially or completely gone to breakfast by the end of the year. thirdly, we are determined to inform the commission of our intentions regarding pilot projects and preparatory measures before parliament's summer break. we expect the commission to leave us in the preliminary draft budget sufficient room for manoeuvre for this parliamentary instrument, in all categories. we have noted that in the tables attached to the president of the european investment bank. - mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, first of all i should like to thank you for giving me this opportunity once again to continue the dialogue with the european parliament. i think it is important that an institution like the eib should be called upon to explain itself regularly to the representatives of the european citizens. i would like to thank mr audy in particular for his report. i can testify that he put a great deal of personal effort into the drafting of this report. he has participated in many working meetings both in brussels and in luxembourg, thus following the line of the constructive dialogue we have started with his predecessors. he stressed two points in his presentation this morning. the first question, which has already been raised in previous reports - i remember mr schmidt's report, mr lipietz's report - is whether the european investment bank, because it is a bank, should be subject to supervision, to banking supervision. this is not provided for in the current state of the texts. there are, of course, controls over the european investment bank: the control of the court of auditors, in so far as the eib uses community funds, and also the control of the audit committee, which is made up of experts appointed by the governors and reporting directly to our governors. but it is true that if we want to apply best banking practice to the eib, it would probably be desirable for a specialised body to be able to verify that these practices are indeed correctly applied at the eib. theoretically, there are three possible outcomes. the first is that which is enshrined in the maastricht treaty, in article 105 (6). this would be the opportunity for the european central bank to exercise this supervisory role. the treaty provides that the council, acting unanimously, may entrust the european central bank with a task of prudential supervision. this is a theoretical possibility, but realism makes it doubtful that unanimity can be found, at least today, among the member states to entrust this new task to the european central bank. another possibility is that which we have engaged in informally, namely the use of a national regulator. at the moment, it is the luxembourg regulator, the luxembourg financial sector supervisory board, which also exercises this task with the european investment bank, in particular to verify the correct application of basel ii. a third possibility that could be explored would be to strengthen the audit committee, as provided for in our statutes, and to transform it into a quasi-banking supervisor. the amending treaty provides for an extension of this audit committee. a first step could be to appoint a number of bank supervisors, who would bring to the audit committee the experience needed to verify that the eib is indeed applying best practice in this area. the second point mr audy stressed was the special role he would like the european investment bank to play in the field of infrastructure and, more specifically, transeuropean networks. as you know, the eib already plays a relatively important role in this area. last year we financed transeuropean networks for almost nine billion euros. we use a number of instruments, including our structured finance facility which allows us to take more risks than is the norm. we did this recently, for example, on a motorway in greece. this is a good concrete example of the use of this special facility to encourage the private sector to take more risks in operating a motorway. and then, very recently, with the european commission, we have developed a new guarantee mechanism to cover a particular type of risk, the risk of insufficient traffic during the first years of operation of an infrastructure. experience has shown that the first four or five years are often the most difficult. these are years in which income is not necessarily at the expected level. this creates problems for the private operator and so, in order to encourage the private sector to finance this infrastructure, we have developed a new guarantee mechanism together with the commission. i would add that the european investment bank has taken the initiative of launching a european centre of expertise in the field of public-private partnerships in order to share our experience in this field with national representatives. this is certainly an area in which the eib is prepared to continue its work. mr staes asked a question about the anti-fraud policy. we have just published our anti-fraud policy after a consultation procedure which has required several successive rounds. in relation to the particular issue he raised, of a debarment system, a system which would therefore prohibit companies guilty of fraud or corruption from further participating in projects which we finance, we announce in this policy that we hope to be able to use the same system as the one which the commission is striving to put in place. if it was not - and we should have that clear by the end of the year - if for legal reasons we could not use the same system, then we would set up our own system of discharge. as regards our energy financing, we have revised our policy on financing energy projects in the light of the european guidelines on combating climate change. in this context, we have decided to give priority to investments that reduce co2 emissions, and this is already reflected in the figures for 2007, since the financing of projects for the production of electricity from fossil fuels now represents only 25% of our financing in the energy sector. in 2007, for example, the amount spent on renewable energy far exceeded the amount spent on these more conventional forms of energy production. finally, as regards the millennium development goals, we are of course trying to ensure that our projects contribute to the millennium development goals as much as possible. but i would draw your attention to the fact that when we act outside the european union, we act on the basis of specific mandates given to us by the european council. and the millennium development goals are not listed as such in the mandates we have received from the european council. which is why we may not be able to make a direct connection as you would have wished. finally, to mr dillen, who, as i understand it, has mentioned a project which we have financed in the democratic republic of congo, i would like to say that for several years we have not financed anything in the democratic republic of congo. our board of directors has approved the principle of funding a mining project in katanga but nothing has been disbursed for that project yet. the loan agreement hasn't been signed yet. why signing of the contract until a satisfactory agreement has been reached between the developer and the congolese government. that, mr president, is a few of the things i could say in reply to those who have spoken, and i would like to thank parliament again, and in particular the committee on budgetary control, for the excellent cooperation we have had. all the court judgments concern cases where the trade unions have taken internationally recognised collective action to combat social dumping. in all three judgments, the european court of justice has recognised that these measures are a legitimate trade union right. however, this right has been called into question by the court of justice in relation to the internal market. in the laval and rüffert cases, the statutory minimum standard was interpreted as the only maximum standard applicable in the internal market. the european court of justice thus interpreted the posting of workers directive in a very specific direction. but that is not what the legislator intended. the recital in the preamble to the directive calls for the promotion of the free movement of services in the context of fair competition and for the protection of the rights of workers. in addition, the posting of workers directive contains a first-preference clause for workers, and this has not been taken into account in the court's judgments. the court is now creating a situation in the european union where the posting of workers directive is being transformed from a minimum to a maximum directive and where it is legitimate to gain a competitive advantage through social dumping. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the draft directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to carcinogens. i may be criticizing the court's decisions. but a union without the equivalent elements of social europe, such as collective
