president of the republic of slovenia. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, it is a great honour to be invited to address this house. it is only a month since we celebrated the 50th anniversary of the first session of the european parliamentary assembly. the anniversary is a great opportunity to reflect on the present and the future of the european union. today i am granted the special privilege of sharing my thoughts with you as the elected representatives of the peoples of europe. this parliament and, of course, the european union as a whole, are the magnificent creation of a great vision, a vision of lasting peace and prosperity, brought to the people of europe by a spirit of cooperation and ever-increasing integration. the fathers of this vision jean monnet, robert schuman, konrad adenauer, alcide de gasperi and others could probably not have imagined that 51 years after the creation of the european communities, slovenia would preside over a highly interconnected european union, the first of the new member states following the great enlargement of the european union in 2004, and that the slovenian president would address the european parliament. however, their sense of satisfaction would likely override their sense of surprise. the european project has not only succeeded, but has also proved to be a project with great transformative power, creating a completely new type of europe, one that had not been known in previous periods of its long history. more importantly, the european union has already established itself as a global actor, a global player, through the european project. and that's what i want to talk about today. what made this incredible success possible, this emergence of this great and important global player? how should we understand the lesson of this success today? are we able to apply the lessons of the past to the challenges of today and tomorrow? these are the questions we must ask ourselves all the time. the european union will continue to face complex issues in an increasingly globalised world and will need to have credible answers to them. the european union will continue to be a great success story if it maintains its dynamism and proves to be a global political actor with increasing weight, i would add, political weight. moving on is a prerequisite for success. what is required of the european union at this stage is that it takes on the role of world leader. in many areas, its world leadership is either already established or eagerly awaited. i would like to mention two at this point: global warming and human rights. last year, the european union put environmental issues, and in particular global warming, at the heart of its policy-making. this was undoubtedly the right and wise decision, for climate change and environmental degradation are proven to be the most serious threat and the greatest challenge facing us all. the european commission has defined specific objectives that enable the european union to play a leading role on a global scale. the key objective is to achieve a 20% reduction in greenhouse gas emissions by 2020 compared to 1990. the achievement of this objective is defined as a stand-alone commitment. the initiative for an even more ambitious target should be part of a global international agreement involving other key actors. in this case, the european union would be prepared to achieve a reduction of as much as 30% over the same period, as proposed by the european commission. these goals are so important, so ambitious, that they truly enable a transformative vision of action in the face of global warming and a much-needed example of global leadership. but are these goals attainable, or will they become another insurmountable obstacle? the answer is not yet clear. last month, the european council welcomed the commission's proposal as a good basis for an agreement. consultations this year and next will show how much can be achieved in practice ahead of the international conference in copenhagen scheduled for december 2009. the european parliament, and i want to stress this in particular, has already recognised the importance of this issue by setting up a special committee on climate change and will have a very important role to play in this respect. the task ahead of us is likely to be difficult. the turmoil that is beginning to be felt in the european media offers a whole range of mixed messages. there are expressions of support, but also of scepticism, which point to the concerns expressed by some european industries, as well as to the fact that the current global economic difficulties are making it more difficult to compete, and that environmental issues are relatively less important. tough times like this are a real test of leadership. clearly, global warming has already reached the point where the international community faces a stark choice: either to continue with growth methods and finally accept disaster, or to summon the courage for a transformative approach that can adequately mitigate the effects of global warming and prevent the worst. we're not gonna make it with a growth mindset. transformation, though difficult to achieve, is the essence of the agenda. and i hope that this year we will choose the path that leads to transformation, to transformation. in this effort, the line of defence will need to be significantly widened. but there are many who feel the need to move on to transformation. ngos, the media and other civil society actors are being mobilised. there is a strong drive in the business community to develop new technologies based on clean energy. and more and more people are willing to change their spending habits. it's about connecting the tendencies into a meaningful movement. the time frame is known. so is the location. the action plan adopted in bali last december envisages the conclusion of negotiations next year with the adoption of a global agreement to replace the kyoto protocol in 2012. although the negotiations will take place in the united nations, it is important that they find support everywhere. time and space allow us to combine our efforts. and this is the time when the european union must take the lead. respect for the environment is not the only area where the european union needs to take on the role of world leader. a stronger role for the union in the promotion of human rights in the world is also urgently needed. the european union's commitment to human rights is, of course, unquestionable. the european institutions are based on the rule of law and human rights, and europe is a human rights area. the ratification of the lisbon treaty in all member states by the end of this year, the year in which we celebrate the 60th anniversary of the universal declaration of human rights, would also mean that, for the first time in the history of the union, the full range of civil, political, economic and social rights of citizens and residents of the union, as laid down in the union charter of fundamental rights, would become legally binding. and the world situation, globally, is not encouraging. human rights are being violated in many parts of the world in a massive and systematic way. this is partly due to the ruthless pursuit of economic gain, regardless of the needs of the local population and the environment. in many places, especially among the poor and the indigenous, poverty and hunger, and in some cases extinction, are threatening. atrocities amounting to crimes against humanity continue to be committed in armed conflicts in many parts of africa and asia. the european union must be active by proposing economic models for sustainable growth, it must be active through humanitarian and diplomatic efforts, but also through sanctions that will support the decisions of the international criminal court. the european union's leading role is particularly needed at this stage, as global human rights action is lagging behind. the united nations human rights council continues to strive for proper working methods. its efforts to establish a system of universal periodic review of human rights in a global framework are promising but not yet effective. his action against the massive and systematic violation of human rights is not comprehensive enough. all of this can be remedied over time, but not without effective leadership, not without effective leadership by those united nations member states that are truly committed to human rights. in reality, this cannot happen without a stronger leadership role from the european union, which is the most important group of influential states in the united nations. some other traditional supporters of human rights have recently become less active and have not run for membership of the united nations human rights council. the increasing concern about terrorism and other security threats, together with the sometimes ill-considered responses to these threats, has clearly reduced the level of sensitivity to human rights. the european union must fill this gap. the union must also seek new ways of cooperating with the united nations security council. the work of the security council in darfur has helped establish the role of the international criminal court in efforts to prosecute the perpetrators of some of the most heinous crimes of our time. almost exactly a year ago, the international criminal court issued arrest warrants for some of these perpetrators. efforts to bring these individuals to justice must continue and cooperation with the security council will remain critical. however, even without the security council, the european union must consider measures to contribute to the effectiveness of the international criminal court. i would stress that international justice is the backbone of international human rights action today and that it requires effective support. the european union should also be committed to the emerging democracies in the world that are genuinely committed to human rights. they are interested in international action, but they must take into account their regional and other affiliations and these aspects are not neglected in all international action related to human rights. but these countries are partners of the european union and we must nurture this partnership. ladies and gentlemen, international human rights action, in its various forms, can only be effective if it is based on a solid foundation, on consistent respect for human rights at home. this includes protecting the human rights of migrants and asylum seekers and the prudent application of the law in cases involving terrorism charges. however, the building of that foundation still needs to continue. the lisbon treaty incorporated the charter of fundamental freedoms of the european union and an improved decision-making process that will facilitate the adoption of bold and creative solutions in the field of human rights. the need for creativity in europe is not new. the european creative turmoil, as german president horst köhler explained in his speech to this parliament two years ago, this creative turmoil has helped europeans to face the various social and political challenges in commitment, freedom and truth, with the ability to realise solidarity and create greater prosperity for all. nowhere will creativity and creative disruption be needed more than in the area of immigration management and integration. europe is ageing and will no longer be able to play the role of world leader without a successful population policy. these policies will necessarily include the management of immigration. europe needs newcomers, positive in spirit and able to do their part in creating prosperity for all. however, it is clear that the policy measures that can help in the process of integrating immigrants are diverse and must be properly tailored to the circumstances of each country of immigration. at the same time, some elements have wider applications and in some respects the european union can learn from non-european countries such as canada. immigration policies will require a set of coordinated objectives at the level of the european union as a whole. the objective of a common european asylum system by 2010 seems both ambitious and urgent. improved coordination between immigration and development aid policies is also needed. the european union must strengthen its role in the united nations high-level dialogue on migration. at the same time, it requires creativity in terms of the inclusion of immigrants and their communities. economic prosperity and greater upward social mobility are key to successful immigration policy. for example, business activities run by ethnic minorities provide jobs and make a significant contribution to the economy of host countries. on the other hand, governments can do their part by providing appropriate regulations, training programmes and general support for entrepreneurship. inclusion must include effective access to quality education, including language education, and access to universities. education is the key to successfully integrating immigrants into wider society. and success is about making it visible. successful people of immigrant origin should be given the opportunity to appear on television and in other media and be held up as examples of success. this will help the wider public to understand that diversity and inclusion are compatible and that non-discrimination and the use of equal opportunities are among the most important civic virtues. there's nothing more successful than success. and there's nothing on television that looks better than the success of those who started on the sidelines. i have shed some light on the issue of immigration and integration because of their importance for the future of europe and also because they represent another area where european creativity will be put to the test. in the past, europe has managed to solve most social issues, and has thus become a world example of social justice and economic prosperity. so there is no reason why our generation cannot find good solutions in the field of immigration and integration. europe has much to gain from integrating people who are capable, skilled and willing to contribute to its future and prosperity. ladies and gentlemen, today, without a doubt, we need leadership, we need vision, and we need creativity. at the same time, the european union must demonstrate its ability to continue to find answers to the various challenges by finding pragmatic solutions. we must not forget that pragmatism was the key to the creation of the european communities more than five decades ago and remains the key to their success today. the establishment of the european communities for economic purposes was a highly pragmatic idea that made possible all further integration. the development of the european economic community towards a customs union and beyond, the ability to develop new forms of cooperation and new institutions with additional powers, and the capacity for geographical enlargement, all illustrate the importance of pragmatism in the history and development of the european union. today, the union is also facing new challenges that require pragmatic adaptation. among these, its further expansion stands out. while it is clear that all those who seek membership, all candidates, will have to meet the criteria, none of them should be prevented from joining simply because of political problems or cultural prejudices. i would like to thank the commissioner for his reply. i welcome market-based instruments for policy enforcement, including in environmental policy. however, i would like to point out that a policy instrument is not automatically good just because it says 'market-based'. all the instruments we use to achieve policy objectives must be able to withstand a number of questions. is the instrument tuned to a specific target? if you mix up several objectives, none of them will be achieved properly. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. does it really help to achieve the goal? you have to check it afterwards, periodically. is the instrument tuned to other instruments? is it efficient, so is the benefit in relation to the cost? i see some points in this report where i have doubts that these criteria are met. emissions trading systems work well in theory, but the reality is different. the european carbon trading system is in a state of chaos. wealth was destroyed and the real goal was not achieved. well, it was a test run, we're still practicing, but we certainly can't afford many of these expensive tests. the next example is tax policy. taxation has no place in an eu green paper on market-based instruments. an instrument is not market-based simply because it affects elements of the market. i am not opposed to taxes being levied to achieve environmental objectives, but i am in favour of their being levied only if they meet the criteria mentioned. i am in favour of setting targets that must be achieved. the choice of the means of achieving the objectives should be left to the market participants.

member of the commission. − madam president, i would like to thank the committee on economic and monetary affairs and in particular the rapporteur, mr radwan, for the considerable work that has gone into this comprehensive report. it raises important issues for the future development of european and indeed global capital markets. in this brief intervention i cannot address all the issues raised in the report. let me therefore focus on three points. one, governance issues; secondly the eu’s input to the international accounting standards board, the iasb; and thirdly the project to develop an accounting standard for small and medium-sized enterprises. on iasb governance, your report rightly highlights the fact that our shared objective is to develop high-quality global accounting standards. the eu’s decision to require listed companies to use international accounting standards was a bold and visionary step towards this objective. a single set of globally accepted accounting standards would provide significant benefits for our companies, our capital markets and our economy. we must continuously strive to ensure that international accounting standards remain relevant in the face of changing economic circumstances and that they represent the interests of all stakeholders in a balanced manner. to ensure that these conditions can continue to be met, progress should be made as a matter of priority in three areas. firstly, the accountability of the international accounting standards committee foundation (iascf), needs to be enhanced, in particular towards public authorities. the latter should play an active role in the selection and appointment of trustees. in this respect, the proposal that i, together with my counterparts in the us sec, the japanese fsa and the international organisation of securities commissions, made last november goes in the direction advocated by your report. secondly, we need to look at how the iasb’s agenda-setting process can be improved. in particular, the process through which priorities are set needs to be made more open and more transparent. thirdly, the iasb’s due process should be enhanced, mainly by ensuring that standards are subject to a full impact assessment before they are adopted. your report makes constructive suggestions about these and related points. the forthcoming review of the iascf’s constitution provides the opportunity to implement the necessary reforms. the committee will pursue them in consultation with this house, the member states and our international partners. now, turning to the eu’s input to the iasb. your report argues that the eu needs to strengthen its capacity to make its views on accounting matters heard at the international level. i agree. in particular we should seek means to ensure that the views of european stakeholders, especially proactive input to the iasb’s agenda-setting process, can be put to the iasb in a more timely and coherent manner. i see this as an evolutionary rather than a revolutionary process. we should build on the european financial reporting advisory group and i am ready to pursue this as a matter of urgency, including the possibility of using funding from the community budget to support such a structure. i must, however, sound a clear and unambiguous warning. this structure will in no circumstances become an embryonic european standard-setter, nor can there be any question of developing european interpretations of international accounting standards. europe must and will remain part of the movement towards a single set of globally accepted accounting standards. anything else would damage the international competitiveness of our companies and our capital market. turning now to the iasb’s project to develop an accounting standard for smes, let me begin by stating that the commission currently has no legal basis to endorse this standard. moreover, we have never made any commitment to take over whatever standard the iasb produces. we would only do so if we were genuinely convinced that the iasb produces a standard that meets the interests of european users. the iasb has not yet finalised its project. however, at this stage the commission’s views are clear. the current exposure draft published by the iasb remains too complex to provide a satisfactory accounting framework for european smes, especially for smaller companies. our focus remains the simplification of the regulatory environment for smes, including in the accounting area.
draft opinion of the consultative committee on legal affairs. the commission has already made a number of proposals. the ias system makes sense for large, publicly traded companies that operate globally. this is why parliament, on the basis of a proposal from the legal affairs committee, adopted the ias regulation in the last parliamentary term. the aim was indeed - as my colleague mr radwan has said - to achieve convergence in the end, at least with the united states and, if possible, worldwide. it makes no sense for small and medium-sized enterprises, which do not need the global financial markets, access to wall street and other things in general. in view of this, it is more than questionable why smes ifrs should be developed at all. in addition, and i think commissioner mccreevy has said this quite rightly, what is now on the table is nothing but a watered-down version of the already extremely complicated international standards which do not fit the structures of smes in europe. this is particularly the case where they are family businesses run by owners for generations, who have already written off land they own, where fair value valuations only create desirability and where, in the end, the structure of these companies is such as to jeopardise their future prospects. on the other hand, we must be realistic. there will also be a sort of pressure for harmonization in the long term on the question of standards among smes in europe. we want comparability, at least in the european single market. i therefore believe it is important that we give serious thought to the question of how we can develop european alternatives to the proposals from london, with the aim of achieving greater standardisation here too, but in a way that is appropriate and appropriate to smes, and that is oriented towards the long term rather than short-term evaluation. i would like to make one further comment on the ias bodies. there is a real problem here, and mr radwan has raised it. we may have a certain geographical balance, but we have no balance in terms of economic power. europe is by far the largest bloc, the largest area in the field of validity of ias rules. that is why we need a proper voice, and we are not to be compared with australia. australia is the size of a medium-sized state in the european union or a large region, such as north rhine-westphalia. we must find a better balance here.
member of the commission. − madam president, i would like to thank members for their comments. it was certainly a very wide-ranging debate with diversity of views on many of the issues and we have taken note of them. i would like to emphasise again that high-quality international accounting standards are crucial for the effective functioning of both the european and global capital markets. the process through which these standards are developed should therefore be subject to robust governance. it should be characterised by a high level of transparency and it should ensure a balanced consideration of stakeholder interests. the iascf and the iasb have over recent years implemented significant reforms of their internal procedures but i cannot deny that further improvements are necessary. moreover, i recognise that we in europe should better organise ourselves to guide and provide input to the iasb standard-setting process. in short, even if the iasb’s governance and due process were perfect, international accounting standards will only meet the needs of european stakeholders if their views are presented in a coherent, a convincing and a timely manner. nearly all that the ifrs would become the rule for listed companies. it was some years ago that this decision was made, together with the european parliament, and that in itself gave greater importance to the iasb and to the process. i would say – and i have said this repeatedly to the iasb also – that road testing – you can call it impact analysis – should be done before standards are adopted, particularly by the iasb, and with input from the eu and other bodies as well. we should not be waiting until the standards are endorsed by the iasb. we had the job here of either agreeing to them or rejecting them. we do not have the role of changing them. i think that they should be road tested enough beforehand to see if there are going to be problems, rather than finding out about serious problems after the whole iasb process has been gone through. we made this point repeatedly to the iasb. hopefully, i think the new governance structures have been appreciated by most of us. i accept automatic and not cause any great headaches for anybody because all the work will have been done previously. we will not have difficulties then.

member of the commission. - thank you very much, mr. president. ladies and gentlemen, we are celebrating the 10th anniversary of the historic decision to introduce the euro, to launch the third stage of economic and monetary union, which was adopted by the european council on 1 and 3 may 1998. this decision has shaped the european union's development over the past ten years. today, inside and outside our borders, the euro is a symbol of european integration used daily by 320 million european citizens. the commission has seen that, at the end of this first decade of a major political initiative and after a full economic cycle, it was worthwhile to take stock and reflect on the challenges facing economic and monetary union in the years ahead. that is the purpose of the communication adopted this morning by the commission and which i have the honour to present to you. the communication is based on a comprehensive report by the commission's directorate-general for ecfin, which analyses in detail the functioning of economic and monetary union and the effects of the euro over the past ten years, and also analyses the prospects for the future. the conclusion of this evaluation of the euro's first decade of existence could not be clearer: the euro is an undeniable economic and political success. thanks to the euro, europeans today enjoy greater macroeconomic stability, lower interest rates, much more moderate price developments than in previous decades, despite what we are seeing lately with inflation. thanks to the euro, the european union - and in particular the 15 countries of the euro area - is a much more economically integrated area, with greater trade, greater opportunities, more employment and more efficient markets. thanks to the euro, our economies are better protected against external shocks and have gained weight and influence on global markets. all this has resulted in many tangible benefits, but the greatest of them all, if i may quote, has been that in the last ten years 16 million jobs have been created in the euro area. the euro has made europe stronger today. it is better able to cope with the turbulence and crises that we have experienced in recent months, and thanks to the euro we have a stronger basis for sustaining our growth and our social protection model in the future. but, positive as our assessment may be, it does not mean that all the hopes we had for the single currency ten years ago have been fulfilled. firstly, economic growth over the last ten years has been below our expectations at the time. secondly, divergences between the economies of the area still persist, as a consequence, inter alia, of the lack of sufficient incentives to undertake all the necessary structural reforms. thirdly, we have not yet articulated in the euro area a strong and homogeneous external presence that would allow us to weigh globally in accordance with the size and importance of our economy and our currency. finally, the public image of the euro - a currency that is broadly identified with the image of the european union - does not reflect all the objective benefits it has brought to our citizens. this diagnosis is enough to make us think about what remains to be done, and our conclusion is that much remains to be done. but we must also take account of the new challenges that we are facing in these years, with an enlarged europe, with the acceleration of social, economic and technological changes, with underlying trends as profound as globalisation, ageing or climate change; we must update the foundations and the vision that inspire the project of economic and monetary union. it is obvious that the new context in which we live today was not easily foreseeable twenty years ago, when it was decided what was to be included in the maastricht treaty, or ten years ago, when it was decided to launch the third phase of economic and monetary union. we must now work on the basis of these parameters to achieve a stronger economic and monetary union, with a more efficient internal operation and a more homogeneous external projection. in the communication we adopted this morning, the commission does not want to simply take stock of the past, but we propose to open a debate on what needs to be improved in the future. as an initial contribution to that debate we propose an agenda based on three pillars. the first concerns the internal functioning of the union. the interdependence between the economies of the area is greater than ever; we must be aware of this and move decisively, in the interests of the economic and monetary union as a whole and of each of its member states in particular, towards a real coordination of their economic policies. how can we do that? the budgetary surveillance regulated in the stability and growth pact should be deepened by broadening that surveillance, by deepening it in relation to the quality of public finances or their long-term sustainability, by broadening the scope of surveillance to macroeconomic aspects beyond strictly budgetary ones, and by establishing a closer link between budgetary surveillance and the development of structural reforms. the second pillar concerns the external agenda. the euro has become - and this is a pleasure for all of us - the second world currency of reference in a very short time. but it is pointless, while we welcome the euro's pre-eminent position on global markets, to renounce our collective action in a way consistent with this new status. the position achieved by the euro on international markets brings with it undoubted advantages, such as greater protection against external shocks. in the last decade we have experienced critical moments in which this protective role has been put to the test. but the status of the euro also carries with it responsibilities and risks. europe must take full responsibility for achieving greater global economic stability. to do this, it must define a strategy that is in line with the interests of the euro area and defend it consistently abroad, and there is no doubt that the best way to ensure that consistency is through a single representation of the euro abroad. although i know that it is difficult to achieve in the short term, given the interests at stake, i also assert to this parliament - and i know that parliament agrees with my view - that it is a strictly necessary objective. finally, the third pillar of our agenda for the future is the improvement of the governance of economic and monetary union. the institutions and instruments governing this union are appropriate, especially when we take into account the improvements introduced by the treaty of lisbon. the question now is not to change the instruments, but to use them, and to use them fully. the best governance of the euro area will come from a full partnership of the ecofin council in matters of economic and monetary union; it will come from a deepening of the agenda and discussions of the eurogroup, in particular as regards the coordination of economic policies to which i have referred; and it will come from an even closer dialogue between the commission and parliament, as well as between the eurogroup and parliament. in the next few years, the composition of the eurogroup will also be brought closer and closer to that of the ecofin council itself. this morning, without going any further, the commission adopted the convergence report paving the way for slovakia to join the euro area on 1 january 2009. in the coming weeks i shall have the opportunity to discuss this report and the related proposals with the honourable members. it should also be a collective concern of our institutions to communicate to the public the issues related to economic and monetary union, so that the public's perception of the euro is in line with the objective advantages it brings to us as citizens who have this currency in our pockets. i'll finish up now, mr. president. we have a matter of paramount importance on the table which fully deserves this first debate we are having today. i cannot, of course, go into all the details of the analysis contained in our communication and in the report, but you can count on my full availability to discuss it in the coming months. the commission's objective, as i have said, is to build a strong political consensus on the steps to be taken to ensure that economic and monetary union can meet the enormous challenges that lie ahead. these and not others are the questions which we feel should be given our attention in the debate which is opening up today. the people who drew up the maastricht treaty and decided to set up economic and monetary union ten years ago were then up to the task, creating an instrument which has brought us protection and benefits. the hard part is done: the euro is here and it is a success. we can therefore face the new stage with confidence and optimism, but we must also do so with the same determination and with the understanding that what benefits economic and monetary union benefits the european union as a whole, all its member states and all its citizens. thank you very much, mr. president.

the commission is therefore proposing to amend the proposal. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. in the past, there have been various attempts by politically sovereign states to create a common monetary union. these trials have lasted for different periods of time. in the end, they all failed. it was therefore not surprising that in the 1970s the outside world reacted very critically to proposals to start such an initiative in europe. pierre werner, the former prime minister of luxembourg, and also valéry giscard d'estaing and helmut schmidt, when they were state secretaries in the ministry of finance, have presented attempts in this direction. even in the early 1990s, the move towards economic and monetary union was viewed very critically. many experts - including nobel prize winners from america - have dismissed it as unrealistic. against all expectations, the euro was finally introduced and it was a success. the european economic union is indeed something of a small political miracle, and it is a case sui generis. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. the introduction of the euro has, however, been greeted with great scepticism by the population of many countries. if there had been a referendum in the first 12 member states of the euro zone, we would not have the euro today, at least not in these many countries. however, the public is now somewhat more positive about the euro. i am sure it is not 100% yet, but it is probably a majority. the sometimes melancholy memories of the old currencies - whether the mark, the guilder, the schilling or the franc - have largely given way to the conviction that the introduction of the euro is also beneficial for the individual citizen, not just for the economy as a whole. the citizens themselves are the first to feel this when they travel: there are no longer any passport controls in the schengen area and the costly and tedious exchange of money is gone. but a large number of citizens have also understood that without the european central bank and the single currency we would not be able to cope with the financial crisis we are facing as well as we are at present. the effects of the strong currency were also somewhat dampened by the rise in commodity prices. nevertheless, there is still a section of the public which has had a negative experience of the euro. in particular, price increases are often attributed to the teuro in english it would be: to expensive euro . the fact is that the euro is stable! it has proven to be a stable currency. the inflation rate in recent years has been lower than in previous decades. and this is true even in countries as stable as germany. this stability has helped the euro to gain international importance and to become the second most important international reserve currency after the dollar. the stability of the euro is due to the independence of the central bank, and it is therefore incomprehensible that this independence is constantly being undermined. the first presidents, wim duisenberg and jean-claude trichet, have done an excellent job in this respect. the fact remains that a common currency without a common fiscal and economic policy is and will remain a risky undertaking. the eu faces major challenges: persistently high unemployment, demographic change, migratory pressures, increasing poverty among some groups and increased competition as a result of globalisation. the euro area can only meet this challenge if the economic policies of the member states are more closely interlinked. the appointment of a president of the euro zone was a first step in this direction, but only a first. there must be more to follow. the eurozone must above all act in a uniform way internationally. this is also true of organizations such as the international monetary fund and the oecd.

the next item is the report by mr hartmut nassauer, on behalf of the committee on legal affairs, on the proposal for a european parliament and council directive on the criminal protection of the environment (com (2007) 0051 c6-0063/2007 2007/0022 (cod)) (a6-0154/2008).
i have to say that i am not in favour of this. - mr president, i have to say something. the european union is resorting to criminal law. the european union will therefore also be imposing penalties, firstly for breaches of environmental law. this is a far-reaching and remarkable step, because criminal law is effectively withdrawn from the european union. it is even a core area of national sovereignty in the member states. the commission has also been asked to draw up a report on the implementation of the directive. the council, the commission and parliament have long agreed that environmental law may also be enforced by means of penalties: it took several years to determine who could operate here: the member states in the framework of framework decisions or the community in the form of the directive. the european court of justice has, not surprisingly, agreed with the commission's position. the new treaty of lisbon addresses this problem and resolves it in favour of the community even more profoundly than the decisions of the court of justice have done so in the past. this is why we have concluded a first reading agreement. we wanted to avoid having to start the procedure again if a solution was not found this year. in view of the changes in the substantive legal bases and the forthcoming european elections, it would undoubtedly have taken considerable time to produce a law to this effect. we therefore agreed that we must do everything possible to achieve a solution at first reading. by 'we' i mean the slovenian presidency of the council - i am extremely sorry that it is not here today, especially as i have put on a discreet tie for this very occasion - the commission and - and i would like to emphasize this in particular - the shadow rapporteurs, who have been very collegial and cooperative and have worked very objectively. the work was a joy. the new law contains three pillars, which i would like to quote at least briefly. firstly, we have not only defined the criminal offences that will be punishable in the future, but we have also laid down in an annex the specific provisions which can be used as a basis for criminal offences. this is in accordance with the principle of criminal certainty. it is not just any environmental violation, but the violation of laws precisely laid down in an annex, that constitutes a possible offence. it was important that this was anchored here. the second point is to take account of the principle of proportionality. the club of criminal law cannot be wielded against every offence, however ridiculous, but it must be of some weight. that is why petty crime has been excluded from the criminal law. thirdly, we have also established that only unlawful conduct can be a basis for criminal liability. we have unanimously incorporated these three principles into the draft. we have also improved the definitions. i look forward to the debate. i would like to thank once again all the colleagues who have made this compromise possible.
thank you very much, mr. nassauer. you mentioned the special quality of your tie. i noticed that too, but i didn't dare to comment. but since you did it yourself, i'd like to confirm that i noticed that, too.
i would like to thank the commissioner for his reply. it is indeed very welcome that the commission has not been intimidated by the eu member states and has put forward a proposal to punish environmental offences. it would be desirable if there were an agreement at first reading, because environmental violations can no longer be considered a cavalier offence. it is also positive that, just as the un conference on the conservation of species has started, the nature reserves are being defined better and more clearly in the proposed legislation and that it is becoming clearer what constitutes a violation. however, it is regrettable that there are no sanctions and that a breach is not generally considered a criminal offence. unfortunately, this creates loopholes, especially in the protection of fauna and flora, where violations are not generally punished and many can hide behind their ignorance. it would therefore have been good if genetic engineering had been covered by this directive. environmental crime must be punished and i hope that we can set a milestone to make it clear that the environment is a good worth protecting and that we must do everything possible to ensure that environmental violations are punished.

poverty alleviation and development. development is indeed a key issue in this context. i will therefore briefly touch on development issues, before addressing our concerns and actions regarding the proliferation of measures restricting access to raw materials. the fight for poverty alleviation and development, as well as food security, is high on the commission’s agenda. you are well aware that the european union is the world’s largest donor of development funding. also in the specific field of raw materials, the commission has undertaken several development-oriented programmes: for instance, through flex, the commission supports developing countries’ national budgets, where there has been a drop in export-related fiscal revenue. the commission also promotes the transparent management of tax revenues generated by the exploitation of raw materials and natural resources through several initiatives such as eiti, the kimberley process and the flegt programme. let me also refer to our everything but arms programme, which grants duty-free access to imports of all products from least developed countries (except arms), allowing them to diversify their exports. let me now turn to our key concern, which is from the trade perspective. it takes two to trade. we need to import and we need to export. it is therefore critical to ensure that access to raw materials in third countries is free from unjustified distortions such as quotas, export duties and export bans. today, unfortunately, this is not the case. on the contrary, third countries’ appetite to impose export restrictions is increasing. our specific concerns are those imposed by some key emerging economies as part of their aggressive industrial policy objectives. let me underline that we are not focusing on poorer developing economies but rather on large emerging economies. measures imposed by these countries result in distorted competition at global level which damages european industry. unfortunately, the size of the problem is growing. by now at least 20 countries have put in place measures affecting exports of importance to the european union. we have counted over 450 restrictions affecting various raw materials. most, if not all, european industrial sectors are concerned, directly or indirectly. what can be done? the work carried out so far shows that there is no quick-fix solution even if the elimination of export restrictions is high on our agenda already, be it in bilateral free trade agreements or in the world trade organisation, but we will do more. first, it will be important to develop an overall strategy for access to raw materials. in this respect, the commission is working on a communication which will include an important trade component. any such strategy evidently should fully and coherently take up all policy areas, including critical issues such as food security, development and the environment. all means will have to be used to their maximum. a sustainable and coherent policy on access to raw materials would therefore combine: firstly, negotiations securing international commitments in the wto and bilateral context; secondly, enforcement of wto rules and existing agreements; and thirdly soft measures such as dialogue and alliance-building. while none of these elements is new, it is their combination and their coherent use which will determine their strength. this will be discussed at a conference with stakeholders later this year. considering the importance of access to raw materials, the commission welcomes the discussions in parliament on this issue. the commission particularly welcomes the amendments to the first draft of the report. the report now highlights more clearly the significance of this issue. it proposes ways to tackle this issue in a constructive manner, such as enforcement of agreements and negotiations with partner countries. we stand ready to fully cooperate with parliament in designing and implementing our further strategy.

member of the commission. − madam president, mr posselt, mr crowley and mr ebner have all asked about the state of play of accession negotiations with croatia and i can respond to them jointly. these negotiations with croatia are progressing well overall. so far negotiations have been opened on 18 chapters out of 35 and we have closed two of these chapters. as regards opening benchmarks, 11 sets of benchmarks have been set. the commission has assessed the benchmarks as being met in seven of these 11 cases. in these cases our recommendations are now under discussion among the member states in the council or negotiation positions are being prepared. in the remaining chapters, such as competition policy and public procurement, opening benchmarks were already set by the union in the first half of 2006 – that is two years ago. but croatia has been slow in taking the necessary measures to meet these opening benchmarks. croatia is still working on opening benchmarks for the chapter on the judiciary and fundamental rights, where there are many difficult challenges in areas such as judicial reform, the fight against corruption and refugee return. while croatia has done plenty of good work aligning with the key 16 chapters where we have closing benchmarks, croatia has not done enough at this stage to meet all closing benchmarks in any of these 16 chapters. with the remaining conditions still to be met by croatia it unrealistic to assume that accession negotiations could be concluded this year in 2008. croatia has nonetheless made good progress overall and therefore 2008 could be a decisive year in croatia’s eu accession negotiations. provided a number of conditions are met by croatia, the commission will in this autumn’s enlargement package present an indicative timetable or a conditional roadmap for the conclusion of other technical negotiations in the course of 2009. the first condition to be met is that croatia should meet all opening benchmarks by june this year, i.e. next month. secondly, croatia must comply with all legal obligations under the stabilisation and accession agreement and it must also continue to comply with the general conditionalities of the stabilisation and accession process. and thirdly, croatia needs urgently to improve its management of eu financial assistance under the phare and ipa programmes. the president of the commission will continue to provide substantial financial and technical assistance for croatia in order to help it fulfil the requirements of eu membership. once sufficient progress has been made by croatia in meeting opening or closing benchmarks, the commission will prepare and submit in good time the necessary recommendations to the member states for the positions to be taken in the member of the commission. - madam president, ladies and gentlemen, first of all, let me thank you for putting burma on the agenda of this session. in view of the scale of the disaster caused by cyclone nargis on 2 may, we have proposed to the presidency that an extraordinary meeting of the council of ministers for external relations of the european union be convened. this council meeting was called as soon as possible by the slovenian presidency, to which i would like to thank, and it took place on 12 may. at this meeting, the european union called for greater cooperation by the burmese authorities to facilitate access to and distribution of international humanitarian aid. i have decided to respond directly to this call by going to burma myself from 15 to 16 may. during my mission, which i have made clear is strictly humanitarian and not political in nature, i had the opportunity to meet the burmese authorities, representatives of the humanitarian organizations present in burma, and i was able to make a field visit, supervised by the authorities, to the disaster areas around yangon. i had, for two and a half hours, rather close talks and discussions with the minister of planning - who was obviously the most authoritative, if not the most authoritarian, personage of the three i met - the minister of social welfare and the minister of health. it is clear from my mission that the burmese authorities remain very reluctant to create the operational conditions normally required for a humanitarian response that is international in scope. it is equally clear that any approach to impose international humanitarian assistance on the burmese authorities seems to me, given the means at our disposal today, doomed to failure and perhaps even counterproductive. all the humanitarian organizations there told me this and confirmed to me that the problem is obviously not the lack of organizations there, nor even the lack of money, because of course the lack of resources also depends on the access of international experts and international professionals, but the lack of access. my mission certainly contributed, in a modest way, to opening a very small gap that allowed for the gradual creation of a minimal humanitarian space for international humanitarian assistance. the burmese authorities have partially responded to the various specific requests: for example, visas for commission experts have been extended by two weeks. we had visas, these people had visas for three days, they were extended for two weeks. we asked for a month. we also clarified a situation that seemed really serious, that in some places the local burmese authorities were demanding that even local staff, that is even operators that our agencies are occupying, un agencies are occupying or ngos are occupying, that local staff also have to present a permit, that is a written authorization, which was obviously, in most cases, impossible. this has been clarified and, obviously, no permits are required for local staff. in any case, it is no longer necessary to travel to the disaster areas, and especially to the airport in pathein. i also asked for a second airport to be opened for the landing of planes carrying material goods, the pathein airport, which is a military airport. i was told that this was not possible because the technical standards of the control tower were not in line with international standards and that it would not make the job any easier, as the communication routes between yangon and the delta, which is the most affected area, are more car-friendly and easier. unfortunately, i haven't been authorized to visually verify this sort of thing. i think it is important to continue to maintain strong international pressure, both from the they got that permission. so there are 140 doctors who have deployed, including medical personnel from laos, cambodia, india, bangladesh and thailand. so they were able to deploy to the worst affected areas. the role of the countries of the region is crucial and i had the opportunity to have a rather long conversation with secretary-general ban ki-moon when i was waiting for my plane back to humanitarian coordinator, john holmes, in recent days, secretary-general ban ki-moon will visit burma tomorrow to discuss the delivery of international aid. the humanitarian situation in the country remains dire, with the risk that the first disaster caused by the cyclone will be followed by a second humanitarian disaster due to the risk of famine, as crops have been destroyed, and epidemics among the survivors, whose living conditions are deplorable. there's a risk of an outbreak. at the time we were there, the world health organization didn't see the risk of cholera, but there were a been destroyed. a practical problem arises: these lands should be planted in such a way as to ensure the october harvest. the time limit is therefore three to four weeks at most. now, a number of that is, toxic - and radioactive. du ammunition is also a waste product of the nuclear industry, resulting from the enrichment of uranium or the production of nuclear weapons. the problem is also the use of nuclear energy. du is a long-acting weapon. du is released at high temperatures when it hits a fixed target and burns to du oxide, producing fine alpha-radioactive toxic dust that can be easily inhaled and dispersed by wind and water. this dust is difficult to remove from the environment and becomes trapped in the lungs when inhaled. there's the gulf war syndrome, the balkan syndrome, and it's the same phenomenon over and over again, that soldiers obviously get cancer, for example, lung cancer. there is also an increase in such cancers in the population in the areas where these weapons have been used. interestingly, du ammunition as such has very little military effectiveness, but carries a very large number of incalculable risks. nato used du ammunition in the war of aggression against yugoslavia. in iraq, the us army has used du munitions - a total of 300 tons. there's an increase in the number of malnourished children, especially in baghdad. the afghan government has now called for an investigation into the use of du ammunition in afghanistan, and they say that the us military did not inform them that du ammunition was used mainly in eastern afghanistan. in the lebanon war du munitions were used by israel in particular, and in the first gulf war du munitions were also used very extensively. we're talking about 66,000 soldiers who are contaminated. the problem is obvious. meanwhile, the first veterans are receiving pensions as a result of this du munition, such as kenny duncan from the uk. if du munitions were cosmetics or a food-related substance, they would have been banned long ago. soldiers are instructed to wear protective suits when dealing with du ammunition. the euromil soldiers' association is calling for a ban on these weapons. belgium has banned du ammunition. congratulations on this. in the united nations disarmament committee vote, 122 countries voted in favor, 35 abstained, and 6 voted against, including france, great britain, the netherlands, and the czech republic. what we need is a ban on the use and production of du munitions.

the next item is the joint debate on the report by mr jacek saryusz-wolski, on behalf of the committee on foreign affairs, on the annual report from the council to the european parliament on the main aspects and guidelines of the common foreign and security policy (cfsp) submitted to the european parliament under point g.43 of the interinstitutional agreement of 17 may 2006 (a6-0189/2008) and the report by mr helmut kuhne, on behalf of the committee on foreign affairs, on the european security strategy and the european security and defence policy (2008/2003) (a6-0186/2008).
i have to say that i am not in favour of this. - mr president, i have to say something. in our report we wanted to avoid duplication with statements in previous reports on the european security strategy. we may not have been entirely successful, but i believe we can go further in this direction in the future. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. we want this to be a real institution and not just a virtual institution. since december 2003 the adoption of the european security strategy time has passed very quickly by european standards, perhaps not necessarily by objective standards, but it can already be said that in this period the european security strategy has made significant practical progress. here we can show some successes. i am not going to list the various missions, civil and military. but what we can demonstrate structurally is that we have also had a civilian control and planning instrument on the council side for about a year now, that there is now a clear line from across the building down to those who have to carry out what we call activities on the ground. in the military field, we have increased operational capability beyond the use of nato capabilities under the berlin plus agreement. we've got the battle groups that are supposed to rotate operational. we have continued to carry out operations which we can say were successful, such as the rule of law missions in georgia and the like. but there are still problems to be solved and where i believe there are still shortcomings, and it does not make the security strategy any worse by writing these points down. the participation of the member states in the missions, particularly in the civil sector, is uneven in relation to the population of the member states of the european union. we therefore propose that member states be obliged - whether by moral pressure or otherwise - to draw up action plans on the human resources they can make available to the european union when needed, including statements on the future career prospects of people returning to their home countries after eu missions. we cannot afford to continue to have the torturous mechanism of troop deployment that we have had in the past for military action along the lines of darfur and chad. we propose a number of options. we also make a number of proposals to solve the helicopter crisis and to increase the availability of helicopters. in the long term, we must stop flying around the european union in 24 different types of helicopters. there are also some new developments which need to be addressed in the further reflection on the security strategy. we have a blurring of the internal and external borders in connection with terrorist activities. the security of energy supplies must be addressed by diplomatic, economic and technical means - and i say explicitly not military means. the protection of sensitive infrastructures against electronic attacks is something that has been brought into the consciousness. all these things should be taken into account when considering what should be added to the security strategy. mr solana, the high representative of the eu, has a corresponding mandate from the council to think about such things. we're supporting him. we want the outcome of these discussions to be presented in the form of a white paper by the end of the year, so that there is a common reference point for the european debate, not only for the debate between mr solana and the governments, not only between him and us, not only in the national parliaments, but also among the interested european public, from poland to portugal.
high representative for the common foreign and security policy. − mr president, let me start by thanking parliament for inviting me to this important debate on the european union’s foreign policy, security and defence in the plenary sitting of the european parliament. however, before entering into the substance, let me at once condemn the terrorist attack against the danish embassy in islamabad ago and i would like to report on that trip, if the sitting allows me the time. i wish to thank the two rapporteurs, mr saryusz-wolski and mr kuhne, for their reports. i think that there are many excellent points in these reports on how we can strengthen the european union's overall impact around the world, in line with our values, in line with our interests. i would like to congratulate them and reassure them, and all of you, that we will take as many of the remarks as possible into consideration because i think they are very constructive, very positive and because of that they will be considered by me. this is a very important session and i would like to address some of the issues which are in both reports. in the time allowed me i would like to talk about those issues that are more pertinent today on the international affairs agenda, to see how we can contribute to the resolution of the problems of today. i should like to say a couple of words about the treaty that has been referred to by the rapporteurs. in both reports there are many references to the treaty of lisbon and it is very clear why. those reports ask for more efficiency. the main point of the treaty is to make the european union’s work more efficient, more visible, especially in foreign and security policy. i am convinced that the treaty will solve many of the problems identified in the report in particular by mr kuhne. the first priority for all of us is to get the treaty ratified. we all still have to work in that direction in the coming days. i would like to underline that the slovenian presidency was mandated by the december european council to take forward the work on preparing for the smooth entry into force of the lisbon treaty. the work, as you know, has been guided by a few basic principles that we share. the starting point of all this discussion is the treaty itself. it has to be respected in full. the second thing is that the overall aim is that the treaty enters into force as previously agreed and that means on 1 january 2009 if things can go smoothly. many aspects of the treaty are of fundamental interest to you, to the european parliament and – as we are talking about foreign and security policy – on that particular issue. both the presidency and the commission and myself have had the opportunity to discuss many of these issues with some of you, and i would the smooth implementation of the treaty. let me say a word about the european external action service. as you know, i have a mandate as high representative in office from declaration 15 of the treaty to carry out preparatory work with the commission and with the member states. i am doing that. i am implementing this mandate with the clear objective of having the decision to establish the eas adopted as soon as possible after the entry into force of the treaty. mr kuhne mentioned the european security strategy. let me make some comments on how i see the situation today. the mandate that i received, the mandate from the council last december, asked me to produce another report by december 2008. i will follow up with discussions with you all in order to obtain the best modifications necessary. the strategy has proved very useful. that has been recognised by the rapporteur and i thank him for that. in the last four years i think it has been an instrument that has done good service. the document was short but at the same time it is a document which is readable and therefore i think it has complied with this purpose. i think that this strategy reflects our values, it reflects our principles, it reflects how we should come back to foreign and security policy. i think the task mandated by the european council last december is not about changing the text; it is more about improving the text and complementing it wherever possible. it is important to reflect on the international situation at the moment it was written – remember it was 2003. things have taken place in this period of time – probably not fundamental enough to change the content of the strategy – but they complement the issues from this period. lessons have been learned and debates have taken place in parliament and in the institutions. therefore i consider the input from parliament to be very valuable, also through the report of the rapporteur, mr kuhne, which is most welcome. i will report orally to the european council in two weeks’ time about this issue, how the work is being done. at that moment i will get something back from the member states on the thinking about this issue and i will listen to you and all the comments you have made today. there will then be further discussion and an informal meeting of foreign ministers – the gymnich – in the month of september and we will continue talking about these issues among ourselves here in parliament. i think that the timing is very important. december 2008 will be the fifth anniversary of the ess. hopefully by then the lisbon treaty will be ratified, therefore improving the coherence of our action. on the key threats that the strategy contemplates, i think those identified in 2003 were the right ones. i think we would agree on that. weapons of mass destruction, terrorism, organised crime, regional conflicts – basically those have not changed. it is still as relevant today, as i said, and we have to continue fighting actively along these lines. the strategy was based on an analysis of the major global challenges at that time, but today, as i said, some are more relevant than others five years ago, and we also have new ones. remember – as has been mentioned already by the rapporteurs – climate change and its effects on international security, energy security – which now has to be contemplated in depth – were not contemplated in the strategy. the same applies to migration – illegal migration in particular – and information security. they were not contemplated, and should be now. we have to take those developments into account. let me say a word also about the esdp, which the rapporteur mentioned. i think we can say without exaggeration that it has been a success. it has been an important and very visible part of the cfsp. over the last five years – and it is good to recognise that – we have deployed more than 15 missions – in fact 17. we now have 14 of them – civilian and military – in action on three continents: europe – in the balkans, africa, and the middle east and asia. that is well recognised in the reports and i appreciate that very much. however, mr kuhne’s report highlights some of the challenges and shortfalls we face in the esdp and i agree with most of the things that have been said. we are working on it: we are taking into account the lessons learned from the missions; we are adapting our structures, both on the civilian and on the military side; we are trying to make it so that there is more civilian and military cooperation, i.e. to have a comprehensive approach, which i think is also the intention of the report. good progress was made at last week’s council meeting with the foreign affairs and defence ministers. an important decision was taken. the rapporteur mr kuhne mentioned the key word ‘helicopters’, which, as you know, is one of the difficulties that the international community is facing now with regard to crisis management operations. the capabilities we need are not here and the capabilities we have are not ready or not the most suitable for the challenges of today. the decision for the defence agency to concentrate on that tactical vice-president of the commission. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council and parliament. first of all, i would like to thank the rapporteurs, mr saryusz-wolski and mr kuhne, for the constructive, comprehensive and forward-looking approach which underpins both reports. in view of the wide range of topics covered in both reports, i would like to focus on a few aspects which are particularly relevant to the commission, namely the implementation of the lisbon treaty, the european security strategy, the neighbourhood policy and the question of common action, in particular the role of the commission in crisis management. the commission, like most of you, hopes that the ratification process for the new reform treaty will be successfully completed this year. the treaty is essential to enable us to better represent the interests of all citizens of the european union on a global scale. a secure, economically and socially balanced and stable europe, which also plays a leading role on the world stage commensurate with its economic strength, needs a strong eu foreign policy. the european parliament has a duty to support the efforts of the european union to achieve a common foreign policy. this is not primarily an institutional problem, nor is it a problem of procedures, nor even of the legal basis. it is a political problem. to make the eu's foreign policy more effective, all member states must have the political will to promote the common interests of the european union. it would be in everyone's interest to do so. we can be strong together, but we can also be weak individually. we have a choice. the commission is currently preparing its contribution to the review of the european security strategy. we are facing new threats and challenges to which the narrow security concept of 2003 can no longer adequately respond. the concept of threat should be broadened today. the link between security and development, security and energy, security and climate change, and even the issues we are currently facing, the evolution of prices and the availability of raw materials, the threat of food shortages and the problem of immigration, deserve greater attention. the cfsp annual report and the ess/esdp annual report contain many points in this respect which are also shared by the commission. i expect these points to be adopted by the european council in december 2008. the promotion of the democratization process in other countries must continue to be a central element of our foreign policy strategy. we have experience of this - enlargement is a successful example. we have gained valuable experience in this area which we can use for the european neighbourhood policy. the neighbourhood policy is today one of our most important instruments - if not the most important instrument - for strengthening peace and stability in our part of the world and promoting prosperity and security. the commission's proposal is to be incorporated as far as possible into community policies. the european union is not only a political force, but also a political force, and it is a political force, and it is a political force, and it is a political force. the overall development of the european union and its global influence depend on the optimal use of all its resources and instruments. luckily, we're not starting from scratch here. a number of community instruments, in particular development and humanitarian aid, have already been deployed to support eu crisis management efforts from afghanistan to kosovo, from the middle east to chad. the cfsp budget managed by the commission has also been massively increased by almost 10 times since 2002. currently, 11 esdp missions are being carried out in the areas of police, rule of law and monitoring and two others in the military area. the commission is now systematically involved in the planning of these missions from the outset. this has already been the case in operations in kosovo, chad and the central african republic. in this context, let me say a few words about the instrument of stability. this important new community financing mechanism now adds a crisis management and conflict prevention instrument with an average annual budget of over eur 200 million for the period 2007-2013. the commission considers that the first year of implementation of the stability instrument has been a successful one, both in terms of the management of funds and the quality of the measures. the commission would very much welcome closer interinstitutional cooperation on the external action of the european union if we could ensure in this way more coherence, efficiency and visibility of the eu's external policy. the commission believes that we should join forces. that is what europe needs. that is what the people of europe expect of us. and that is what the international community expects of us. thank you for your attention.

member of the commission. − mr president, let me first apologise on behalf of peter mandelson, who is not able to be here to discuss with this house the regulation on the generalised system of preferences (gsp). he has asked me to speak on his behalf. i thank you for your work and the valuable comments made on the proposal for a gsp regulation for 2009-2011. the commission considered it important that parliament should be able to express its opinion, and we really appreciate the effort you have made to examine the proposals and provide an opinion, even in a rather short timetable. we therefore welcome the opinion and the opportunity to engage with you and explain the commission’s position. the gsp scheme is an important pro-development instrument of eu trade policy. the commission therefore appreciates the recognition in the opinion that the eu’s gsp is the most important such scheme among the developed countries and that it continues to make an important contribution to the objective of promoting development and poverty reduction in the developing world. we share the objective expressed by parliament that the scheme should continue to operate in a stable, transparent and predictable manner. these aspects are important for the beneficiary countries themselves, giving them and economic operators within the eu a firmer basis for their own decision-making on trade and investment opportunities. the commission considers that all three components of the scheme – the standard gsp for all beneficiaries, the ‘gsp plus’ for those countries that make specific commitments in terms of adherence to international standards for good governance and sustainable development, and the everything but arms initiative for the least-developed countries – are operating well and in line with the overall policy orientations put in place for the period 2006-2015. that is why the basic approach underpinning the proposed regulation for 2009-2011 is one of continuity in substance, combined with some technical updating. we are working actively with the member states in the council towards agreement on the final regulation. the presidency has set the objective of achieving this before the end of june. that is something the commission supports, since an early decision is important to ensure that beneficiary countries and all other interested parties, including business operators, have sufficient notice of the changes to be made next january. another very important reason for an early decision is that all those countries that wish to apply for ‘gsp plus’ treatment will have to do so by the end of october and need confirmation as soon as possible of the relevant criteria and the process they will have to follow. i would note that some of parliament’s comments and suggestions in fact relate to issues that go beyond the scope of this regulation, even if they are certainly issues of importance from a development perspective. reform of the ec’s preferential rules of origin, including for the purpose of the gsp, is being taken forward in a separate exercise headed by commissioner kovács. a number of comments also touch on the need to ensure that developing countries are able to access sufficient and good-quality aid for trade to help them build trade capacity and harness the potential of trade to drive their own economic growth and sustainable development. here the european union has already demonstrated its strong commitment and, in the eu aid for trade strategy of october 2007, has put in place a firm basis on which to make yet further improvements. in conclusion, let me repeat that we very much appreciate the interest shown by parliament in these proposals.

vice-president of the commission. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the commission has already made a number of proposals. we are talking today about a project which is a pilot for one of the
