economy and thereby contribute to job creation. the commission is clear that cutting red tape must never lead to less security for our citizens. so it is not a question of lowering standards, but of enforcing standards in such a way as to avoid unnecessary bureaucratic burdens on our companies. this principle has been strictly observed in this case as well. let me emphasize that the commission does not intend to change the substance of the food hygiene regulations in the slightest. the identification of hazards and the identification of process steps in the manufacturing process at which hazards can be eliminated remain the central concerns. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the draft directive on the protection of the health of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos. we want to ensure that the existing flexible provisions on reporting obligations are applied more efficiently. this does not impose any additional burden on the competent authorities in the member states, since the responsibility for compliance is already with the food manufacturers and not with the authorities. we want a system for small businesses which will be exempted from certain requirements of the existing regulation. it is about the very small family businesses: bakeries, small grocery stores, market stalls, cafes and bars, petrol stations, small supermarkets. the question is why we are asking these small family businesses, none of which have anything to do with the single market, to be subjected to the same bureaucratic procedures as the largest supermarket chain. that is the question at hand. i would like to stress that the relevant regulations apply to all food manufacturers involved in the production, processing and distribution of food, irrespective of their size. the rules do not apply to food intended for private domestic consumption. nor are producers of small quantities of unprocessed products for local retail outlets such as farming, hunting and fishing affected. the existing flexible reporting requirements do not differentiate between different sizes of enterprises. so you get this straight: the small shop on the corner where you can still shop at 10 p.m. here in brussels has to meet exactly the same regulations as the huge supermarket chains. i really wonder if that can be right. the nature of the business is such that these very difficult and very extensive regulations are easy to cope with for large companies, but not for small ones. the formal application of the haccp system requires food manufacturers to carry out a hazard analysis. this can be a complex and demanding task requiring expertise. to reduce the burden of such analysis, the regulation already allows small food manufacturers to use a guide to good practice. this guide is produced by the sector relevant to their activities. it is already available for bakeries, breweries, butchers and restaurants in several member states, but not everywhere. the commission proposal aims to ensure that the possible derogations already covered in principle by the regulation and the accompanying guidelines are used more efficiently. in practice, this would mean, and this is the crux of the matter: if a food manufacturer can demonstrate during the initial steps of testing under haccp that there are no hazards to be avoided, eliminated or reduced to an acceptable level, in other words that there is no risk at all in such an establishment, or if he can demonstrate that identified hazards are sufficiently controlled, he should be exempted from all other requirements of the haccp directive. this flexibility - to put it very clearly - is already provided for in the existing directive. it is only not applied by all member states. the commission's proposal is a fast track action, an immediate and rapidly implemented measure within the framework of our action programme on reducing bureaucracy. the proposal has been met with resistance in the council and in some member states, i know that. these member states do not seem to attach the same importance to reducing administrative burdens and red tape costs - especially for their small and medium-sized enterprises - as the commission and the european parliament. however, we have had to give the impression that the discussion among the member states has so far been a purely official discussion and that the political leaders in the member states have not yet addressed this issue. i do not think that the political leaders in the member states whose officials have so far resisted can represent it to their public when hundreds of thousands of micro and small businesses in those countries could get the relief that the commission is proposing but the member state is rejecting. at that moment all the agitation and propaganda we often see against brussels - the 'allegedly so regulatory monster' that wants to regulate everything and wants to restrict everything - would collapse into itself and it would become clear who is really responsible for unnecessary bureaucratic burdens. the commission regrets this, since this proposal is an important substantive and symbolic element of our action programme to reduce administrative burdens. i thank mr schnellhardt for his report and his active support. i urge you all to support this report because i am convinced that a clear political opinion from parliament, as can be given today, will also create the necessary political momentum in the council to push through this proposal.

member of the commission. − mr president, whenever we speak about international trade or european integration, we have to think of customs, which is responsible, at the eu external borders, for the correct administration of all the measures designed to tackle the dual challenge which customs is facing today: to facilitate trade while also protecting european citizens and the environment. during the last 40 years, european customs has done its best to work efficiently together like one single administration. it has often been the avant-garde in european integration. it is truly remarkable that a policy which does not very often hit the front pages has nevertheless managed to play a pioneering role in opening new paths both for the economic development and the integration of the community. today the role of customs remains important, difficult and, regrettably, not as highly valued by the public as it should be. however, the correct work of customs forms the basis for the success of our single market and the free movement of goods, persons, capital and services. customs action touches the very core of community work and impacts on the daily life of our citizens, often without people realising it. in order to raise our citizens’ awareness about the crucial role of customs, i have launched an eu-wide communication campaign on the occasion of the 40th anniversary of the customs union. member states’ customs authorities have backed this idea. last week i visited three main points of entry for goods at the eu’s external borders – the port of rotterdam, frankfurt airport and the röszke crossing point at the hungarian-serbian border – with a view to highlighting the everyday work and the high motivation of our customs officials. this is the subject of a news package now available to the media in order to inform the public in the coming months. coming back to the core issues, customs today have to meet five strategic objectives: the first is to protect the financial interests of the community and its members. in 2007 the total amount of custom duties transferred to the eu budget amounted to eur 16.6 billion, which represents 16% of the community budget. the second is to facilitate legitimate trade and to support the competitiveness of european companies: the modernisation of the community customs code and the introduction of ecustoms are two instruments to this end. the most recent concrete achievement was the introduction of the authorised economic operator concept as of 1 january 2008. the third is to protect the safety of our citizens against terrorists, drugs and counterfeited and pirated goods that can even endanger their health and life, by controlling the supply chains used for the international movement of goods. the fourth is to maintain, develop and enhance cooperation between the customs authorities of the member states, between customs and other government law enforcement agencies and, furthermore, between customs and the business community. the fifth is the cooperation between the european union and third countries – cooperation with other target countries for fake goods and terrorist devices, like the us. our approach is based on exchange of information, cooperation on risk analysis and risk management, the mutual recognition of security standards, findings of security controls and the customs-trade partnership; but also on cooperation with countries of origin of counterfeited and pirated goods, like china, where 60% of the fake goods come from. in 2005, we signed a customs cooperation agreement and established a joint customs cooperation committee which meets annually. last year we launched a pilot project on smart and secure tradelanes between european and chinese ports and recently we have started to develop a programme of action to be signed at the december eu-china summit. we need to establish similar cooperation with other countries like india, turkey, the united arab emirates and others. since 1993, once a consignment is cleared by a national customs authority, it is free to circulate amongst all the other member states. this means that customs have one single opportunity to control goods and seize any illegal traffic. the result is that the customs union is as strong as its weakest link. by this i mean that it would be very easy for traders to spot the point where controls are less accurate or less strong and divert the illegal consignments to these points. it underlines the responsibility of the customs authorities of member states with external borders. in view of the ever-increasing international trade and this responsibility to combat counterfeiting, customs activity remains high. i will give you some figures to illustrate the workload in 2007: 183 million customs declarations were processed, which means around 5.5 customs declarations every second; 1 545 million tonnes of seaborne cargo and 3 million tonnes of airborne cargo were handled; 43 cases of fake goods were found and seized, which amounted to 79 million counterfeited and pirated articles, and the trend is upwards. we will only be able to meet the dual challenge that customs are facing if we rethink our working methods. this means, for example, moving from the current transaction-based approach of customs formalities and controls to a system-based approach focusing on the internal control systems and supply chain of the economic operators. of course this does not mean abandoning the control of individual shipments but basing these controls on risk analysis. such a new approach implies new working and control methods and a common risk management strategy for all eu customs services. it will also offer a platform for working with the member states on the most appropriate operational structure to be put in place in future for an efficient functioning of the customs union. new working methods also imply that all national customs authorities are well equipped with skills, competences and resources that can maintain and increase their efficiency and effectiveness. to reach these objectives, the commission proposed, in its communication on a strategy for the evolution of the customs union, the development of a strategic plan. this long-term planning should allow national authorities to forecast their needs for resources, training and equipment so as to permit the developments to be made in a synchronised and harmonised way throughout the 27 member states. this permanent channel of communication will also help us to ensure a simultaneous implementation of the new measures. on the eve of the 40th anniversary of the customs union, i am asking for your political support for the commission’s initiative for a strategy on the evolution of the customs union. i am glad that the text of the resolution to be voted on thursday takes into account most of the commission’s ideas about the major axes of evolution of the customs union on closer cooperation, addressing security and enhancing the efficiency, effectiveness and delivery of customs for the benefit of the internal market. i would not like to conclude this statement without thanking the european parliament for all the support it has given to customs throughout the years.
the socialist group will be voting in favour of the report. the commission is not the european union is not a party to the treaty of rome, but it is a party to the treaty of rome. the 40th anniversary of the customs union is a remarkable date. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. i think it is important that we keep telling the citizens this, that we make it clear to them what they have from the european union, what we achieved in this context. i would like to say that the commission has not been able to take the necessary steps to ensure that the budget is properly implemented. the work you are also doing with china and the european union countries you mentioned, these are important steps for our economy, but also for our consumers in the european union. because we want to have safe products and safe services that we can move forward. and that is of great importance. we have now also brought modernity into our last guidelines for the customs union by introducing electronic customs. i think that's also very forward-looking. if we succeed in bringing these positive aspects of european union policy to the outside, if we succeed in making it clear to the citizens what they have from the european union, then we will be able to lead them back to the european union. this is what we should be doing together. i would like to thank you very much, commissioner, for the work you are doing in this connection in the european commission.

the commission's vice-president - mr president, i too would like to thank our minister, mr dragutin mate, president of the council. i would first like to say that this case really proves that the codecision procedure is effective, even when it comes to complex and difficult cases. the european commission advocates an integrated approach to migration, and this coherent approach requires a consolidation of the channels of regular immigration, the integration of immigrants in local situations, an effective and generous asylum system. but of course, if we accept this regulation of the conditions for admitting third country nationals to the european union, we must also provide for rules applying to those who do not or no longer meet the conditions. otherwise, our immigration policy would lose its legitimacy. it must be recognized that there is a risk of a vicious circle. by not doing anything about illegal immigration, we make life more difficult for those who are at risk of exploitation by malicious employers and we also make it more difficult for those who are there, the regular immigrants, to integrate. so i think we must break this vicious circle by the balance that minister mate spoke of. the directive incorporates into community law the relevant provisions of the european convention on human rights. its adoption will enable us to apply the community control mechanisms designed to monitor compliance with the acquis. whether it is the priority given to voluntary return, the right of irregularly staying persons at risk of return, the retention of these conditions, the protection of the best interests of the child, respect for family life in the context of return or respect for the principle of non-refoulement, the directive reduces the grey areas and thus makes it possible to better combat the exploitation of children by illegally staying third-country nationals. the directive obliges member states either to take a decision to repatriate or to grant a right of residence to a third-country national. this approach enhances legal certainty for all concerned. the directive therefore also has the advantage of giving the commission the possibility of monitoring its implementation and i can assure you that the commission and myself, who am in charge of this dossier, will ensure that the fundamental principles of respect for the rights of migrants are respected. in particular, we will assess the impact of certain provisions on detention, entry ban and legal aid. as mr mate said, the directive will oblige all member states to pay particular attention to the rights of the child. the implementation of these rules must be in accordance with the european convention on human rights and the united nations convention on the rights of the child. the commission will take particular care to ensure that the specific situation of these most vulnerable persons is adequately taken into account. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank in particular mr manfred weber, the fictitious rapporteurs and your committee for the extremely important work that has been done in the pursuit of what i believe is a in writing. − why i voted against the deportation directivethe directive, which has been negotiated by eu interior ministers, not only includes a possible period of detention for so-called 'illegal immigrants' of up to 18 months, but also a five-year entry ban for refugees once deported. the directive threatens deportation and expulsion to the 'home country' of some 8 million non-eu citizens who do not have a valid residence permit. the directive also provides for the possibility of detention and deportation of unaccompanied minors. this is clearly in breach of the un convention on the protection of children. the plan is to deport migrants to transit countries other than their home countries. many procedural safeguards and legal rights for migrants to challenge their expulsion have disappeared from the final text, which also jeopardises the rights of those migrants who can apply for asylum. overall, the directive creates a basis for stigmatisation and criminalisation of migrants who are deprived of their liberty and detained in inhumane deportation prisons without having committed any crime. the directive lowers european and international human rights standards by further worsening the living conditions of migrants. this new step is the logic of the immigration and asylum policy practised by the eu states since 1990, which is characterized by a permanent reduction in the rights of migrants. now we must resist the implementation.

member of the commission. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, we are still discussing a subject which concerns the safety of citizens on the roads of europe. i think we should insist on this. i had am glad that we can conclude today, once again, legislation concerning road safety and therefore the safety of all european citizens. in the 2001 white paper on european transport policy, commissioned by mrs loyola de palacio, the commission proposed an ambitious target of halving the number of lives lost on the roads by 2010. this initiative was welcomed by parliament and has always been supported by parliament. i said that, unfortunately, the results have not been as positive as we would have liked, after a series of extremely positive data in recent years. and we are all aware, of course, that the vast majority of accidents are mainly due to human error or carelessness. however, road conditions, combined with increasing traffic volumes, also often play a decisive role in causing accidents. it has been shown that the condition of the road infrastructure plays a decisive role in one in three accidents. for this reason, in addition to initiatives aimed at improving user behaviour and the level of vehicle safety, infrastructure should be the third pillar of any road safety programme based on the principle of the integrated approach. the proposal for a directive on the safety management of road infrastructure offers a good mix of preventive and corrective measures. the procedures introduced by the directive aim to ensure the integration of safety at all stages of planning, design, construction, as well as the management and operation of the road infrastructure. the directive is certainly not intended to teach civil engineers how to build roads and it is certainly not an incentive to build new roads. it is rather a tool which aims to extend to all member states procedures which are already in use, sometimes in different ways. the added value of action at european level is to generalise and disseminate these best practices to member states that do not yet apply them. mr markov and his colleagues in the committee on transport have worked hard on the proposal and have helped to improve its outcome. the text of the proposal has been amended as it has passed through the institutions. many administrative and information requirements have been removed in order to alleviate the bureaucratic burden of the proposal. the annexes, which list the elements to be considered for the procedures introduced by the directive, have been made non-compulsory. some definitions have been revised to make them consistent with existing practices in some member states. however, the main elements of the initial proposal remain unchanged and the present text is therefore acceptable to the commission. once adopted, the directive will be the first european union instrument directed at road infrastructure as a whole and will be a particularly important and powerful instrument. i would remind you once again that this directive, if applied to the transeuropean network, will save more than 600 lives and prevent some 7,000 accidents every year. it is clear that the directive will also have a significant social and economic impact. it will start a long process. the aim is to change the cultural approach to safety in the design, construction and maintenance of roads. in this sense, it is a directive which looks to the future and which can be valid for the next 50 years. thank you again, mr. markov, for the work you've done, and thank you again for your attention.

acting president of the council. - madam president, i would first of all like to express my gratitude to the slovenian presidency, to the rapporteur of the draft in parliament and to the commission, who managed to combine their efforts to reach an agreement on the inclusion of aviation in the european emission trading system, and i know that it was difficult. this agreement is a very important political signal and at the same time an instrument for achieving the ambitious objectives we have set ourselves to combat climate change. it is also an ambitious undertaking that is part of a broader political context, that of the ongoing negotiations on the energy/climate package in europe, and the ongoing negotiations in the world on the fight against climate change. finally, the international economic and political context is difficult and has made the negotiation of this text particularly difficult. several factors had to be taken into account: the rising price of oil, the concern to preserve the international competitiveness of european airlines, the desire and commitment of the union to combat climate change and the pursuit of an international agreement in copenhagen in 2009. it was necessary to take account of the interests of each individual, the interests of regions which, because of their geographical situation, are very much dependent on aviation for their development or for their links with metropolitan areas. we have also taken into account airlines in the new member states, which have a low but rapidly growing mobility rate. finally, the special situation of small and mediumsized enterprises is also taken into account, so that the compromise which you have before you today is a balanced but ambitious package of measures. this compromise recognises that aviation will also have to contribute to the effort to reduce co2 emissions and, at the same time, it allows this industry sector, which is obviously very important, to prepare and adapt to the new environmental requirements. the quota rate being auctioned is moderate, very moderate, and the ceiling on which the allocations to be allocated to the various operators will be calculated remains realistic. this agreement is international in scope, covering european companies as well as those from third countries. it will have to take account of the equivalent measures that these third countries could take and, above all, it should be seen as a precursor to a future global agreement on the participation of international aviation in the carbon market. that's our ambition. the member states and the commission therefore wish to continue discussions in the various international fora to create the conditions for such a global agreement, or at bilateral level to forge links between the european system and other national or regional systems to come. finally, we have taken care to send a particular signal to developing countries, many of which could see their airlines exempted from the system thanks to the de minimis clause which has been incorporated into the text of the agreement. in conclusion, in the same spirit, it is stated that the proceeds from the sale of allowances by auction should be used - the term has been weighed - to combat the effects of climate change in europe and outside europe through a whole series of measures which are listed in the text. the focus was on measures to facilitate adaptation to climate change in developing countries, aeronautics research and low-emission transport.

expected to double again by 2020. it is therefore necessary to take decisive action, which is not possible at the level of the member states but only at the level of the european union. the agreement continue to work within the united nations framework convention on climate change and the international civil aviation organisation to achieve an effective global agreement to address aviation member of the commission. − madam president, i would like to thank all the contributors for their very positive positions. by reaching an agreement on this directive the community institutions are demonstrating their determination to adopt the concrete measures which are necessary to implement the european union’s ambitious climate change goals. this directive is the first of a series of measures which are designed to deliver on the european union’s greenhouse gas objective by 2020. its adoption is a positive signal for the forthcoming negotiations on the climate and energy package and the international negotiations in poznań and copenhagen. i have just been informed that the g8 have agreed on a long-term reduction target of 50% in 2050. although we welcome this, it is only a partial step forward because they failed to agree on a mid-term target despite the fact that both the european union member states and the commission insisted on the necessity of a mid-term target. today, on the basis of the agreed text, all flights to and from the european union airports will be fully included in the european union emissions trading scheme from 2012. this means that from 2012 aircraft operators will need emission allowances to cover their flights into and out of the european union. in 2012 the number of emissions allowances allocated to the aviation sector will be 3% below the sector’s average annual emissions for the years 2004-2006. from 2013 the number of allowances will be 5% lower. like other industries in the scheme, they will be able to sell any allowances they do not need on the market, but if their emissions are higher they will need to buy more allowances or emission credits from clean energy projects in third countries. this is how the emissions trading scheme creates an incentive for participants to minimise their emissions. the majority of allowances to airlines will be free but 15% of allowances will be auctioned. the revenues from this auctioning should be used to tackle climate change in the european union and third countries, especially developing countries. this level may be increased from 2013 as part of the ongoing discussions to revise the emissions trading directive. in january this year the commission proposed that 20% of allowances for aviation should be auctioned in 2013, increasing to 100% in 2020. while supporting this agreement, the commission position in the context of the revised emissions trading directive remains that the auctioning level in the aviation sector should be 20% in 2013 and increased in line with sectors other than the power sector. for these sectors it is proposed to auction 20% of allowances in 2013, increasing to 100% in 2020. as regards the issue of nitrogen oxide emissions, the commission indicated in its original proposal that a separate measure would be proposed to address nitrogen oxide emissions and can make the following declaration:‘the commission recalls that it intends to issue by december 2008 a legislative proposal to introduce measures to limit nitrogen oxide emissions from aviation, in particular to address effectively the climate change impact and to avoid any negative incentives to reduce carbon dioxide emissions at the expense of nitrogen oxides.’ in conclusion, the commission is very pleased. i would like to particularly thank dr liese for his excellent work and results. we are very pleased with the outcome of the negotiations. the commission can accept the proposed compromise amendments in full. the next item is the report by olle schmidt, on behalf of the committee on economic and monetary affairs, on the annual report of the ecb for 2007 (2008/2107 ((ini)) (a6-0241/2007).
president of the european central bank. mr president, mr rapporteur, ladies and gentlemen of the european parliament, it is my honour to present to you, as required by the treaty, the 2007 annual report of the european central bank. our relations go far beyond the obligations imposed by the treaty, and the european central bank welcomes the very close relationship we have with parliament. this is the fourth time this year that i have spoken before you. my colleagues in the executive board have also been in close contact with the european parliament, particularly on subjects such as the enlargement of the euro area, payment systems and the tenth anniversary of economic and monetary union. i will first give you a brief overview of the economic developments in 2007/2008 and explain the monetary policy measures of the ecb. i would then like to make some comments on the points and suggestions you have made in your draft resolution to the ecb annual report 2007. in 2007 the ecb operated in a challenging environment with rising and volatile commodity prices and, since the second half of 2007, heightened uncertainty stemming from the ongoing correction in financial markets across the world that was mentioned by the rapporteur. despite these developments, the euro area economy continued to expand at solid rates in 2007, with annual real gdp growing by 2.7%. in the first half of 2008, moderate ongoing growth in real gdp has continued, although the quarter-on-quarter profile is likely to show significant volatility owing to temporary, in part weather-related, factors. it is therefore important to focus on the medium-term trend when assessing growth developments. looking ahead, on the external side, growth in emerging countries should remain robust, supporting euro area foreign demand. on the domestic side, the economic fundamentals of the euro area remain sound and the euro area does not suffer from major imbalances. unemployment rates and labour force participation have increased significantly in recent years, and unemployment rates have fallen to levels not seen for 25 years. that being said, the uncertainty surrounding this outlook for growth remains high, with downside risks mainly related to further unanticipated increases in commodity prices, possible further spillovers from continuing tensions in financial markets to the real economy and increasing protectionist tendencies. turning to price developments, in 2007 average annual hicp inflation in the euro area was 2.1%, slightly above the ecb's definition of price stability. however, at the end of the year, substantial increases in international oil and food prices brought inflation to levels well above 2%. since then, inflation in the euro area has risen further and, in the wake of renewed sharp commodity price increases, reached the worrying level of around 4% in mid-2008. looking ahead, the annual hicp inflation rate is likely to remain well above the level consistent with price stability for some time, moderating only gradually in 2009. risks to price stability over the medium term remain clearly on the upside in 2007 and have intensified over recent months. these risks include possible further rises in commodity prices and unanticipated increases in indirect taxes and administered prices. in addition the governing council is strongly concerned that price and wage-setting behaviour could add to inflationary pressure through broadly-based second-round effects. first signs are already emerging in some regions of the euro area. in this context, indexation schemes for nominal wages are of particular concern and should be avoided. as in 2007, the monetary analysis in the first half of 2008 has continued to confirm the prevailing upside risks to price stability at medium to longer horizons. in line with our monetary policy strategy, we take the view that the sustained underlying strength of monetary and credit expansion in the euro area over the past few years has created upside risks to price stability. to contain prevailing upside risks to price stability over the medium term, the governing council further adjusted the monetary policy stance in march and june 2007. after a period of unusually high uncertainty in the context of the financial market correction, in july 2008 the governing council brought the minimum bid rate in the main refinancing operations of the euro system to 4.25%. this action underlines the governing council's strong determination to prevent second-round effects and maintain longer-term inflation expectations firmly anchored in line with price stability. this is the contribution of the ecb's monetary policy to preserving purchasing power over the medium term and supporting sustainable growth and employment in the euro area. following last week's decision to raise rates, in the governing council's current assessment the monetary policy stance will contribute to achieving price stability over the medium term. we will continue to monitor very closely all developments over the period ahead. in the draft resolution you raise a number of issues of relevance for the ecb. i would like to assure you that we will consider the remarks which have just been made and all the remarks which are in the resolution with great care and we will report back to you accordingly. let me perhaps very briefly elaborate on some of these points. on the monetary policy strategy, i would like to start by welcoming the positive assessment made by the committee on economic and monetary affairs on the ecb's monetary policy strategy. our two-pillar framework ensures that all information relevant for the assessment of risks to price stability is taken into account in a consistent and systematic manner when taking monetary policy decisions. in 2007 the governing council launched within the euro system a research agenda to further enhance its monetary analysis, as also proposed in the draft resolution to continue to improve the ecb's analytical infrastructure. on transparency, i would also like to welcome the committee's recognition that making the minutes of the ecb governing council meeting available to the public would not necessarily be advisable. such a measure would draw attention to individual positions when, in a euro area of 15 and very soon 16 countries, what counts is the position of the collegial decision-maker, the governing council, the college. it could also lead to pressures on governing council members to abandon their necessarily euro area perspective when taking monetary policy decisions. as already emphasised on previous occasions, i see the introductory statement i present on behalf of the governing council at the monthly press conference as an equivalent to what other central banks call summary minutes. together with the ensuing question-and-answer session, the introductory statement provides in real time a comprehensive overview by the governing council of the current monetary policy stance. this communication instrument has served us well in guiding financial-market expectations. in the field of fiscal policies, the ecb shares the view expressed that all member states must fully respect the stability and growth pact. a renewed increase in the euro-area aggregate fiscal deficit ratio is projected for 2008. there is a clear risk that some countries will not comply with the provisions of the preventive arm of the stability and growth pact. achieving sound and sustainable budgetary positions and on this basis allowing the free operation of automatic stabilizers is the best contribution we trust fiscal policy can make to macroeconomic stability. the draft resolution also refers to the risks posed by economic differentials across euro area countries, which to some extent reflect structural rigidities and/or inappropriate national policies. it goes without saying that economic divergences across euro area countries cannot be addressed by monetary policy. in order to avoid a protracted period of either low growth and high unemployment or overheating, as a country response to asymmetric shocks, reforms to enhance the resilience to such shocks should be undertaken at the national level. these include well-designed structural reforms to enhance competition, increase productivity and foster labour market flexibility. let me emphasize again that there is a need for lucid monitoring of national competitiveness developments including unit labour costs as recouping ex post loss of competitiveness is a difficult exercise. in this regard we support parliament's call for responsible wages and price policies. let me now turn to the issues highlighted by the financial-market correction for crisis prevention and crisis management, which also figures prominently in parliament's analysis. as regards crisis prevention, the market correction highlighted issues for both supervisors and central banks. supervisors should make further efforts to reinforce cooperation and exchange of information on a cross-border basis. it is of crucial importance to further exploit the potential of the lamfalussy framework. the ecofin council has agreed on certain measures to that end, and attention should now shift towards implementing those guidelines. the market correction, in our view, has not provided any convincing evidence for an overhaul of the current supervisory framework, for example through the setting-up of a new authority for eu supervision. central banks, including the ecb, have to a great extent been effective in identifying the weaknesses and risks to the financial system that materialised as the turmoil unfolded. i will not elaborate on that. looking for the lessons for crisis management, the main issue that emerged during the turmoil concerns the need for a smooth flow of information between central banks and supervisors during the unfolding of a crisis. central banks may need supervisory information for the effective performance of their functions in the management of the crisis. this applies to the eurosystem as it applies to all central banks. supervisors from their side may benefit from central bank information. therefore, the envisaged strengthening of the eu legal basis for information exchange between central banks and supervisors is very strongly supported by the ecb. let me conclude with some remarks concerning the integration of europe's payment systems. we noted with satisfaction the positive assessments in the draft resolution about sepa and target2. as regards the eurosystem's target2-securities initiative, the governing council will decide in the coming weeks on the continuation of the t2s project. it is important to note that all major csds have responded positively to our initiative.

(applause) i would like to thank secondly, i understand that for a number of countries - i am thinking in particular of those that joined us in 2004, where the bulk of energy is fossil fuels - the effort required is considerable. and these countries tell us, "we've had growth for ten years, don't come and break the growth we have". there is no doubt that there is a way to bring everyone together, and we must work with the president of the commission to ensure that everyone can say to himself that he will not be condemned to recession, misery, poverty and unemployment. but this energy-climate package is our top priority. the world can 't wait; europe must lead the way. secondly, we are now 24 of the 27 countries in the schengen area, which means 24 of the 27. you say 23? well, 23 if you like, but that's not bad, not counting those who are not part of the european union, but are part of it - that's why there are often debates between us - about the schengen area. but it doesn't matter. what does that mean? this means that we have therefore decided to allow full free movement between the countries of the schengen area. i would like to say to the group chairmen and to the members that on behalf of france, on behalf of france, with bernard kouchner and jean-pierre jouyet, we have taken a decision which was not so easy to take. since 1 july, there are no longer any barriers to access to the french labour market, as i have announced that i will remove all the restrictions that had been negotiated by my predecessors; all workers from all european countries can come to work in france. (applause) i would like to thank it wasn't that simple. it wasn't that easy. moreover - and i am speaking under the control of french parliamentarians of all persuasions - i was told the worst would happen if i announced this decision and, as usual, the decision was taken, and the worst did not happen. i did not like the controversy over the famous 'polish plumber', which gave a very bad image of my country and a very bad image of europe. that is not why we have both built the european union. (applause) i would like to thank but, since we no longer have borders between us, is it legitimate, is it reasonable to continue to define, each on our own, an immigration policy that ignores the constraints of others? the european pact for immigration is an essential document for the french presidency in two respects. firstly - and i would like to speak to the left of the house first - if we all, the european countries, adopt a european immigration policy, we will remove immigration from national debates where the extremes use the misery of some and the fear of others in the service of values that are not ours. the only way to make the debate on immigration responsible is to make it a european policy, free of political bias and forcing countries with different sensibilities to work together. what was proposed by brice hortefeux, adopted by all the ministers, and which must be discussed in coreper and then in the european council, seems to me to be a priority which will demonstrate that europe does not want to be a fortress, that europe does not refuse to welcome, that europe needs labour immigration, but that europe cannot welcome all those who would like to come to europe. i would add that, as far as political asylum is concerned, it is not normal that one person can lodge 27 applications in 27 democracies and that the responses of these 27 democracies are not the same when faced with the same problem. i would add that, for development with africa, we will be stronger by working together; this is the second priority of the french presidency. thirdly, we want to promote a concept which has been discussed a great deal in europe but which is making little progress, namely european defence. i am well aware that there is a great deal of disagreement on this issue. but i would like to be allowed to express my convictions. how can you expect europe to be a political power with a loud voice if europe is not able to defend itself and to put resources at the service of its policy? let us take kosovo as an example, which i believe is a success of the european union. this is a european problem, which must be solved by europeans. how can the europeans continue to solve it if the europeans do not have the military and human resources to enforce the decisions we have taken together? how can we imagine making europe the most prosperous economic area if we are not able to defend ourselves? of course there is nato and it does not occur to anyone, certainly not to me, to question the usefulness of nato. it is not european defence policy or nato, it is nato, the alliance with the americans, and an autonomous european security policy. it's both, not one against the other. i would add that we cannot go on with a europe which ensures its security through the contribution of only four or five countries, while the rest is dependent on the efforts of these four or five countries. we cannot continue to build aircraft in our own backyard, to have a competing arms industry which is going bankrupt and ultimately weakening, simply because we do not have the strength to conduct a european defence policy. the fourth priority is the difficult question of the common agricultural policy. and i will come to my conclusion, which is related to this. it is precisely because it is difficult that it is appropriate to talk about it. i am well aware that there are agricultural states among us which are ardent defenders of the work of their peasants and that at the same time there are states which think that this policy is too costly. ladies and gentlemen, may i appeal to your common sense. by 2050, there will be nine billion people on the planet. already, 800 million people on the planet are starving. there's a child starving to death every 30 seconds. is it reasonable to ask europe to reduce its agricultural production when the world has never needed food so much? i am not going to go into detail. i would like to begin by welcoming you all and making a few remarks on the plenary session in strasbourg. as you know, the partial collapse of the ceiling of the plenary chamber in strasbourg on 7 august has made it necessary to hold this first plenary session of the european parliament in brussels in september as an exception. i have taken this decision in the interests of the greatest possible security for members and staff, after reviewing the preliminary expertise carried out and after consulting the chairmen of the political groups and the french presidency. the decision also takes account of the need for continuity in the legislative work of the european parliament. according to the preliminary findings, the partial collapse of the retracted interlayer is due to the breakage of components connecting the interlayer to the actual roof structure. the ongoing investigations, carried out by several independent international civil engineering firms commissioned by parliament, will reveal further details and the responsibilities associated with the collapse. these investigations are carried out in close cooperation with the responsible municipal authorities and with a high-level expert on building safety appointed by the french government. the liability and responsibilities between those involved in the construction of the original ceiling will be determined after the final results of the investigation are available. the ceiling in the plenary hall is now completely suspended by a new technique previously approved by the independent experts and the local building authorities. although every effort is made to move forward with the work as quickly as possible, the necessary procedure is lengthy. we hope that all the safety and repair checks will be completed before the second plenary session in september. in all our deliberations and decisions, safety is our paramount concern.

acting president of the council. - madam president, ladies and gentlemen, it is a great honour for me to speak before you today and to tell you of my deep attachment to the values of the european union. at the heart of these values is, of course, justice. you have wished to open your plenary session with a joint debate on justice issues, which is a sign of the interest your assembly takes in the decision on the european judicial network, the decision on eurojust and the framework decision on the enforcement of judgments in default. these three texts will advance judicial cooperation within the european union, and they will also change the way the member states work. these three initiatives are also awaited by those who are at the service of justice in our countries. the jha council meeting of 25 july reached political agreement on the draft decisions on the european judicial network and the strengthening of eurojust. the joint efforts of the slovenian and french presidencies have made it possible to achieve this in less than a year. these two draft decisions are aimed at greater protection of european citizens and at strengthening judicial cooperation in criminal matters. it is a sign of a european union which acts and progresses taking into account fundamental freedoms and rights. as regards the european judicial network, the draft decision which should replace the 1998 joint action clarifies the obligations of eurojust and the network. it takes account of the wish of the member states to maintain its two structures and to strengthen their complementarity. the secure communication channels between eurojust and the judicial network will allow for effective judicial cooperation and greater mutual trust. the european judicial network is a well-known and recognised tool, it has proved its usefulness in promoting contacts between the actors on the ground, and the report by your colleague, sylvia kaufmann, emphasises the usefulness of the network and its success. it highlights the adaptability of the network to the needs of, in particular, the judiciary. the report also stresses the need to maintain this flexibility and the decentralised way of operating. madam president, you have taken up and supported the main lines of the original proposal, and i thank you for that. you also mention some concerns. you have rightly other. after six years of operation of eurojust, experience shows that there is a need to improve the functioning of this judicial cooperation unit. eurojust is not sufficiently informed, particularly in the field of terrorism. the powers of the national members are not harmonised and eurojust's operational capacity is not sufficiently developed. the text on which a comprehensive political agreement was reached on 25 july is an essential step in the construction of the european judicial area. as you know, the fight against all forms of serious crime is a priority for the european union. for example, eurojust received 14 cases of trafficking in human beings in 2004 and 71 in 2007. this is proof that we must have effective tools to combat trafficking of unprecedented proportions, which is affecting thousands of our fellow citizens. eurojust must also become a leading unit of european judicial cooperation. this text, which the jha council agreed on, will make eurojust more operational and responsive, and is therefore an important step forward for us. i would like to pay particular tribute to the work done by your colleague, renate weber, and thank her for her support. i know his commitment and his desire to make this proposal work. with the strengthening of eurojust, the prerogatives of the national members will be strengthened. an emergency coordination mechanism will be established and the transmission of information will be improved to better respond to the challenges posed by new forms of crime. some would have liked an even more ambitious approach. the institutional framework does not allow this, so all possibilities must be used to strengthen eurojust, at all times, without delay. some of your concerns have also been addressed. the information your parliament receives in connection with the operation of eurojust in this capacity will be carefully considered. as regards the application of the principle of mutual recognition, which is also one of the cornerstones of the construction of an area of justice, freedom and security, the framework decision on the enforcement of judgments in default will strengthen existing instruments, such as the european arrest warrant. a judgment given in the absence of the person by a member state must be enforceable throughout the european union. the framework decision will also be accompanied by a strengthening of the procedural rights of individuals. it is a question of being able to execute default sentences while respecting the rights of the defence. the aim of this framework decision is not to amend national regulations, however, but of course to improve the enforcement of judgments in default. your report, mr france, stresses the need to harmonize the existing instruments, the right to be heard during the procedure must be guaranteed. the diversity of legal systems must be respected, i am thinking, for example, of the manner in which the summons is issued. the council therefore hand, and i do not forget that you are the representatives of the peoples of europe. through these three texts, judicial cooperation in criminal matters is advancing and the common good is advancing the rapporteur. - madam president, i have to say that i am very sorry. i would like to take all my speaking time right now. i am glad that the president of the council and the vice-president of the commission are here. the committee unanimously adopted my report on the judicial network. there has been very constructive cooperation and i would like to thank everyone for it, in particular mr popa, mrs gebhardt and mrs weber, the eurojust rapporteur. the european judicial network ejn has now been in existence for ten years. it's been proven in practice. it has continued to be important since the creation of eurojust in 2002. the ejn is not concerned with coordinating investigations, but with providing direct contacts, assistance in legal aid procedures and information. it is therefore important to leave the flexible decentralised structure of the ejn intact. changes should be made only where necessary or where they are the result of the practice of recent years. an example of this is the establishment of national contact points, which perform coordinating functions within their member state and are responsible for liaising with the ejn secretariat. an important innovation is the establishment of secure telecommunications links. i was pleased to hear that the president-in-office of the council had also raised this question. personal data, such as sensitive data such as fingerprints, are exchanged between the authorities of the member states in the context of a european arrest warrant. in order to ensure security, secure telecommunications channels are needed, since such data cannot be transmitted by fax, for example. the ejn was established in 1998 with the aim of creating a secure telecommunications system, but the details were not agreed, apparently also for cost reasons. the report proposes that secure telecommunications be introduced initially only for the contact points. however, in order to ensure that all contacts between competent authorities are as direct as possible, a second step should also consider the possibility of involving all competent authorities responsible for legal aid in their respective member states in the secure telecommunications. the report makes reference to the relevant data protection provisions because of the sensitivity of the data, and i would like to stress once again the importance of a strong framework decision on the protection of personal data in the context of the third pillar. this would apply to the exchange of data between the member states' respective contact points. the commission has also proposed that the council should adopt a framework decision on the protection of personal data. the functioning of the ejn depends to a large extent on the contact points. therefore, guidelines were developed to ensure that the selection of contact points should be based on certain criteria. those acting as contact points should have a good command of at least one other language of the european union and experience both in the field of international cooperation in criminal matters and in the judicial, prosecutorial or other judicial field. it is important that member states follow these guidelines and, of course, they must also ensure that the contact points have sufficient resources. in order to improve cooperation between the ejn and eurojust and to coordinate their activities, members of eurojust should be able to attend the meetings of the ejn upon invitation and vice versa. the eurojust decision sets out the timing of the notification of cases by the judicial authorities of the member states, including the ejn contact points. this decision complements this obligation by requiring both the ejn and eurojust to inform each other of all cases where they consider that the other body is better placed to deal with the specific case. this flexible and needs-based system aims to avoid excessive notification by national authorities to eurojust and at the same time to 'flood' eurojust with information that the authority cannot process. finally, as regards reporting on the management and operation of the network, this should be done by the ejn itself, not only to the council and commission, of course, but also to parliament. i am glad that the commission is expressly supporting this. this decision adapts the european judicial network to developments in recent years and further defines its relationship with eurojust. in this way, the european judicial network will be able to cope with the task of judicial cooperation in criminal matters, including and in particular in the event that the treaty of lisbon may still enter into force, thereby bringing the field of judicial cooperation in criminal matters into the community.
the socialist group will be voting in favour of the report. the commission has already taken a number of measures to combat fraud. i am very pleased that we can discuss such an important package together today and that we will probably take decisions tomorrow by a very large majority. i would like to thank in particular my two rapporteurs, for whom i was a shadow rapporteur, mrs kaufmann and mrs weber, for their excellent cooperation, because this is a basic condition for us to be able to do a good job. this good work is very important in this area and i am also pleased that the european judicial network has succeeded in ensuring that the work being done there is actually being continued. the commission has already taken a number of initiatives in this area, including the creation of a european centre for the development of vocational training. and that's what we wanted. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. however, as more and more data is exchanged, of course, data protection becomes more and more important, and so does the security of telecommunications and the exchange of this data. i am therefore very pleased that parliament, the commission and the council have reached an agreement, which is very important and which i can only welcome. i am also very pleased that we will be able to have a very large majority in all the reports tomorrow. the extension we have proposed, which i hope the council and the commission will agree to, the addition by parliament, which we owe to mrs weber, of the sexual exploitation of children and child pornography to the list of facts which have not been included so far, is, in my view, a very important issue in our society, which i would like to stress once again. what is particularly important for us social democrats in this context - president of the council. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, ladies and gentlemen, you have kindly waited until the extraordinary european council has finished and i am in a hurry to come and present the results. we wanted - the french presidency wanted - that you be immediately informed of the decisions taken, not only because we want to keep a constant record of our work, but also because the european parliament has been extremely active on the georgian question for several months. thank you, commissioner. we wanted to thank you for this and to tell you what happened, as you know, at the council meeting on 13 august and at the foreign affairs committee meeting on 20 august, where jean-pierre jouyet came to present our provisional conclusions. i would remind you that the conflict began 20 years ago, in 1991/92, but the last phase of the conflict began on the night of 7/8 august. it would be good to look back at this very special beginning, and it would be necessary for journalists and historians to look at the facts, at the way in which they took place in ossetia and more particularly in tskhinvali, the capital of south ossetia. so the battle raged through the night, then on 9 and 10 august, and we decided with my colleague alexander stubb, the finnish foreign minister, who is also the chairman of the osce, to meet in tbilisi from sunday 10 august. we have proposed to president saakashvili a ceasefire agreement, which he has accepted. of course, i'm going over quickly, but it was important, about what we found there, what we saw in gori, on the roads, in that painful episode of the entry and rapid penetration of russian troops. at the moment, the first thing to say is that we feared the arrival of russian troops in tbilisi. the troops were in gori, which is 45 or 50 kilometers from tbilisi. the road was straight and there weren't many obstacles. and so we thought, and we had some reason to think, that the purpose of the russian troops was, as they said, to respond to the provocation and liberate south ossetia, but also to go to tbilisi and impose a change of government. so it was absolutely necessary, or at least we thought it was, that the troops stop and the ceasefire should come as soon as possible. we wanted to see a ceasefire as soon as possible. i joined president sarkozy in moscow the next day, but before that, after speaking with refugees on the georgian side and with the victims i met in the gori hospital, i held out, the presidency of the european union wanted to go and listen to the story of the refugees on the other side, in north ossetia, who came from south ossetia after the bombing of tskhinvali on the night of 7 to 8 august. and i've heard stories that, unfortunately, were similar in terms of suffering but, obviously, had very different interpretations. we met with president sarkozy in moscow, where there were long talks, for five hours, between president medvedev, prime minister putin, the minister of foreign affairs, sergey lavrov, president sarkozy and myself. at the end of these rather tough discussions, there was a press conference, during which president sarkozy and president medvedev explained the six points that made up the french protocol of agreement, a protocol that had to be brought back to tbilisi for acceptance, since changes had taken place between this first round trip and what was to be our last stay in tbilisi the next day. two amendments were accepted by president medvedev and in particular one point on the final status, which he understandably did not want to be included in the text. the ceasefire agreement was accepted by president saakashvili and thanks to this mediation, which you can at least recognize that, even if it was not perfect - because nothing is perfect in a situation like this - it was quick. this mediation has thus brought about an effective ceasefire, with a few sad exceptions. on the ground the russian troops because it was the second of the six points of the document began to withdraw on august 21, that is to say in reality almost eight days later. but there were movements that were interpreted differently, as is always the case, because tanks came in one direction and then also came in the other. today, this withdrawal is not complete. i don't know if it's finished, but it's definitely not done in full. the war ended rather quickly, because on 10 and 11 august the major operations of the war, the operations of the war, were actually completed, according to a number of observers, including our french ambassador, eric fournier, who is here. but what was not finished, and what caused the damage, were the actions of the militias of ossetia, abkhazia, who, behind the russian troops, of course, looted and sometimes killed, although, i must say with great caution, the damage was not considerable. i mean, the damage from the bombing wasn't that extensive. they are still far too serious, far too large, they have caused far too many casualties, but compared to what we were told, the damage was not as great as we feared, which is a good thing. what we didn't see, and what we should have seen, and the accounts were very partial, is what had happened in ossetia. because if it was possible to see, quite quickly, things in georgia, it was not possible to enter ossetia, at least not easily, and only a few managed to do so. in fact, the accounts of each of them differed greatly. so the ceasefire and this was the first of the six points was immediate and effective. there was a temporary ceasefire and a permanent ceasefire. the second point was the withdrawal of troops. it was specified that the withdrawal concerned, for the georgian troops, the withdrawal to their barracks and, for the russian troops, the withdrawal beyond the lines that prevailed before the crisis. there were a number of other points including access to humanitarian aid for all victims. the specific points which were problematic were point 5 and point 6. we had agreed in our negotiations to a zone around the border between south ossetia and georgia so that, temporarily, while waiting for the osce or eu volunteer observers, russian patrols would be tolerated. after that, it was necessary to write a specific letter from president sarkozy, which was published, in agreement with president saakashvili, to specify that it was in the immediate vicinity of the border. the border is in some places two kilometers from the main road that crosses georgia, so it is not easy. so there were a few points that had been agreed upon while waiting - it was very specific in the text - for the arrival of the international observers. we have put "observers" not "peace keepers", all of this will obviously have to be clarified. and then, point 6, which was, in some ways, the most important, concerned the political settlement and the discussions, the international negotiations, which were to preside over the political settlement. so this memorandum of understanding, which was signed by president saakashvili, through, incidentally, mrs condoleezza rice - because the first document was signed but it was amended - then the document with mr medvedev, finally the third and last document with president saakashvili, we did not have it signed. it was midnight or one o'clock in the morning, there was a big smes. the results of these workshops must also be incorporated in the future commission document. the resolution also makes it clear that the final academic framework can serve as a toolbox. he has it in his possession because of his publication. the community legislators will have to base future community private law legislation on the reference framework. the common reference framework may be transformed into a so-called optional instrument at a later stage. the parties should be able to choose voluntarily an alternative civil law system for their legal relationship. this is the way forward if we are to solve the problems which are clearly still present in the internal market. however, in order to give a new impetus to the operation of the internal market, an optional instrument must go beyond general contractual arrangements. it must therefore, for example, contain, in addition to rules on the conclusion of a contract of sale, provisions on the transfer of ownership and rules on the recovery of unlawful transfers of assets i.e. the right of enrichment . parliament is particularly concerned that it is fully consulted and regularly involved by the commission throughout the selection process. we certainly need to think about how we can take greater account of the importance of this project in the future, particularly in the legal affairs committee. the european commission must, however, already now consider mechanisms for adapting the future commission document to new developments. the commission must already take into account in its planning for the ongoing selection process the changes that will be included in the final academic reference framework. all this shows that with the reference framework we are breaking new ground in european contract law. the european parliament, the commission and the council must make a clear commitment to this, perhaps the most important project of the next legislature. this project will benefit everyone: consumers, because they will soon be able to shop across europe on the basis of european contract law, and businesses, because they will be able to serve new markets with increased legal certainty and significant cost savings through a single set of rules.

second point: the legal expenses, which are very important for the consumers and for insurers as well. your report considers several pros and cons of a system where legal expenses would be compulsorily covered, eu-wide, by the motor insurance policy of the liable party. as stated in the commission report of 2007, we are convinced that such a solution would be very unlikely to provide clear benefits for road traffic accident victims; it might even lead to a distortion of well-established national systems of motor claims settlement. in addition, premiums are likely to increase in those countries where either no or limited reimbursement of legal costs has been the practice so far. i am pleased to see that your report reflects some of these concerns and that it gives preference to market-led solutions, such as the use of voluntary legal expenses insurance. it seems to be evident, though, that in some markets this type of insurance cover is hardly used, and that better promotion is needed. this is a mission the market should accomplish itself, as the commission should not promote particular insurance products or particular lines of insurance business. finally, let me address the issue of the awareness of tools and mechanisms under the eu motor insurance directives. the commission agrees that there is room for improvement, especially in relation to the new member states, as regards the degree of citizens’ awareness of the tools created by the eu motor insurance directives, such as the claims representative mechanism or the existence of national information centres. the insurance industry can and should play a major role in this area. the commission has contributed to the information need of both traffic accident victims and motorists through the publication of a number of motor insurance leaflets placed on the ‘your europe’ portal. many other information sources exist at national level, such as automobile clubs, motor insurance bureaux, claims settlement agencies and others. in conclusion: over the last years, regular reporting to the european parliament on motor insurance issues has become a well-established practice and i am looking forward to our continued good cooperation.
