president of the council. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, it is both an honour and a pleasure for me to address you today for two reasons: firstly, because your assembly represents the heart of european democracy. the french presidency is very respectful of your action in the service of european construction and the best proof of our willingness to move forward together in the construction of europe was given by the president of the french republic in his speech in strasbourg in july. i am encouraged by this attitude and my colleagues in the french government share it. secondly, because the draft budget for the financial year 2009, which i am presenting to you today, was unanimously adopted by the council on 17 july. this unanimity proves that this draft budget is balanced and allows all the governments of the european union to recognize it. our first contacts laid a solid foundation for the budgetary procedure. the trilogue and the consultation took place in a constructive atmosphere. we have already agreed on six declarations and i am confident that we will be able to reach agreement on many other matters of common interest. i can assure you that the council is ready to continue this high-quality dialogue in order to reach an agreement on the 2009 budget that is satisfactory to all. this agreement will have to meet three principles: ensuring the financing of the political priorities of the european union and we have defined a financial framework for the period 2007 to 2013, which we must implement in order to achieve our objectives in terms of competitiveness, cohesion and growth. secondly, to respect the rules of budgetary discipline and sound financial management laid down in the interinstitutional agreement. expenditure must remain within the limits set by this agreement and sufficient margins must be maintained under the ceilings of the various headings. finally, appropriations must be adjusted to the strict reality of the needs. in particular, lessons should be drawn from past executions to determine the actual capacity to implement sectoral policies. since the financial perspective was introduced in 1988, the community budget has consistently been under-implemented in payment appropriations. implementation is improving thanks to the action of commissioner dalia grybauskaite, but uncertainties for 2009 are still obviously high and there is no indication at this stage that 2009 will be any different from previous years. it is also important to safeguard the interests of european taxpayers - this is all the more so in the present economic context - and therefore any credit that cannot be used should be avoided as far as possible. the objective of a realistic and balanced budget has therefore been the guiding principle of the council's work. before i present the result, i would like to say a word about the ease of responding to the soaring food prices in developing countries. this will be the focus of our discussions over the next few weeks. the european council of 19 and 20 june gave a strong political impetus by welcoming the commission's intention to submit a proposal for a new fund to support agriculture in developing countries. but the mandate of the european council on this subject is very clear: a solution must be found in strict compliance with the current financial perspective. i know that this view is not shared by the european parliament today. the council will, however, follow this line of reasoning when examining the proposal adopted by the commission on 18 july. finally, i would remind you that the european council recently reaffirmed its willingness to support the reconstruction of georgia, including the areas of south ossetia and abkhazia, in addition to the eur 6 million in emergency aid already released. the union will therefore take the initiative of convening an international conference at the earliest opportunity to assist in the reconstruction of georgia. the european council of yesterday finally asked the council and the commission to start preparing it. i would now like to present the main lines of the draft budget for 2009 drawn up by the council. we are proposing a budget of eur 134 billion in commitment appropriations, which is a reduction of eur 469 million compared with the preliminary draft budget. the increase in commitment appropriations compared with 2008 is therefore 2.8% and the union's commitment capacity is therefore fully preserved. as regards payment appropriations, the council made a limited adjustment of eur 1.7 billion compared with the preliminary draft budget. as you have requested in previous years, the council has not made blind cuts across all the headings. this reduction is based on a detailed analysis of implementation in 2007 and 2008 and on a realistic approach to the implementation and execution capacities of community programmes. the draft budget therefore amounts to eur 115 billion in payment appropriations. the decline in the level of payment appropriations in 2009 is not - i would like to stress this point - a surprise. it had been anticipated since the adoption of the 2007-2013 financial framework. the ceiling for payment appropriations for 2009 is therefore considerably lower than that for 2008 and 2010, in particular because of the evolution of cohesion policy appropriations, which will be marked in 2009 by the end of the 2000-2006 programming period and a gradual increase in the 2007-2013 programming period. we have no indication that new programmes will be started any sooner. on the contrary, the monitoring system for the adoption of management and control systems and major projects shows the delays affecting their launch. thus, out of 433 programmes, only two in hungary have received interim payments. the level of payment appropriations in our draft budget is therefore realistic and adapted to the needs of the union. some points should be emphasized under each heading. on the competitiveness for growth and employment front, the council attaches great importance to the implementation of the lisbon strategy. it has therefore ensured that adequate funding is provided, in particular for research and technological development programmes, trans-european networks and the improvement of the quality of education and lifelong learning. the council has limited the increase in commitment appropriations on the basis of an analysis of the capacity to implement the programmes, as i said. i would like to stress, however, that in this context the increase in commitment appropriations for priority programmes remains very strong. the research framework programme is up 10% compared with 2008, the programme for innovation and competitiveness is up 16% and the programme for lifelong learning, which is essential for european citizens, is up 6%. these examples illustrate the targeted strategy adopted by the council. the council also reduced payment appropriations (eur 471 million) by reducing the appropriations for several targeted lines in order to draw the consequences of implementation. under heading 1b 'cohesion for growth and jobs', the council accepted the amount of commitment appropriations proposed by the commission in the preliminary draft budget. as regards payment appropriations, we have taken a balanced approach, increasing them by eur 50 million for the convergence countries and regions and reducing them by eur 300 million for regional competitiveness. this leads to a reasonable overall reduction of eur 250 million in payment appropriations and i am pleased that we have reached a joint declaration on the structural and cohesion funds and on the rural development programmes. under the heading 'conservation and management of natural resources', the council decided to reduce the appropriations for commitments by eur 382 million and those for payments by eur 497 million. it mainly concerns budget lines related to market interventions and clearance of accounts and, to a reasonable extent, rural development. i would point out that the line on the food programme, free distribution of fruit and vegetables, milk for schoolchildren and promotion measures has been preserved. we have also maintained the amounts proposed by the commission for environmental policies. under heading 3 'citizenship, freedom, security and justice', the council increased the margins available under the ceilings slightly to reach an overall level of eur 76 million by making targeted cuts of eur 20 million in commitment appropriations. i would like to stress in this context the importance which the french presidency attaches to the immigration programme. the amount proposed in the preliminary draft budget for the frontex agency has thus been taken over. on heading 4 'the european union as a global partner', we wanted to anticipate the needs of palestine and kosovo without waiting for the commission's letter of amendment, which is due to be adopted next week. we have therefore set aside an additional amount compared with the preliminary draft budget of eur 100 million for palestine and eur 60 million for kosovo. as regards the cfsp, the council accepted on a provisional basis the commitment and payment appropriations entered in the preliminary draft budget which are in line with the amounts provided for in the institutional agreement of 17 may 2006. the reduction in payment appropriations amounts to 393 million, but half of this reduction is in the reserve for emergency aid and, as you know, the council believes that the financing of this reserve can be obtained by redeploying payment appropriations, as has been the case in recent years. finally, on the administrative item, the council decided on a controlled increase in administrative appropriations of 3.8%, which it considered compatible with the proper functioning of the institutions. the margin available for heading 5 therefore amounts to eur 224 million. the council of course accepted the 250 posts linked to the 2007 enlargement. we have also made targeted cuts based on past implementation, rather than the almost traditional horizontal cuts. finally, a final point on decentralised agencies: we have taken account of the life cycle of agencies. we cannot treat the agencies in the cruise industry in the same way as those whose competence is being developed, i.e. those in the development phase, and we have taken account of the surpluses generated by some agencies in previous years. this is the case for frontex and eurojust, two agencies which are among our priorities. in conclusion, it seems to me that this draft budget for 2009 represents a point of balance between the ambition we all have, of course, for our european union and the fair budgeting we owe to the citizens. this is of course essential to share the necessary confidence in the european project. the perception of your house will probably be different, but we are only at the beginning of the budgetary procedure and we have time to reconcile our views on the architecture of the 2009 budget and to respond to the challenges posed by the new commission proposals. i am sure that the three institutions will therefore do their utmost to reach a comprehensive agreement on all these matters by the november consultation, which is two months away, and i hope that this agreement will be the best possible compromise for both the institutions and the european citizens. you can of course count on my full commitment to this prospect.
i would like to thank you very much, mr woerth. they deserved a little more of our presence here. but we decide a lot of things with the quality of the members. today we are discussing the first of these matters, and a former minister who once held your office is also here.

president of the council. - mr president, madam commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, to appreciate the strategic importance of telecommunications and new information technologies for europe, one need only look at a few figures: telecommunications technologies alone account for a quarter of european growth and 40% of our productivity gains. and if you look at a number of studies, you see that the growth gap between the united states and europe over the last 12 years is half related to the differential development of our information and communication technologies. it is therefore necessary for our continent, for our countries, to invest sustainably in this sector. the rapid revision of our european regulatory framework for electronic communications is therefore of major importance to foster competitiveness, growth of the european economy. as i said at my hearing before the itre committee, the aim of the french presidency is to reach a political agreement at the council meeting on 27 november, the content of which will of course have to be based as much as possible on the european parliament's positions. to this end, the council has scheduled some 15 working meetings throughout the second half of 2008. i should therefore like to share with you in a few minutes the prevailing position today at council level on the main issues raised by the three rapporteurs, mrs trautmann, mrs del castillo and mr harbour. my colleague, eric besson, will be dealing with mrs toia's report on the digital dividend issue. i would like to commend the very considerable work done by the three rapporteurs whose topics i will be discussing. i think they clarify the situation and allow the council to start its discussions on a new basis, and i would like to stress the convergence of views between our two institutions, parliament and the council. i would first like to congratulate mrs catherine trautmann on the work she has done so far as rapporteur on the directive amending the framework directives on access and authorization. i would like to welcome its willingness to take account of the challenge of deploying the next generation networks, which is a concern shared by all the players in the sector and by the member states. the council's view is that your report, madam president, stresses the need to continue to promote competition, particularly competition through infrastructure. your report suggests that geographical segmentation of markets should be used more frequently so that ex ante obligations can be lifted where competition is effective. this second point is the subject of more debate in the council. the commission's proposal to extend the commission's veto power to remedies proposed by regulators. the commission is also proposing a co-regulation mechanism to bring the renewed group of regulators to court, for example, where the remedies proposed by one of the regulators are challenged by the commission. the rapporteur of the parliament is thus seeking a compromise between the status quo and the veto power which was originally proposed by the commission and which - as you know - is opposed by a number of member states. it is a real step forward from the original text on a subject which is extremely sensitive for the council and which does not seem at present to be fully prepared to give the commission such power. another hotly debated topic is functional separation. the report by mrs trautmann proposes to maintain the introduction of functional separation as an exceptional remedy for national regulatory authorities. this exceptional remedy would be more closely linked to its application, since the commission's prior agreement would be required with a favourable opinion from bert. in general, the approach adopted by the rapporteur seems to be in line with the compromise reached in the council on this subject, namely to maintain the introduction of this remedy while avoiding its trivialization. finally, another important point in this negotiation is the management of frequencies. your rapporteur, like the council, is in favour of a gradual approach to the evolution of spectrum management which reconciles the principles of neutrality put forward by the commission with the complexity of managing this rare resource. the report from the itre committee votes also introduces a new element by recommending the creation of a radio spectrum policy committee (rspc) to advise both the european parliament, the council and the commission on spectrum policy. this committee would be responsible for establishing a strategic legislative programme on spectrum use. on this point, i think the council has taken up the legitimate request of the european parliament to be better associated with the definition of broad guidelines for frequency management, but you know that the council is also committed to not multiplying the bodies responsible for this resource and to preserving the reactivity that is necessary on these markets and on this resource which is strategic for innovation. the report by mrs pilar del castillo on european authority, whose quality i would like to commend, is a very sensitive report and one which shows that parliament and the council are still in agreement. the report, madam member, concludes that the european authority, in the form originally proposed, is not the appropriate solution to strengthen cooperation between regulators and promote harmonization of practices, and that is also the council's position. you oppose the creation of a european super-regulator and propose the establishment of an entity closer to the regulators, the bert, more independent of the european commission and with a simpler organisation and governance than those originally proposed. the council is sensitive to all these arguments, but as you know, a majority of member states are still reluctant to the principle of the creation of a community entity. the council will therefore have to strike a balance in the coming weeks between two options: the institutionalisation of a private law entity bringing together european regulators or the creation of a community entity whose independence must be guaranteed. finally, mr president, my final comments will be on the report by mr malcolm harbour, whom i would like to thank for the quality of his work, and i particularly welcome the fact that it takes into account the fundamental interest of consumers. parliament, like the council, supports the commission's initiatives to strengthen consumer protection, a subject which has recently gained momentum with the growth of the communications service in the lives of our citizens. the report by mr harbour proposes, in particular, to specify the information to be included in contracts, to strengthen the measures to be taken by the member states in favour of disabled users and to reduce the portability time in order to strengthen competition. the council broadly endorses all these provisions. the issue of privacy, which was dealt with in enhanced cooperation with mr alvaro in the committee on civil liberties, also seems to me an important point to be addressed and i welcome, for example, the consideration of unsolicited communications via sms. finally, on the specific issue of copyright, mr harbour's report proposes to maintain a general obligation for the providers of electronic communications networks to inform subscribers about illegal uses of networks and services. it also proposes to encourage cooperation between stakeholders in order to promote the dissemination of legal tenders. these provisions seem to be balanced but the great sensitivity of this subject must be borne in mind, both for your assembly and for the council. in conclusion, mr president, before i give the floor to my friend eric besson on the digital dividends, on the subjects for which i am responsible, we feel that the positions of parliament and the council are converging with, it is true, a number of nuances on the degree of precision to be given within this directive. we will naturally endeavour to continue close cooperation in order to make compromises in the three institutions possible as quickly as possible.

regulation aims to ensure that all hydrogen-powered motor vehicles on the road in the european union are as safe as conventional vehicles. this should also help to build public confidence in an president of the republic of costa rica. mr president, i greet you on behalf of a small american republic, in which a little over four and a half million people dare to live and dream every day; in which the ideal of a society without an army has been made possible, and in which we will soon be celebrating 110 years of democracy. i greet you on behalf of a small american republic which in the second half of the 20th century witnessed the parade of the most abominable dictatorships around it, without ever being the scene of oppression; which refused to be a pawn in the chess game of the cold war, and refrained from using arms to achieve peace. i greet you on behalf of the republic of costa rica. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, two events precede me today, separated by centuries and decades, but as close to the present as the dawn of this morning. 225 years ago today, the american war of independence came to an end, with the signing of the treaty of paris, the first wave of the independence movement of virtually the entire american continent. and also 69 years ago today, world war ii began, with the declaration of war on germany by france and the united kingdom, and the emergence of the allied bloc in which much of america would participate. i am noting these facts because, as i approach this podium, a symbol of communion between different peoples, i am aware of the historical baggage i carry on my shoulders, and which you also carry in the past of each of the nations you represent. we are not here to establish relations between our two continents, but to recognize that these relations have existed for a long time, and that any attempt to improve them must start from an attempt to understand them in their entirety. with the frankness that must prevail among friends, we must recognize that the genesis of our common history is the domination of one civilization by another. america knew europe by its strength, rather than its ideas. fear characterized the conquest, indignation characterized the colony. and yet, we couldn't help but admire this millennial culture. despite the struggles we faced, it is undeniable that europe lit the light of reason in our land, and that it instilled in us an attachment to the best causes of humanity, causes that we did not abandon with independence. twenty-one years ago, those were the causes that brought me to europe, during my first administration as president of costa rica. i came to ask for the strength of this continent in the search for peace in central america, where five nations were struggling for life and death in the midst of civil war. threads of blood divided our villages, and pitted brother against brother. in a cruel experiment, the powers of the time used us as a test ground for the demonstration of their power: they put the weapons, we put the dead. the death toll was, by some estimates, 350,000. that's the equivalent, proportionally, of almost four million americans dying today in the iraq war. only by achieving peace could we secure a future for our region. europe was then the answer to our prayers. the moral support of this continent legitimized our efforts to find a diplomatic solution to the conflict, a central american solution to the central american problems. the international aid you gave us in those days was wide and generous, and it was a symbol of the true european will to assist the progress of the central american nations. twenty-one years later, i'm back in europe, and like brother luis de león coming out of his four years of imprisonment, i feel compelled to start with a "we said yesterday"..., because in many ways, we have to pick up where we left off. the relationship between europe and central america, so intense in times of war, became distant in times of peace. the aid from europe to central america, which was so abundant in times of oppression, became more moderate in times of freedom. we never imagined that by crossing the threshold of peace, we would enter the realm of oblivion. i would like to think that this will be the time to show that the friends who supported us in dark days, also know how to do it in light days, and precisely because the day is light. today i would like to propose three courses of action with which we can deepen our relations and fight, shoulder to shoulder, in building the utopias that you yourselves taught us to pursue: the signing of the association agreement between central america and the european union, the consensus of costa rica and peace with nature. i know this room is full of all kinds of opinions about free trade. but i also know that those opinions are expressed from the head of someone who has the good fortune of living in a developed nation. i'd like to give you the view from the plain today. for a country like mine, one of the smallest in the world, there is no possibility of producing all that we consume. we are doomed to be the phoenicians of modernity. in times of globalization, the choice facing developing nations is as stark as it is simple: if we are not able to export more and more goods and services, we will end up exporting more and more people. it is clear that europe must look after the interests of europeans. but it is also clear that the interest of europeans, and of every race in the world, is increasingly determined by the common destiny of human beings. no nation can remain calm while hunger, ignorance, violence and disease are rampant beyond its borders. as long as the disparities between our nations remain so wide, a global diaspora will continue to take thousands of human beings across oceans, rivers, walls, to seek opportunities that they could not find in their own countries. the association agreement between central america and the european union, the first region-to-region agreement that the european union could conclude, is the closest, clearest and most immediate opportunity for europe to strengthen its presence in latin america. since the creation of the central american common market, few initiatives have harbored greater potential to accelerate the economic growth of the central american isthmus, to modernize our institutions and to provide new opportunities to those central americans who still live in poverty. the agreement would mean that europe would regain the leadership it had lost and take the vacant position at the forefront of the struggle for the development of our latin america. yesterday we were allies in peace, today we can be partners in development. central america and europe, however, have colossal differences that must be considered. the first is the difference between our two models of integration: europe must accept that central american integration takes place in the form and to the extent that our institutional evolution allows. we are already the most integrated region in the developing world, and therefore we consider it unfair that conditions should be imposed on us in terms of our integration in order to make progress in the negotiations; conditions which central america can hardly meet, and which, moreover, are not demanded of other regions of the world. the second difference between our regions, and perhaps the most important, is the difference between our levels of development: it is crucial that the trade component of the agreement should grant asymmetrical treatment in favour of central america, and above all avoid the painful practice of maintaining barriers in areas where it is precisely central america that has comparative advantages. if we reach an understanding on the basis of these assumptions, europe would be making a giant leap for the benefit of central americans, but also for europeans, because in times of international crisis this continent could benefit greatly from an economy which has been growing at about twice the european rate for the last five years. europe can start a new role in the developing world, but first it must ensure that this role is in the interests of development. goethe said that "nothing does more harm to a new truth than an old error". we cannot enter a new stage of international cooperation bearing the burden of the past, particularly the burden of military spending which is, in and of itself, a real insult to the almost 200 million latin americans who languish in poverty. it is time for the international financial community to learn to separate the chaff from the wheat, and to recognize, with evidence in hand, which expenditures translate into a better standard of living for human beings, and which do not. it is no badge of honour that in 2007 military spending in latin america amounted to 36 billion dollars, in a region which - with the sole exception of colombia - is not currently experiencing any armed conflict. with the money spent on a single sukhoi su-30k aircraft, about 200,000 computers from the mit media lab xo could be bought for our students. with the money spent on a single black hawk helicopter, a $100 scholarship per month could be paid to 5,000 latin american youth for a year. the developed nations of the world cannot support, with aid and resources, the decision of those who would rather open their soldiers than educate their children. that is why, ladies and gentlemen, my government has announced the costa rican consensus, an initiative to create mechanisms to forgive debts and to provide financial support to developing countries that invest more and more in environmental protection, education, health and housing for their people, and less and less in arms and soldiers. i hope that the costa rican consensus, with your support, can one day become a reality. i also hope that we can approve a very related draft: the arms transfer treaty that costa rica has proposed in the united nations, which prohibits countries from transferring arms to states, groups or individuals, when there is sufficient reason to believe that these weapons will be used to violate human rights or international law. i don't know how much longer we can survive without realizing that killing many, little by little, every day, lethal than nuclear bombs, and is one of the main drivers of civil insecurity at both national and international level. fear of death cannot be the key to writing the future of our peoples. today we can do something to ensure that this is not the case. there is only one issue that i have left to mention to you, and it is one that has to do, also, with violence and destruction, but not only against human beings, but against all forms of life. every forest we cut down, every ton of carbon dioxide we put into the air, every river we pollute, brings us one step closer to the gates of extinction for our species, at the threshold of which, like dante's gates of hell, we must abandon all hope. i refuse to witness the passage of humanity through those gates. sixty years ago, former costa rican president josé figueres had the vision to abolish the national army and thus declare peace to the world. we have now made the decision to declare peace with nature. we have set ourselves the goal of becoming a carbon neutral country by the year 2021, when we celebrate 200 years of independent life. last year, we became the country with the most trees per capita per square kilometer in the world, by planting five million trees. in 2008, we will plant 7 million more trees. we are leading an international crusade against global warming, and today i humbly ask you to join us. the increase in the planet's temperature has made it possible for olive trees to grow on the coasts of england, a truly alarming sign to the scientific community. contrary to the biblical story, this time the dove will not bring the olive tree as a sign of calm, but as a sign of danger. today i ask you to send that dove to the farthest corner of the globe, so that it returns bearing the will for change of all the nations of the world. only together will we succeed in founding a new covenant, no longer of god with man, but of man with god's creation. mr president, the great argentine writer jorge luis borges used to say that he was an exiled european, referring to the european ancestry of a large part of the population of our american continent. after centuries of interbreeding and exchange, it's likely that there are many americans in exile here as well. we are exiled by the geographical fate of an ocean, and the historical fate of a pendulum that unites and separates us as circumstances come. i think it's time to let go of that fixed pendulum of union, to go back to the path that the winds took 180 million years ago, before the earth suffered the original rift, when europe collided with america, and it would have been possible to walk from paris to new york. we are members of a single species, still able to harvest the best flowers from the garden of life. our dreams are our common heritage, and our decisions impact the lives of everyone else, whether we like it or not. i believe that, far from being a threat, it is a wonderful opportunity. i think, as the greatest costa rican poet, jorge debravo, would tell us, that "it is wonderful, above all, to know that we have the virtue of making the most distant things we touch come alive, of stretching our gaze and not finding edges, because all the things we look at become, with us, infinite". i have no doubt that we will be able to use this infinite virtue for the good of all, europeans and americans, and that we will follow side by side the star of a morning of greater justice and freedom. member of the commission. − mr president, the proposal the honourable members are debating today seeks to modernise rules adopted in 1989 on the market for the distribution of airline services. computerised reservation systems (crs) act as intermediaries between airlines and travel agents in the sales chain for air tickets. in the early 1990s, computerised reservation systems were practically the only channel for the sale of airline tickets. in addition, all the crs were controlled by airlines. the latter were therefore more tempted to abuse their position in the crs, for example, by biasing displays in their favour. the code of conduct for the use of crs establishes a number of safeguards to prevent abuse. it complements competition law since it adds measures to deal with sector-specific risks. it requires that all companies participating in the system are treated on a non-discriminatory basis. for example, the same fee is to be paid by all airlines. the code also lays down special obligations for parent carriers – i.e. those which own or control the crs. the code of conduct has been very effective in preventing all kinds of abuse. however, since the code of conduct was introduced, the market for the sale of air tickets has changed considerably as alternative sales channels have developed. today, nearly half of all reservations no longer go through a crs but are made on internet sites or through airline call centres. the competitive pressure of these alternative sales methods has significantly reduced the risk of abuse through a crs. the new situation also requires an adjustment of the code of conduct. the rules laid down in the code of conduct significantly restrict the margin for negotiation between the crs and airlines. the crs are therefore not genuinely in competition with each other, and the fees paid to them by airlines and passengers are escalating. the commission’s proposal seeks to allow for more negotiation and, in particular, the possibility to set prices as regards the fee for the use of a crs. this will enable airlines to negotiate the reduction of rates with the crs. boosting competition between the crs will help to reduce costs and to improve the quality of the services they provide. at the same time, the proposal maintains and strengthens the safeguards for the prevention of abuse and protection of consumers, and in particular the neutrality of information provided and the protection of personal data. in addition, the proposal continues to impose special obligations on crs parent carriers. the definition of ‘parent carrier’ has led to heated debates, since the obligations imposed on those companies are very burdensome. modernisation of the code of conduct will make it possible to reduce the cost of distribution of their services while guaranteeing the protection of consumers’ interests. this is urgently required from the viewpoint of the competitiveness of our industry, as our companies’ competitors already benefit from a liberalised environment and lower sales costs. i am therefore pleased at the speed with which parliament has taken up this issue. i wish to express my appreciation of the work performed by your rapporteur, tim kirkhope, and the tran committee, as well as the committees which expressed their opinions.
the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used effectively. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your work. on behalf of my group, i would like to thank the rapporteur, mr timothy kirkhope, very warmly. he has presented a very balanced report and worked very closely with the shadow rapporteurs. the text of the directive, which was negotiated with the french presidency, provides for better protection of consumers against fraudulent offers on air and rail transport, and ensures fair competition between rail and air transport companies, as a result of clear transparency rules. the new view also confirms that the epp-ed group was the first group to have rightly stopped the commission's attempt in 2005 to repeal this regulation as obsolete. we need it and we will prove it by our vote to protect consumers. although more and more travellers are actually booking their tickets directly with airlines or on the internet, the majority of consumers continue to rely on their travel agents, who in turn need to be able to rely on non-discriminatory, truthful and low-cost offers in the computerised reservation system. the prices must now include all costs, including fees, so that travel agencies can actually provide consumers with transparent and comparable offers. the commission has also proposed that the rules on the transparency and competition of parent companies should be strengthened to prevent the systems from giving preference to their offerings to the detriment of other airlines and consumers. i am glad that the commissioner has taken this opportunity to speak to the house. i believe that the text we have agreed with the french presidency on parent companies provides sufficient protection against the preferential treatment of certain airlines, and that is why amendment by the famous amendment no 48 is completely unnecessary, and if it were to be adopted tomorrow it would delay or even call into question the adoption of this whole complex. i appeal to you to make a clear, final decision tomorrow to protect consumers.
i would like to thank the commissioner for his reply. i want to focus on the controversial issue of the definition of parent companies. the objective of the definition is to prevent airlines with shares in a crs from abusing their position in an anti-competitive manner. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the aid is not used to finance the restructuring of the airline industry. the commission's practice of carrying out a case-by-case examination of suspected market abuse has proven to be effective. cases of improper influence have been investigated and punished. it's happened twice before. there is no reasonable reason to change this basic best practice. the definition of a parent company that has been found, based on the competition law term of decisive influence, is consistent with this best practice. the term has been around for 40 years. the commission has also proposed that the member states should be allowed to apply the principle of equal treatment to all airlines. for the air transport market, this means a massive and unnecessary intervention in the current competitive situation. the consumer would not benefit either. the laughing fours would be british airways, american airlines and others who would benefit from such a shift in the competitive situation. the only european computer reservation system would also have to face a competitive disadvantage vis-à-vis its us competitors in the highly competitive european market. i think that is politically inappropriate, even negligent, and i therefore recommend that we accept the compromise that has been reached.

(interception)... and above all with the plane. the shift of freight from road to rail remains a key objective. the report therefore calls for at least 40% of eu transport funding to be invested in rail. in europe, only about 17% of goods are transported by rail, while in the highway country of the usa the share is 40%. the eu will only be able to cope with the growth of freight transport if it improves its rail infrastructure. the transport ministers of the member states are urged to overcome national bias and to encourage the investment needed for europe in their countries. the link between modes of transport is also important. the commission has already proposed a number of measures to improve the quality of the transport services provided by the community, such as the introduction of a single transport document for ships, railways, lorries and aircraft, a european maritime transport area without frontiers, a european but also a world standard for intermodal loading units and, in particular, better links between sea and inland ports and the road and rail network in the hinterland. despite the unanimous vote, my group has tabled amendments because some votes in committee were extremely close. the most important of these concerns the request to the commission to identify the main bottlenecks and problems in european rail freight transport. this is precisely the kind of analysis that is needed to quickly address the weaknesses in the railway network and thus create greater capacity. the european commission itself has very much welcomed this idea, and i hope that we will get a majority for this tomorrow at the plenary vote . i would like to thank all the members for their attention.

transport in europe. these communications are: firstly, the eu’s freight transport agenda, boosting the efficiency, integration and sustainability of freight transport in europe; secondly, the action plan for freight transport logistics; thirdly, towards a rail network giving priority to freight; and fourthly, the multiannual contract for rail infrastructure quality. i am particularly pleased to the rapporteur, mr michael cramer, for the work that he has done, and all the members who have contributed to it. in terms of tonnes per kilometre, the white paper of 2001 foresaw a 50% growth in goods transport in europe between 2000 and 2020. the commission will update that estimate next year, but it is already clear that it was pretty accurate. the major challenges presented by this growth, the fight against congestion and climate change, reductions in pollutant emissions and guaranteed security of the energy supply are more topical now than ever they have been. the choice of means of transport should, therefore, be directed towards the least pollutant ones, although each means of transport, including road transport, should be used where it is most efficient and most suitable. there is also a need to improve the efficiency of the european transport system by implementing measures aimed at introducing information technology on a large scale, in administrative simplification as well as enhanced service quality. i welcome the fact that the draft report is encouraging the commission to pursue a goods transport policy that places a greater emphasis on sustainability. our wish is to create a transport system that is reliable, effective and viable, both financially and environmentally. to this end i am convinced that co-modality – that is, the rational and optimum use of all modes of transport on their own and in combination – must become one of the guiding rules behind our thinking and action. in addition, the various modes of transport must meet a number of performance criteria that are essential to competitiveness. in particular, punctuality, regularity, reliability, high quality, sufficient capacity, interoperability and transnational coordination on international corridors are some of the watchwords for an array of services that has the customer absolutely in mind. it is through specific, immediate action at a controlled cost such as those contained in the text of your resolution, together with other european initiatives such as the green paper on the future of the ten-t, that we will be able to increase the efficiency of the european transport system.

member of the commission. − mr president, i would like to thank the committee on economic and monetary affairs and the committee on legal affairs and in particular their rapporteurs, mr rasmussen and mr lehne, for the work done in the preparation of these two reports. few would have predicted one year ago that the situation in financial markets would be as serious as it is today. and the effects of the crisis will continue to be felt for some time. it started with reckless selling of mortgages in the united states, promoted by banks and others who did not care about lending standards because they could offload the loans to others through securitisation. credit-rating agencies then gave respectability to these high-risk products by assigning low credit-default risk to them. financial institutions around the world bought up these products without, it seems, doing any serious risk assessment of their own. in the light of events over the past year, it has been incredible to see how little understanding senior managers of financial institutions had of the risk they were taking on board. no doubt the size of the profits that were rolling in blunted serious risk analysis. supervisors seemed to have no better idea of the risk in these hugely complex products. things were so sliced up, diced up and repackaged that no one knew where the real risk was. one observer referred some months ago to this unfolding crisis as like watching a train crash in slow motion. last week the crisis went into hyper speed. the concerted actions of the world’s major central banks and the announcement of the support measures by the united states authorities have restored some calm to the markets. we must welcome this given the extreme situation faced by regulators. i also welcome that the united states authorities have shown recognition of the need to address in their proposals similar assets held by some non-us financial institutions. one thing we can be thankful for in europe is that we have not seen the same scale of destruction as has happened in the united states. although banks in the eu have been suffering from a similar lack of confidence in lending to each other, there has not been anything on the same scale as experienced in the united states. but no one is out of the woods yet. there are difficult trading conditions ahead. the downturn in economies will have its effects. vigilance and transparency are key if confidence is to be restored in markets. at eu level we must continue to improve our supervisory arrangements for cross-border supervisory financial institutions. there is a window of opportunity that must not be missed. all of this leads me to believe we are going to have a different financial services sector when this is all over and we will have a different regulatory framework as well. if moral hazard cannot be shown to work then the taxpayer cannot be expected to pick up the bill for the excess and irresponsible risk-taking of private institutions. the ultimate shape of whatever new regulatory approach will be adopted will be designed over the coming period as the lessons from this crisis and the appropriate responses become clearer. we need to continue to work closely with other regulatory authorities and to the extent possible dovetail our responses. as many of you will be aware, we have already been taking action. for a year now the commission has been working on a detailed road map agreed by the council of finance ministers and endorsed by the european council. we have been refining our response as the turmoil unfolds. we have already taken measures to improve convergence and cooperation between supervisors. a new memorandum of understanding was agreed by eu supervisory authorities, finance ministers and central banks setting out common principles including the establishment of cross-border stability groups. this is now being implemented. we have been reviewing enhancements of deposit guarantee schemes. a special group which will report by the end of this year has been set up to look at the pro-cyclicality effects of current instruments including basel 2 and ifrs. in close cooperation with the financial stability forum, the iasb has set up an advisory panel on fair valuation. work on off-balance-sheet items is also under way in the iasb. industry has come forward with valuable data which improves transparency for regulators of the securitisation market. the commission is pressing industry to refine this information so that transparency for regulators is improved. in the light of these activities, and others i will refer to, it should come as no surprise to members when i say that i can welcome many of the points set out in mr rasmussen’s report. what is important is that we are able to identify the key measures we should take now and get them implemented. as i said earlier, the market turmoil exposed failings in the risk management of large financial institutions. it also highlighted a number of areas of regulatory weakness. it is on these areas that regulatory attention must now be focused. mr rasmussen has flagged in his report many of the most pressing areas: conflicts of interest in credit-rating agencies, the need for improvement in the valuation of illiquid assets and the misalignment of incentives in the ‘originate and distribute’ model. over the past year i have kept members informed, both in plenary and particularly the committee on economic and monetary affairs, of the work we have been doing on improving capital requirements in banks, as well as my ideas for regulating credit-rating agencies. we all agree, i believe, on the need for a strengthening of capital requirements and an obligation for transparency and due diligence in regards to structured products. we have been working on changes to the capital requirements directive, which will improve the management of large exposures, improve quality of capital through harmonising treatment of hybrid capital. we have also been looking at strengthening the supervision of cross-banking groups. in the next few weeks i will be proposing to the commission two separate regulatory measures to deal with these and other issues: firstly, an amendment to the capital requirements directive and, secondly, a regulation on credit-rating agencies. i look forward to the support of the european parliament for these proposals which are very much in line with what you call for in this report. hedge funds and private equity feature in both reports. we have had some interesting exchanges over the years about the roles of hedge funds and private equity. one thing i believe we can agree on is that they were not the cause of the current turmoil. it has turned out that it was the regulated sector that had been allowed to run amok with little understood securitisation vehicles. i do not believe it is necessary at this stage to tar hedge funds and private equity with the same brush as we use for the regulated sector. the issues relating to the current turmoil are different. let us not forget that these funds are regulated in member states. hedge funds and private equity managers are authorised and supervised entities throughout europe. they are subject to the same market-abuse disciplines as other participants in financial markets. they are bound by similar transparency and consultation obligations when investing in public companies. exposure of the banking sector to hedge funds and private equity is subject to the capital requirements directive. but this does not mean that we are turning a blind eye to hedge funds and private equity. as these business models evolve and their role in financial markets changes, regulators around the world need to remain vigilant. the industries themselves must assume all the responsibilities that accompany a prominent role in european and global financial markets. several recent market initiatives indicate that this message is understood. our role should be to monitor closely these and other developments in the market and be ready to respond if and when necessary. i welcome the constructive suggestions for supporting the functioning of the single market. i would just like to mention at this stage that there is considerable work under way in the commission on private placement and venture capital. i agree with mr lehne that a sufficient degree of transparency is an essential condition for investor confidence. it is, therefore, indispensable if we want financial markets to function effectively. the report sets out a list of transparency rules that apply today to the different players in the financial markets in the eu. to my mind, what is important is that the market is provided with a sufficient degree of clear information that is useful. we need to find the balance between the need for confidentiality of the proprietary information of investment vehicles against the legitimate needs of investors, counterparties, regulators and investee firms. i am, therefore, pleased that the report puts an emphasis on the need to analyse the impact of the existing eu provisions and of additional member states’ rules in this field before one embarks on introducing any new legislation. the commission has already been very active in this field. we have held extensive consultations in the context of our shareholders’ rights initiative, where we looked at a number of issues that are touched upon in the report – stock lending, for example, and the question of the identification of shareholders. furthermore, we have recently published a call for tender for an outside study that will look at the implementation, in member states, of the transparency directive. this study should be available next year and will form the basis for a general evaluation of the directive, including the notification thresholds. as members will recall, the commission adopted, in spring of this year, a communication setting out its policy approach to sovereign wealth funds. we had come to the conclusion that these measures were appropriate but also sufficient to address the issues that currently are being discussed. this approach was endorsed by the european council; i see, though, that the committee on legal affairs does not entirely share this assessment. i shall make some brief remarks in this area. firstly, we should acknowledge that hedge funds and private equity in many senses are not unique – other institutional investors have similar objectives and nowadays use similar techniques. if in that situation we imposed special obligations on hedge funds and private equity, this would result in discrimination of these categories of investors. secondly, we should not make the mistake to perceive all activities of hedge funds as a threat to the market but we should also be aware of the positive effects that their activities have. let me be clear, the eu economy is going to need massive investment in the time ahead: without sovereign wealth funds, private equity and the like, europe’s recovery from today’s turmoil will be all the slower. thirdly, i agree that certain techniques, such as stock lending and the use of derivatives, do pose challenges to established models of governance. this is an area we, in conjunction with national supervisors, will be giving close attention to in the time ahead. in conclusion, these two reports will be significant contributions to our ongoing reflection. i commend members for these reports. the commission will examine your recommendations and report back to you as envisaged in the framework agreement. we remain fully committed to responding to this crisis with the measures necessary to restore confidence and stability.

president of the council. - mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, tomorrow you will be voting on the third maritime security package. as you know, with some 3 million people, the maritime economy is a vital economic sector for our european union. the legislative proposals comprising the package, which the commission submitted in early 2006, were seven. the aim was to implement preventive measures to prevent marine accidents and to establish measures to be taken following accidents, i.e. to analyse their causes and to compensate any victims. the package gives priority to the safety and quality of maritime transport while respecting the environment, and to improving the competitiveness of the european maritime sector. the council, parliament and the commission share the objective of promoting maritime safety. at the copenhagen european council in 2002, the council welcomed the efforts made to strengthen maritime safety and reiterated the european union's determination to 'take all necessary measures to prevent the recurrence of maritime disasters'. the council can moreover fully endorse many of the demands made by parliament in its resolution of 27 april 2004. however, on the third maritime package, some differences remain and will require further consultation between the parties. since the commission presented the package, the council, through the work of several presidencies, most recently the slovenian presidency, has adopted six common positions on the following proposals: post-accident investigations, classification societies, port state control, traffic monitoring and the athens convention, taking into account the opinions of the european parliament as adopted in april last year. from the beginning of its mandate, the french president of the council. - madam president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, on saturday 14 september, almost yesterday, a french tuna boat was being chased by pirates 420 miles off the coast of somalia. this is not an isolated case, since since the beginning of july, 10 ships have been detained and 250 sailors taken hostage. as a result, fishing vessels are understandably reluctant to operate and the 50 french and spanish tuna vessels fishing off the coast of the seychelles and somalia have decided to join the seychelles. in addition to the fact that acts of piracy are on the increase, it is clear that they are no longer limited to the coast and that they tend to spread over larger sea areas, in international maritime areas, seriously disrupting not only the activity of fishing and commercial vessels in transit, but also - and this is very serious - that of vessels acting in the framework of humanitarian programmes, in particular the world food programme, which provides vital assistance to the very large displaced somali populations. this phenomenon has become a matter of concern on a global scale. our president of the republic, mr sarkozy, recently said that these are no longer isolated cases but a real crime industry which is calling into question one of the fundamental freedoms, that of movement, as well as that of international trade. the french president concluded by saying: 'the world cannot accept this!' in this context, the united nations security council adopted resolutions 1814 and 1816 last may and june. in response to the worsening of this phenomenon, it is currently working on a new resolution which aims to mobilise the international community to better apply existing instruments of repression and prevention, within the framework of the law of the sea or within the framework of security council resolutions. the member states of the european union have already taken this step and on 26 may expressed their determination to fight together against piracy off the coast of somalia. a crisis management concept was approved by the council on 5 august. more recently, at the general affairs and external relations council on 15 september, the council adopted a strategic military option for a possible military naval operation under the european security and defence policy. i would like to remind you solemnly that the launching of a naval operation is clearly envisaged, as the french presidency reminded the foreign affairs committee of your assembly last tuesday, at the end of the council meeting mentioned above. but in anticipation of a possible operation, and in view of the urgency of the need to act, the council decided to take the first step by setting up a military coordination unit. it is headed by a senior spanish officer and composed of four maritime experts whose role is to facilitate the exchange of information between merchant navies and warships that may be present in the area, on a regular or occasional basis. this unit, located here in brussels, will be responsible for supporting surveillance and protection actions carried out by member states off the coast of somalia. this initiative should have three components: the escorting of certain vulnerable vessels in transit in the gulf of aden, the protection of humanitarian convoys of the world food programme to somalia, and the monitoring of fishing areas off the southern coast of somalia. member states with naval units operating off the somali coast are therefore invited to inform the security council of this fact, in particular to optimise the possibilities of protecting the most vulnerable merchant ships. in parallel, madam president, the european union will continue to prepare for a possible naval military operation under the european security and defence policy. an information gathering mission, composed of european experts from the eu general staff and the general secretariat of the council, is currently in the region to refine strategic planning. the commission is due to report on its conclusions on 29 september. as you can see, ladies and gentlemen, the european union is not only showing its determination to act, but is also establishing itself as a major force in the international fight against piracy. we must give ourselves the means to act quickly and in a coordinated manner, in the interests of commercial interests, of course, but also in the interests of free movement, which is a global principle, and in the interests of our humanitarian objectives.

of the world against the interests of the member states of the european union, whether acts of maritime piracy or armed attacks against ships in waters under the jurisdiction of a state. such acts affect not only maritime transport but also deep sea fishing and maritime tourism. in addition, these acts make the living conditions of seafarers who already work in difficult conditions even more dangerous. that is why we must not only condemn, we must act, we must realize that there is a risk of going back centuries with an organized presence of criminal networks, of pirates operating in four main areas: the south china sea, the straits of malacca and singapore, the gulf of guinea and the horn of africa. most of the acts are committed in these areas, the intensity and severity of the actions vary continuously. in addition, there is concern about the development and possible spread of piracy to other parts of the world, which shows that these are not occasional incidents, but we are convinced that there is an organized network of criminals who want to scientifically attack cargo, cruise ships and passenger ships. as the european community is a party to the 1982 united nations convention on the law of the sea, the european commission has always been committed to promoting freedom of navigation in all its components and to developing appropriate instruments to prevent illegal acts against ships. in this context, the commission has systematically supported the efforts of the member states and the international community as a whole to develop high-quality legislative instruments within the united nations and its specialized body in the field of maritime transport, the international maritime organization. following the work of the informal consultative process of the united nations on the oceans and the law of the sea in june last year, which dealt in particular with the question of the legal treatment of pirates in the event of capture, efforts are still a writer. the commission has already made a number of proposals. i am very pleased that we have the opportunity today to discuss the international tropical timber agreement. in view of the need to combat climate change, to conserve biodiversity and to protect the rights of indigenous peoples, the protection and sustainable management of tropical forests is becoming increasingly important. accordingly, there is broad support in the committee on international trade for the concept of an international convention. however, as our rapporteur, caroline lucas, has already said - and i would like to thank her very warmly for her wonderful report - there are some doubts whether this agreement will be sufficient to tackle the problem of deforestation seriously. 13 million hectares of tropical forests are cut down every year, and an estimated 20% of greenhouse gas emissions are due to this. the fact that almost a full year has passed since the text was referred to parliament and the agreement is now being discussed in the plenary is not due to the fact that the trade committee wanted to delay this debate or did not give the question the importance it deserved. this is because we believe, and the legal affairs committee in particular, that this agreement requires parliament's consent and not just a consultative procedure. i should like to thank in particular the rapporteur, mrs maria panayotopoulos-cassiotou, and the chairman of the legal affairs committee, mr giuseppe gargani, for their clear and prompt legal advice on the legal basis. in january, in the light of the opinion of the legal affairs committee, president pöttering wrote to the secretary-general of the council, explaining that in our view this agreement creates a special institutional framework and therefore requires parliament's consent in accordance with the second subparagraph of article 300 (3) of the ec treaty. unfortunately, it took until 23 may 2008 for the council to reply to this letter. the answer - four full paragraphs - contained no legal arguments or any other reason for rejecting parliament's request. in this context, the committee on trade adopted the report by caroline lucas, this oral question and the related resolution which we are debating here. i would therefore like to emphasize not only the importance of the agreement itself and the fight against climate change, but also the question of the rights and privileges of parliament. the existing treaties give parliament very little legislative power in the field of international trade agreements, with the exception of those treaties which fall within the scope of the second subparagraph of article 300 (3). the establishment of such a specific institutional framework is the most frequent basis for the application of this provision in the treaty and also provides the justification for the application of the assent procedure to the conclusion of the economic partnership agreements between the eu and the acp states, and of possible agreements with korea or india and with south-east asia, which is of particular importance for the fight against deforestation. why is the application of the consent procedure so important to us? the aim is to provide a parliamentary forum for debate and control on behalf of the european citizens, thereby giving the agreements greater legitimacy and public recognition. it is therefore in the interests of the council and the commission to involve parliament as a co-legislator. in view of the public interest in the conservation of biodiversity and the fight against climate change, i hope that the commission will at least now comply with our request to submit annual reports on the implementation of the tropical timber convention and its interaction with bilateral agreements.
