is the whole point of the road map which we will be proposing and discussing at this european council. the economic and financial situation has already been the subject of many debates in this house. so i would like to recall the main points at a time when europe is being hit hard by the very strong economic downturn. we must be able to react to an emergency. we must show unity and the same decisiveness as we did last october when it was a question of finding a coordinated response to the risks of a collapse of the entire financial sector. it is in this spirit that the presidency of the council will conduct the council's work on 11 and 12 december. the president of the commission, mr barroso, will say it better than i do, the commission adopted on 26 november proposals for a european recovery plan, which were discussed on monday by the competitiveness council and the council of ministers for economic and financial affairs. it is a coordinated european response to the economic crisis, which mobilises the community instruments available and allows member states to take the measures best suited to their situation, in close coordination with each other and in compliance with a number of principles. i would like to say that the commission's proposals are in the right direction for the council presidency. we must try to make financial margins available in the community budget, where they are available, for the european social fund, the globalisation adjustment fund and the structural funds. we must also, as the commission proposes, mobilise more european investment bank funds and we count on your parliament to take full part in the mobilisation of the community institutions in response to the crisis. it is primarily the responsibility of the member states to do everything possible to support economic activity next year, taking into account the forecasts made by the commission and other institutions. the commission proposes a joint effort between what can be done at community level and what is done in the member states of up to €200 billion, or 1.5% of community gdp. i know there are some concerns about these figures. it seems to us, as the presidency, that the effort proposed by the commission is in response to the difficulties we are facing and the necessary stimulus. we know that the community authorities cannot do everything, because the instruments are limited, particularly in terms of budgetary resources and powers, and that not everything can be done at community level. the authorities should nevertheless ensure that national recovery actions are coherent and coordinated so that the overall effect on economic recovery is maximised to the benefit of the union. we believe, together with the commission, that we need targeted, sectoral and transitional support measures. these measures must be consistent with the union's long-term priorities and the lisbon strategy and must be implemented swiftly. we believe that priority action must be taken to target the european industrial base and in particular the most structural industries such as the automobile sector, which, as you know, is being seriously affected by the economic downturn. in conjunction with the european investment bank, member states should be allowed to grant grants to their manufacturers to support the development of new technologies, in particular clean cars. we must also, as was stressed at the competitiveness council, obtain new room for manoeuvre to support small and mediumsized enterprises, which are more particularly confronted with this crisis and which are more particularly, today, faced with the threat of credit restrictions in view of the state of the european financial sector today. we are determined that this council will obtain the most ambitious overall plan possible at its meeting on 11 and 12 december. as regards the energy-climate package, mr president, we will have a debate in this house tomorrow. i would like to thank the european parliament again, on behalf of the council, for its extremely constructive attitude in the dialogue we are having on the energy-climate package. our objective is and remains an agreement at first reading by the end of the month. it is not a question of vanity for the french presidency, it is not a question of whether we are putting another success on the presidency's radar, that is not the issue. the point is that europe, i repeat, must be prepared to meet international deadlines, taking into account the 2009 timetable, must be prepared to take the necessary initiatives both in pozńan, at the conference which has just opened, and in copenhagen next november. your rapporteurs know this very well. your assembly has had many and substantial discussions with jean-louis borloo in order to bring this negotiation to a successful conclusion. what we want, the aim of the presidency, is clear: there are objectives, there is coherence in the package proposed by the commission. these objectives and consistency must be safeguarded. we must not depart from the original logic proposed by the european commission. we must take two things into account: the first is to be sufficiently flexible with regard to countries which, given their geographical situation, given their economic development, have to make efforts to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, and i am thinking in particular of our friends in central and eastern europe; the second is to find, in the light of the economic crisis, the necessary flexibilities for the industrial sectors which are most affected by these energy consumption problems. we are working very closely with the commission and the other member states on this and we must all be united in order to achieve concrete results and to get this package adopted again by the end of the year. the council is the decisive body. europe is at a crossroads on a number of institutional, economic and energy issues. this will be a difficult council. it is in line with the situation in the european union. that is why we, the council, the commission and parliament, must absolutely do everything in our power to achieve success on these various objectives. but we are well aware of the difficulty of the task.
president of the commission. - mr president, mr president-in-office of the council, ladies and gentlemen, first of all, allow me to join you, mr president pöttering, in all that you have said about the mumbai tragedy, and also to say that i share your remarks about the need to put into practice the spirit of solidarity in europe, also the spirit of what genuine european citizenship should be. i think we can all learn from these incidents to put into practice the great ideas of european citizenship and solidarity in europe. in recent months, mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the european union has faced a series of major challenges: a conflict in georgia, but also an unprecedented financial crisis and a sudden economic recession. i am fully convinced that the european union has so far taken the right measure of these extraordinary events and has not been undeserving. the european dimension has proved its usefulness and relevance thanks to the joint commitment and close cooperation of our three institutions, and also, i should like to say, thanks to the energy and competence of the french presidency. we have shown the people of europe in particular, and the world community in general, that the european union is up to the task: capable of a rapid and coordinated response, ready to work hand in hand with its partners at the global level. but let us be absolutely clear and honest with each other: the main work remains to be done in the coming weeks. because we are facing many challenges, including three major challenges, which can only be met if the three major european institutions - the parliament, the council and the commission - continue to work together, each playing its full role in pursuing common objectives: first, to take decisive action, and to do so without delay, to put europe on the path to economic recovery, to respond to the crisis in the real economy; secondly, also to demonstrate that europe is empowered to become the world's first low-carbon economy and to show that we are capable of holding the global leadership position in the fight against climate change; and thirdly, to set out a roadmap for the implementation of the lisbon treaty. there are certainly many other areas i could mention, particularly in terms of external relations, and here i would like to say that today we are proud of the commission for having approved a communication which sets quite ambitious objectives for a genuine eastern partnership policy, but for lack of time i will now concentrate on these three challenges which i see as the greatest challenges for the european council in december. let us look first at the european plan for economic recovery. in the debates leading up to the european council last october, there was already talk of a shift in the problems and a shift from the financial crisis to the real economy. a week later, in a communication which we approved, the commission proposed a european framework for action. we have said that we need an economic response to the financial crisis and that we need to do it in a coordinated way. this framework has generally been agreed, since the last informal european council approved it, as did parliament at its meeting last month. but it also provided the basis for the global strategy that was defined at the g20 summit, as it was the basis for discussion. finally, when defining their own policy, the member states followed the approach advocated by this general framework of reference. while setting out the modalities, the european economic recovery plan i presented last week took this coordination to a new level of ambition. i would like to welcome the impetus which parliament has given to the recovery plan, through the debates in the parliamentary committee, in plenary, but also, more particularly, through the debate i had with the conference of presidents, and i thank the president of parliament and the chairmen of the various groups for having contributed to making this debate possible. the implementation of this plan should benefit from the same sustained dialogue as its preparation. by proposing to inject €200 billion to boost our economy, our recovery plan, which includes ten detailed priorities, reflects a level of joint action unprecedented at european level. the challenge was immense, as was the risk of failure, for an ambitious plan had to be drawn up, one that was up to the task. a plan which does not reflect the lowest common denominator, but which also does not hide the very different budgetary and economic positions of the member states, even though all the member states are bound by the common market and, for most of them, by a common currency. so let us admit that it is not an easy task, that it is indeed, from an intellectual and of course also political point of view, quite difficult to find an economic answer for 27 countries with such different starting situations. that is why we have defined a plan that is not one size fits all, but a coordinated plan, building on the instruments we already have in europe, the stability and growth pact and the lisbon strategy for growth and jobs, but defining common objectives to be pursued in a coordinated way for economic recovery. now we must translate this plan into reality. the idea of coordination must not just be at the time of agreement but at the time of implementation because the price of inaction is unacceptable. we are witnessing this: job cuts are already a daily occurrence. we cannot wait for the recession to accelerate and degenerate into a serious depression. i think we all perceive a change in mindset, even if sometimes this change in mindset has not yet been fully translated into concrete decisions. everyone is well aware that this is not just a general downturn in the economy. we are in a different situation, it is not a simple economic downturn; we are faced, i repeat, with exceptional circumstances, and it is now that we must act. everyone has to take responsibility. the commission has done so in presenting this plan and will continue to do so in implementing it. i hope that parliament will be vigilant in reminding everyone of his commitments. this recovery plan provides the necessary framework for decisive and ambitious action. i think it is both ambitious and realistic; it is no use making ambitious proposals that have no chance of being approved. but at the same time, we must keep this ambition. this plan demonstrates that the foundations laid by the stability and growth pact and the lisbon strategy have enabled us to deliver a truly european solution. europe has a great opportunity here. i think we have a real test for europe here. not just, and that is enough, in the economic response, but also on the very idea of europe. what is our idea of europe? do we want european answers to european problems and to global economic problems or not? europe can prove that it is able to: provide the coordination needed to ensure that everyone throws his or her full strength into the battle; dprovide, at the appropriate scale, the fiscal stimulus required to have a real impact, while ensuring the medium- and long-term sustainability of public expenditure; to enable the intelligent use of short-term tools to boost long-term competitiveness by striking two strikes at the same time: stimulation must both limit the impact of the crisis on households, workers and businesses in the short term, but it must also prepare the transition to a less energy-intensive economy, while supporting reforms for european competitiveness in the medium and long term; and to place all our action under the sign of the major imperatives of solidarity and social justice, which must first be exercised for the benefit of the most vulnerable in times of crisis. so we have set three clear priorities, three pillars of the strategy, but with, let's say, one underlying priority in all the measures, which is to pay particular attention to the most vulnerable. the time is not now for action confined to a national framework. let's be absolutely clear about this. that is the message i would like to send to the european council, and i know that i can count on this parliament to amplify it. only a european-level solution will have the scope to make a difference, to the greatest benefit of all. parliament's support is essential. i would therefore ask you to consider new proposals, to speed up procedures, to adjust the european budgetary framework. we must be clear on this too. i think it would be absolutely contradictory if we were now asking the member states to make an extra effort in budgetary matters, a budgetary stimulus, and we ourselves, at european level, were not able to use all the appropriations available in the community budget. i think the commission has made the right proposal when it says that all the funds not spent should be used to deepen certain programmes and launch certain european actions, whether for interconnections, innovation, climate-friendly energy or a policy of economic recovery which is also fruitful in the medium term. i think it's the least we can do. but above all, i would ask you to explain to our citizens how the european union protects, not by replacing the action of states, but by reinforcing the effectiveness of the action of states by joining forces to stimulate demand and restore confidence, for the benefit of all our citizens. the second item on the european council agenda is climate change. i know how much time and attention this parliament has devoted to the climate change energy package. you have shown how this is truly one of the major political, economic and "civilizational" projects of our time. when we look back at what will be a historic decision, your support for the objective and your input into how it should be reached will prove to have been invaluable. it is now almost a year since the commission made its proposals. in that time we have seen a major economic downturn. we have heard understandable concerns from industry at a time of intense pressure. but the commitment to the core goal has not wavered: to meet the 20/20/20 targets by 2020; to show the way for a global agreement at copenhagen next year; and to prove that we are serious and we mean business when discussing these issues. of course there is much to be done before the council and parliament reach a final agreement. this is how it should be. these are critical decisions impacting on the life of every european. they deserve to be taken seriously. we must get it right. the european council next week will be key to reaching agreement between the heads of state and government of the 27. but while agreement amongst the 27 is a necessary condition for a deal, it is not in itself sufficient. believe me, nobody knows better than the commission the crucial role parliament plays as a co-legislator. you have proven time and again that your input is indispensable, not only for the democratic legitimacy of european legislation, but also for its effectiveness. your work is critical in building a broad cross-party, cross-national consensus on essential pieces of legislation. we will need you to play this role on the climate and energy package too. a lot has already been achieved in recent trilogues. i am confident we can travel the rest of the way together as well. i really believe we can and should reach a deal at the european council and i welcome the efforts of the very hardworking french presidency of the council, with which the commission is actively cooperating. this is why, right after the european council, i propose to take up its outcome in trialogue with the european parliament in order to iron out remaining differences and translate political agreement into legal texts. i am confident that we will be able to conclude work in good time and show that climate action, energy security and economic growth can and must be pursued in a mutually supportive way. this is the best message we can send ahead of the european elections, but also ahead of the coming into office of the next united states president, and in view of copenhagen. i give my commitment that the european commission will work tirelessly with you to make this possible. finally, there will undoubtedly be some who would argue that, in the current situation, discussing the lisbon treaty is a distraction. they would be wrong. the european union today is proving itself more essential than ever in terms of promoting the economic and social well-being of its citizens. giving it the tools to do this task more efficiently, more democratically, is not a distraction. it is an imperative. the crises we have been experiencing have all underlined this need. i believe that the european union has shown a lot of maturity in responding to the 'no' vote in ireland, by respecting the outcome, and by giving the irish authorities time to digest and analyse, time to work out how to address this situation. above all, europe has shown its determination to keep working towards the prize of the new treaty. member states have continued to ratify. the commission, like this parliament, has continued to put the case for the treaty. and we have worked together with ireland not against it to find the right way forward. there remains an urgency to see the treaty in force. there remains a need to respect the decisions of the 25 national parliaments which have ratified. and the overriding goal of the european council must be to set out a credible way forward which will allow ireland to ratify as well. by the end of next week, we need to have a road map that leads us out of this impasse. 2008 will go down in the history books as a year when the european union faced some of its toughest tests. but also, i believe, when it showed itself determined enough, decisive enough, and bold enough to meet the challenge. let us use the next few weeks to leave a legacy of a stronger, more ambitious european union for the future. your excellency, president pöttering, honourable members of parliament, ladies and gentlemen, it is a great honour to speak before you today and i thank you for your invitation. on the last occasion i was here, i gave my speech in tibetan and then read the english translation. i felt that wasted time, so today my written statement has already been circulated. i am not going to repeat what is in there. in fact there are some words i cannot pronounce properly so it is better not to read it! the main points i have already mentioned in my written statement, and i do not want to repeat these things. i am just one human being out of 6 billion human beings. on that level, i believe that every human being wants a happy, successful life; all of us, irrespective of our colour, nationality, religious faith or social status, we all want and all have the right to have a happy life, a successful life. as a human being i believe – and for a number of years, many of my friends have agreed with my views and feelings – that in modern times there is too much emphasis on the importance of material values. we have somehow neglected our inner values. that is why, in spite of materially being highly developed, i have noticed there are still a lot of people – even billionaires – who are very rich but are unhappy on a personal level. so one of the most important factors for happiness or joyfulness is very much to do with peace of mind, a calm mind. too much stress, too much suspicion, too much ambition and greed i also think are factors which destroy our inner peace. so therefore, if we wish to achieve a happy life, there is no point in neglecting our inner values. these inner values are not necessarily what we bring from religious teaching, but i feel they are a biological factor we are already equipped with: warm-heartedness or a sense of responsibility, a sense of community. the biological factor is there because we are social animals. that is what i usually call ‘secular ethics’ and it is the basis of our happy life, our inner peace. the ways i generally emphasise to promote that are secular ways: the secular method means using our common sense and common experience and the latest scientific findings. even for our physical well-being, peace of mind is very essential. i should like to illustrate this by a small experience of my own. i recently underwent surgery to remove my gall bladder. so, in contrast to my previous visit here, i have the same face but one organ is now missing! but, since then i am ok, quite fit! (laughter) seriously, during surgery and also after surgery there were some quite serious complications. usually gall bladder removal takes 15 to 20 minutes, but in my case it took three hours because of complications. however, after the surgery, within one week i had fully recovered. so the doctors were a little bit surprised. i told them that i had nothing special. no miracle power. no healing power. if i had miracle powers or healing power, i would not have needed surgery in the first place. the very fact that i underwent surgery means that i have no such miracle power, does it not? but i really think that peace of mind is one factor in a speedy recovery. so this is my number one commitment, the promotion of human values. number two is the promotion of religious harmony. in that respect – i mean peace of mind – all the major religions have the message of how to develop inner peace. particularly when we are passing through difficult situations or hopelessness, faith provides us with inner strength and hope. so all the major religious traditions basically fall into two categories: one is theistic religion, the other is non-theistic religion. buddhism belongs to the non-theistic religions. buddhism and jainism both form part of the indian tradition. these different philosophies, different ways of approach, ultimately have the same message, the same practice, the practice of love, compassion, forgiveness, contentment and self-discipline. so therefore all the major religious traditions have the same potential but they come from different locations, and different peoples with different mental dispositions. we need different ways of approach. theistic philosophy and non-theistic philosophy have developed: that does not matter. these philosophies matter, but the important thing is the real purpose, the real message. so in that respect, all religious traditions carry the same message, the same practice and the same effect. so harmony among the different religious traditions is quite possible. and yet now – not only in past history, but even today – there are still conflicts happening in the name of religion. so therefore we need a special effort for the promotion of religious harmony. this may be irrelevant, but i see that here among the parliament members there are many women. one of my beliefs (and i am not saying this just to appease the women here!) is that in human history, in the earliest periods, there was no concept of leaders. all family members worked together, all the community members worked together, hunting or collecting fruits or things like that, and they shared equally. eventually the population increased. then stealing, bullying and that sort of thing happened. so then the concept of leadership arose. at that time the brain was not very important. the important thing was physical strength, like other animals. this, i think, is why male dominance developed. then eventually through education, brain development took place and the brain became more important than physical strength. so then male and female had more or less equal weight. and so it is that many members here are female. some are rather beautiful! completed the ratification process of lisbon. on the 26th, the czech republic has just taken an important decision, as the constitutional court has indicated that the lisbon ratification process can take place, and prime minister topolanek, in a courageous and responsible statement, has indicated that his ambition is to propose the ratification of the lisbon treaty. so the irish case remains. this is the agreement we reached unanimously. this arrangement is very simple. firstly, it is to guarantee each member state, if the treaty of lisbon comes into force, one commissioner per member state. i know that this is an effort on the part of some of you, as it is an effort on the part of a number of governments who believed that a smaller commission was needed to be more effective. i would like to ask each of you to reflect on this. if we want lisbon - and europe needs strong and lasting institutions - we can only have it if our irish friends vote and say yes. for them to say yes, we need a new fact. this new feature, the european council proposes that it is one commissioner per member state. second point. we have made a number of political commitments relating to the specific nature of the irish debate, neutrality, taxation, the family. these political commitments were not a problem. what's the matter? it's better if everything is on the table. the problem is the legal force of these political commitments. because in ireland there is a constitutional court and no one doubts that the supporters of the no - and it is their right - will take the irish constitutional court to ask for the force of the political commitments that have been made. this is the compromise that the presidency has proposed: no re-ratification of the lisbon treaty by all those who have done so, no amendment of the lisbon treaty. it seems to me that there is no point in solving one problem and creating 26 others! it's all very clear. on the other hand, when europe next enlarges, probably croatia, probably in 2010 or 2011 - if things go as they should - then, mr president, we will need a new treaty to enlarge europe to the new entrant. we have therefore proposed that at the time of enlargement of europe, and only at that time, we should add two elements to the treaty of accession of croatia: the first element, the so-called 'irish' protocol, and the second element, the question of the number of members of parliament. the european elections will be held on the basis of the treaty of nice. i do not see how we could do otherwise. however, a number of states have been granted more parliamentarians under the lisbon treaty. the first enlargement could also solve this problem. on this basis, the irish government has courageously committed itself to consulting the irish people again on the lisbon treaty before the end of 2009. this means that if things were to go as i would like them to go - but it is up to the irish to decide - the treaty of lisbon would enter into force only a year later. ladies and gentlemen, it was not easy to discuss this, it was not easy to organise, it was not easy for the irish or for anyone else, but the european spirit is first and foremost a spirit of compromise. if at 27 you are not capable of compromise, there is no point in having a european ideal. the european ideal is to listen to each other and try to find common ways of overcoming problems. finally, i would like to end by thanking the european parliament first. i should also like to say that it was very easy, very pleasant and very useful for the presidency to have many contacts with all the groups in your assembly, regardless of their political commitment, right or left, liberal or green, sovereigntist or federalist. you have all shown a willingness to advance europe in your own way. i must say that parliament has been a decisive factor in the presidency's efforts to achieve results. i would even say that it has been easier to discuss, work and negotiate with the european parliament than with - i will not go into details - this or that other interlocutor. at the end of a presidency, we express our congratulations, not our regrets. i would also like to fundamentalism, i forget the word europe and i hear the word fundamentalism, and fundamentalism is never good advice. to want to build europe against the nations would be a historic mistake. every member of the commission. - the mr president, the proposed legislation on carbon dioxide and cars will for the first time set binding emission targets for the automotive industry. it is also an important means of assisting member states in achieving their emission targets under the proposal on the sharing of effort between member states. the compromise agreement reached brings a number of changes to the commission proposal. these include the gradual adoption of the targets between 2012 and 2015, a lower fine for the first 3 grams of exceedance by the manufacturer by 2018 and the provision for taking into account eco-innovations, which are not currently taken into account when measuring emissions in the test cycle. the amendments could also be seen as weakening the commission's proposal. the proposal to compromise on a long-term basis by setting a long-term target for emissions from all new cars of 95 grams per kilometre in 2020 compensates for these losses. by incorporating this target, the legislation will achieve about one third of the reductions needed in sectors outside the emissions trading system, about as much as we had originally estimated for the year 2020. the compromise reached benefits both the environment and consumers, who will save money on lower fuel bills. it will also provide manufacturers with investment stability and predictability, boost innovation and lead to greater investment in research and development. it will thus give manufacturers the advantage of initiative in global markets, where demand for green cars is expected to increase, and will thus improve the competitiveness of the european automotive industry. i would like to thank the rapporteur, mr guido sacconi, for his great contribution to reaching an agreement and i hope that you will support the compromise agreement in the vote tomorrow.

wife of hu jia. − dear friends, i am hu jia’s wife, zeng jinyan. hu jia is currently in prison and so is unable to come to the ceremony to receive his sakharov prize. i do not have a passport so i cannot come to europe either to attend the ceremony for the sakharov prize’s 20th anniversary. we are deeply sorry about this. the good news is that hu jia was transferred on 10 october 2008 from chaobai prison in tianjin to the beijing municipal prison, and that the conditions in which he is being held have improved. as for his health, he is looking a little better. he seems to be in slightly better shape than he was in chaobai prison. however, he had two blood tests in the space of a month and we do not know what the results were. although we asked for them, the results of the tests have not been given to the family. this behaviour worries us. it makes us fear that his cirrhosis has got worse. i visited hu jia in the beijing municipal prison on 21 november 2008. before our meeting, we were both warned separately by the prison authorities that we were forbidden to talk about the fact that he had been awarded the sakharov prize. so, during my visit, neither of us was able to talk about the prize. we were not able to discuss it by letter either, as all our correspondence is inspected. even if all we do is express a view about social phenomena or if hu jia talks about the prison, when the prison authorities are not happy with it, our letters are confiscated or hu jia’s letters are returned to him. we very much hope to be able to communicate more normally, but for the time being it is very hard. at the end of october 2008 or beginning of november, i am not exactly sure which, state security police officers told hu jia he had won the sakharov prize. and when i saw him on 21 november, i could sense that he was very happy about it. i know that hu jia spoke to his mother and to the policemen about it. these are more or less his words:‘perhaps the european parliament was thinking of the work i did in the areas of aids and the environment, because what i did in terms of human rights was very far from sufficient and i will need to redouble my efforts.’ he also said this sakharov prize was very important for china and he was confident that the future would prove him right. obviously, from my personal viewpoint, i hope he comes home as soon as possible. hu jia said one day that he hoped to be china’s last prisoner of conscience but the reality is very different. since the day of his trial, on 3 april, there have been others such as huang qi, zeng honglin and chen daojun who have been arrested by the authorities because they expressed their views publicly. and some of them have been tried and given prison sentences. this shows that the situation of freedom of opinion is still absolutely appalling and that there is no reason for optimism. but even in these circumstances, there are now a great many exceptional people and people of goodwill in chinese society who are going to great lengths to find ways to make the real situation in china known, and to express deeply-felt views, and the internet is providing them with a very interesting platform. but unfortunately there is sometimes a very high price to be paid for this. if the truth be told, sometimes one’s courage is not enough. sometimes the price to be paid is very, very high. there have been cases in which, after human rights activists, writers and others have used their freedom of thought, their relatives have also been harassed by the police, have lost their jobs or have been put under house arrest. and more serious still, some have even been tried and convicted. hu jia had himself been illegally kidnapped several times by the police since 2004, without any form of legal procedure. he was constantly followed and in the end he was given a prison sentence. and i, who am his wife, i am often harassed by the police. others are in the same situation, such as chen guangchen and his wife, guo feixiong and his wife, and even their child, who has been denied his right to education. thanks to many appeals from different quarters, guo feixiong’s children were later able to go back to school although in circumstances that are not very satisfactory. for all these reasons, i would like to respect the desire that hu jia has expressed on many occasions. he has often said he would like to set up a support network to help the families of human rights activists. to provide moral support for the families, to ease their mental and life pressure to which they are subjected. so that they can be strong enough to face the pressure of the authorities in a more active and optimistic manner, and to discourage cruel revenge-taking on families. i cannot at the moment do very much but i would like to use the eur 50 000 of hu jia’s sakharov prize as start-up money, to establish a foundation to support the families of human rights activists and to finally realise what hu jia had always wanted. why is the human rights work done by hu jia so difficult? i think this is mainly because china’s legal system is not satisfactory. there are laws, there are all sorts of articles and regulations, some are well written, but they are not applied. in reality, the situation of the rule of law is disastrous. the judicial system has no independence. until 2004, hu jia devoted most of his activity to the problems of aids and the environment. he spent a lot of the time in the field, on campaigns, where people needed him to take concrete action. then, from 2004 onwards, the police regularly denied him his freedom of movement and he had no other choice but to participate in human rights movements from his home, writing articles and publishing reports from the field. i think that during all these years, the most important and most interesting thing he did was to have constantly persisted in saying the truth. he never stopped writing about the phenomena he observed. he never stopped describing, one by one, all the realities that the chinese media cannot say. he never stopped publishing all this on websites so that the public could learn about the reality of china and understand it. in my view, this has been his greatest contribution. if you look at china now, you see everyone talking, but lying is very widespread. nonetheless, there are people who continue their quest for the truth. because the school textbooks our children study, our newspapers and broadcast media, our libraries and all these documents and files, they all resemble what you find in the novel nineteen eighty-four. they are written in another language to describe a fictitious reality. what is the real situation, the real china? we do not know. that is why there is a group of thinking people, like hu jia, in china who have never abandoned their quest for the truth. but hu jia has paid a very heavy price. our child is now just one year old. this is a key period in her life but hu jia is not able to be at her side. it is very difficult for me to talk about this, but i think… and then hu jia has also always been very optimistic. he said he thought china was experiencing the most open period of its history, that you had to seize the opportunity to more effectively promote a fairer, freer and more democratic society in china. we can indeed see this in our daily life, although the government still has very tight control over the media and over freedom of association, and perhaps even tighter control with the use of new technology. but on the other hand, civil society also uses the new technology and the platform that the internet provides to actively promote a fairer judicial system and a more just society, and to investigate and expose the real china. and to carry out citizen education, to educate citizens about human rights. it is a real hope: whether the government wants it or not, and whether leading figures inside or outside china recognise it or not, china is moving at great speed towards an open and democratic society. i would finally like to say that, whatever happens, we must maintain an active and optimist attitude and pursue our efforts to promote the rule of law in china, to promote democracy and freedom in china. we are full of hope of soon being able to hail the arrival of an open china. we are full of energy for china to become a country at peace. i would like to thank our european parliament friends from the bottom of my heart. the european parliament has from the outset taken an interest in hu jia’s mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your reply. i give the following explanation of vote on behalf of the cdu group of baden-württemberg: we strongly support efforts to significantly reduce the very likely human contribution to climate change. we have not, however, accepted the compromise reached at the weekend between the heads of state or government on the european emissions trading system. legislation in the hau-ruck procedure - that is precisely the point - is intolerable and undemocratic, and the extremely rapid legislative procedure and the submission of the council documents just a few days ago made it impossible, in our opinion, to conduct a qualified review and examination of the documents and thus to legislate properly. this is all the more unacceptable given the particularly high financial burden that this legislation imposes on the citizens of europe. according to various studies, the climate package is costing the european economy and citizens between €70 and €100 billion, and it threatens to relocate entire industries to other parts of the world through carbon leakage. we could not agree to a package of this magnitude under the expedited procedure. such important legislative proposals must be developed in an orderly procedure in several readings.
i would like to thank the commissioner for his reply. i too am in favour of making cars that use less and less fuel. i am also in favour of setting consumption limits, but they must be realistic. i therefore abstained on this report because i do not think it is right that penalties of up to eur 475 per tonne of co2 are imposed for exceeding these low thresholds. there are many ways to save co2 at a much lower cost. this is a one-sided discrimination, especially against high-quality cars made in my home country of bavaria. we can save co2 with much lower costs in building insulation. i've insulated my house, which saves me 7,000 litres of fuel a year, which is more than i can save on my car. that is why we should take the right paths, and that is why i have abstained.
in writing. - mr president, i have to say something. the agreement on the climate package is a modest achievement. the eu has set itself a reduction target of 20% compared with 1990. we have already achieved almost half of this: the keyword is eastern enlargement, where emissions are lower in absolute terms. the target of a 12% reduction compared with 1990 remains. the eu is allowed to achieve three to four per cent of the reduction in developing countries, leaving just under nine per cent. the targets may be missed by up to 5%. that leaves four percent. normally, one should say at this point: lucky, the eu has decided not to export its economy entirely to asia. the compromise is much cheaper than the commission's proposal. that's what allows the fdp to approve. the eu is now playing its own member states against each other: through the energy mix, derogations and clever negotiation, some member states have the advantage. german energy suppliers may soon be able to produce electricity in poland instead of at home, if they are not bought by the french. the fact that eu countries are engaged in such a cow trade does not bode well for a global agreement. the question of the efficiency of the means also arises. governments, the council and the european commission are called upon to ensure efficiency in environmental protection as well as in the economy and growth.

in writing. i voted against the consolidated amendment because i did not see the rights of the european parliament as a member of parliament being respected: parliament has never had the opportunity to form an opinion. instead, it had the de facto only choice of rejecting or agreeing to the european council's compromise. this is not in accordance with the rules of the codecision procedure, which is intended to guarantee equality between the two legislative bodies. i have many reservations about the content of the compromise reached. it is thus creating significant distortions of the market within the eu and imposing unnecessary burdens on consumers. in the unnecessary rush to adopt the reform, alternative systems that could also have achieved the reductions sought were not considered at all. the fact that the economic consequences, particularly on consumers' purchasing power, were not closely examined at the time of adoption only highlights the poor thinking behind this compromise. the majority of the european parliament is also responsible for its entry into force, also in relation to future generations. there were alternatives. they would have achieved the reduction targets at a fraction of the costs now incurred. such policies are not only damaging to the economy but also, and above all, to the eu's reputation.
in writing. - i strongly support efforts to reduce the likely human contribution to climate change. we have not, however, agreed to the negotiated compromise on the european emissions trading system. legislation by the hau-ruck procedure is unsustainable and undemocratic. the extremely rapid legislative procedure and the submission of the council documents only a few days ago have, in my view, made it impossible to examine the documents in a qualified manner and thus to legislate properly. this is all the more unacceptable given the high financial burden that this legislation will place on europe's citizens: according to various studies, the climate package will cost between eur 70 and 100 billion, and it threatens to relocate entire industries to other parts of the world. i could not agree to a package of this magnitude in the fast-track procedure. such important legislative projects must be dealt with in an orderly procedure in several readings.
in writing. − in this explanation of vote, i would like to congratulate fuels quality directive rapporteur, dorette corbey. she has succeeded in incorporating many demands of this house into the final compromise. the european union must base its policies and regulations on sound scientific evidence – a requirement both of eu law and the eu’s trade commitments. as a member of the trade committee, i often hear from trading partners when the eu appears to be regulating by arbitrary or political processes rather than by reference to scientific conclusions. i was therefore pleased that the revised fuel quality directive did not include an earlier proposal to ban the fuel additive mmt. the revised directive provides for the continued use of mmt, in recognition of the scientific conclusions reached by major trading partners, including the united states and canada. importantly, the revised directive also requires the eu to conduct a scientific examination. i strongly believe – and eu and international law require – that restrictions on mmt must be based on science. because other countries often model their fuel standards on those developed in europe, it is essential that the eu ensure its fuel regulations are strongly supported by scientific evidence.

i have to say, madam president, i didn't agree to the toy compromise proposal. there are still too many security gaps, especially with chemicals. poison is not for children, not even in small quantities. the decision today is disappointing and, moreover, not very ambitious. there are too many loopholes. the commission has not yet adopted a proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to dangerous substances. this lax approach to the safety of our children is deplorable. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. it's a trick of the eye. there are improvements, but this should be taken for granted in a directive which was 20 years old and had to be revised. the bottom line is, too much spin and not enough substance. the responsibility cannot be delegated to industry. we are responsible for clear legislation!
i have to say, madam president, what we are witnessing now is the last months of the mugabe regime. but it is also the only positive news from this battered country. the good news from africa is that more and more countries are fighting back against the conditions there. i can report as first vice-president of the acp-eu parliamentary assembly that for the first time, at our meeting in port moresby three weeks ago, we had african colleagues on board in a critical analysis and assessment of the situation in zimbabwe. in south africa itself, pressure is mounting on the government to finally take its protective hand from the zimbabwean regime. this situation is exacerbated by the fact that now in south africa, diseases are also coming into the country with the refugees. hopefully this situation will improve by the time the world cup is over, because that's perhaps why south africa is making a change, because they're afraid that the guests will be out. that alone should be a reason to take that protective hand away from mugabe.
the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used effectively. the commission is not prepared to accept this. we have expressed our willingness to cooperate with russia on many occasions. we want economic exchanges and political dialogue with russia. europe and russia need each other. we are all the more concerned about the development of the rule of law and democracy in this country, whose people have already suffered under soviet dictatorship for so many decades. all democratic indicators have been down since vladimir putin took office: freedom of the press and media, freedom of expression, freedom of assembly, freedom of association - not just for political parties - judicial independence, respect for minorities. the convictions of russia at the european court of human rights here in strasbourg are a sobering testimony to the situation of civil rights in that country. the storming of the memorial research and information centre in st petersburg on 4 december unfortunately shows, among other things, that the present leadership apparently wants to displace the burden of the stalinist legacy and whitewash stalin's terror. this is not a good basis for the development of a democratic society, which is the prerequisite for prosperous economic and social development, but also for the confidence of europe's neighbours in russia as a reliable and peaceful partner. we must press for the return to the rule of law and democracy in russia in the common interest in all contacts with the government and civil society and business.
i have to say, madam president, the rule of law problems in russia are not isolated developments, but a systematically spreading cancer. we are in the second phase of the putin era, garnished by a mr medvedev, and the third phase is being prepared. mr putin began his first era with the second chechen war, a genocidal assault on a small people by massive resource colonial interests. since then, the situation has been spreading, the rule of law and freedom of the press have been reversed, human rights defenders like mrs moskalenko have been persecuted all the way to the european capital, strasbourg, and we are simply seeing no progress and, as i said, not just isolated failures, but a systematic loss of what little remains of the rule of law and democracy. that is why we as the european union must act with much more energy. we owe it to the people who died in the negotiations for an agreement, such as mrs politkovskaya, mr litvinenko and many others, to have dared to investigate or name these developments. anyone who speaks openly about this in russia is already in danger of losing their life. and each time it's supposed to be a mysterious, opaque background. we have therefore a duty, we who live here in freedom and relative security, to ensure that light is finally shed on this darkness and that we here in the european parliament at least do what we can do, namely to speak in a clear and honest language to the russian authorities. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. let us take the example of the courage of elena bonner and andrei sakharov and stop pretending to be anything but. let's put things as they really are. we are doing the russian people the greatest service we can.
madam president, in the first line we want to replace the words ‘xenophobia’ and homophobia’ with ‘violence’, because we think that the violence goes beyond xenophobia and homophobia and also covers national minorities or religious minorities. we would like to say ‘trends of violence’ in the first part, because later we refer to various other issues – nationality, religion and sexual orientation. as they remain in the text, i think it would be too narrow to refer only to xenophobia and homophobia in the first line. could colleagues agree to the word ‘violence’ in the first line?
